=== NOTES 1:170 | Anglo-maratha and Anglo-sikh Wars; Conquest of Sindh; Doctrine of Lapse and Annexations
## SUB 0 | Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775-1818) and Their Treaties
[170:0:0] TABLE head: War | Years | Governor-General | Key events and treaty
  [170:0:0.0] First | 1775-82 | Warren Hastings | Bombay backed Raghunathrao: Surat (1775) → Calcutta's Purandhar (1776) → British trapped near Talegaon → Convention of Wadgaon (Jan 1779); Goddard, Popham (Gwalior 1780), Camac (Sipri 1781) → Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with Mahadji Sindhia
  [170:0:0.1] Second | 1803-05 | Lord Wellesley | Holkar beat the Peshwa and Sindhia at Hadapsar (Poona), Oct 1802 → Baji Rao II fled and signed the Treaty of Bassein (31 Dec 1802); Arthur Wellesley (Assaye, Argaon), Lord Lake (Delhi, Laswari)
  [170:0:0.2] Third | 1817-19 (1817-18) | Lord Hastings | Pindari campaign + Peshwa attacked the Poona Residency; Peshwa beaten at Khirki, Bhonsle at Sitabuldi, Holkar at Mahidpur; Peshwaship abolished (June 1818)
[170:0:1] # Treaties → year and party
[170:0:2] TABLE head: Treaty | Year | With | Point
  [170:0:2.0] Surat | 1775 | Raghunathrao (Bombay govt) | Salsette and Bassein promised to the English
  [170:0:2.1] Purandhar | 1776 | Regency (Nana Phadnavis, Barabhai) – Calcutta Council | Annulled Surat; Raghunath pensioned
  [170:0:2.2] Wadgaon | 1779 | Marathas (after Talegaon) | Bombay gave up all gains since 1775
  [170:0:2.3] Salbai | 1782 | Peshwa / Mahadji Sindhia – Warren Hastings | Salsette kept by the English, rest restored; 20 years of peace; Sindhia the guarantor
  [170:0:2.4] Bassein | 1802 | Peshwa Baji Rao II | Subsidiary Alliance: 6,000 troops, land worth Rs 26 lakh, Surat surrendered, chauth on the Nizam given up – "gave the English the key to India"
  [170:0:2.5] Devgaon | Dec 1803 | Bhonsle of Nagpur | Subsidiary treaty
  [170:0:2.6] Surji-Arjangaon | Dec 1803 | Sindhia | Delhi and the Mughal emperor under the English
  [170:0:2.7] Rajpurghat | 1805/1806 | Holkar | End of the second war
  [170:0:2.8] Poona / Gwalior / Mandasor | 1817 / 1817 / 1818 | Peshwa / Sindhia / Holkar | Third war
[170:0:3] - **Peshwa's end:** Lord Hastings **removed Baji Rao II**, annexed his lands and sent him as a pensioner to **Bithur near Kanpur**; **Pratap Singh** given the small state of **Satara**. Baji Rao II died **1851**; adopted son **Nana Sahib** was refused the pension.
[170:0:4] - **Marathas = the power that opposed the British most vigorously;** the British took India from the **Marathas, not the Mughals**; after **1818** British paramountcy was unchallenged.
[170:0:5] - **Why the Marathas lost:** inept leaders (Baji Rao II, Daulatrao Sindhia, Jaswantrao Holkar), loose confederacy, inferior artillery and military system, superior English diplomacy and spies.
[170:0:6] - **Chronology (asked):** Wandiwash **1760** → Nand Kumar hanged **1775** → Salbai **1782** → Tipu's death **1799**.
[170:0:7] - **Treaties in order:** Salbai **1782** → Seringapatam **1792** → Bassein **1802** → Amritsar **1809** (and 1846) → Sugauli 1815-16 → Yandabo 1826.
[170:0:8] - **Years match:** 1775 First Anglo-Maratha; **1780** Second Anglo-Mysore; **1824** First Anglo-Burmese; **1838** First Anglo-Afghan.
[170:0:9] > **Arthur Wellesley** (Assaye; later Duke of Wellington) is not **Lord (Richard) Wellesley**, the Governor-General.
[170:0:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.134-140; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.18-19, Part 6 p.19; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.29; old app notes row 170
## SUB 1 | Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley, 1798-1805)
[170:1:0] - **Introduced as a system by Lord Wellesley** (Governor-General **1798-1805**); not invented by him – **Dupleix** first hired out troops; **Awadh (1765)** was the first state in the protection trap; Cornwallis (Carnatic, 1787) first barred foreign relations.
[170:1:1] - **Terms:** British force permanently stationed in the state, paid for by a **subsidy or ceded territory**; a **British Resident** at the court; no Europeans in service without consent; no war or negotiation without the Governor-General; in return protection and (nominal) non-interference.
[170:1:2] - **Order of acceptance:** **Hyderabad (Sept 1798, 1800)** → **Mysore (1799)** → Tanjore (1799) → **Awadh (Nov 1801)** → **Peshwa (Bassein, Dec 1802)** → Bhonsle (Dec 1803) → **Sindhia (Feb 1804)** → Rajput states, Holkar (1818). Hyderabad was the **first**.
[170:1:3] - **Wellesley against Napoleon:** while Napoleon broke the empires of Europe, Wellesley's forward policy (Mysore 1799, Marathas 1803-05, Tanjore, Surat, Carnatic) **kept the British flag flying high** – "converted the British Empire in India into the British Empire of India".
[170:1:4] - **Effects:** states lost independence and revenue; rulers became irresponsible; the Company spread its troops at strategic points and kept the French out.
[170:1:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.151-154; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.39; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.42; old app notes row 170
## SUB 2 | Anglo-Nepal War and Treaty of Sugauli; Burmese and Afghan Wars
[170:2:0] - **Anglo-Nepal War (1814-16):** under **Lord Hastings** (Governor-General 1813-23); Gorkhas had taken **Butwal and Sheoraj**; **Ochterlony** forced terms after Almora (1815).
[170:2:1] - **Treaty of Sugauli (Sagauli):** signed **2 Dec 1815**, ratified **March 1816** – with **Nepal**. Nepal accepted a **British Resident** (at Kathmandu), ceded **Garhwal and Kumaon**, gave up claims to the **Terai**, withdrew from **Sikkim**.
[170:2:2] - **Gains:** empire reached the Himalayas; trade with Central Asia; **sites for hill stations – Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital** (Spectrum); **Ranikhet and Nainital** are in Kumaon; **Kathmandu stayed Nepal's capital**; Gorkhas joined the army.
[170:2:3] TABLE head: War | Years | Governor-General | Treaty
  [170:2:3.0] First Anglo-Burmese | 1824-26 | Amherst | Yandabo (1826) – Assam, Manipur, Arakan, Tenasserim
  [170:2:3.1] First Anglo-Afghan | 1838/39-42 | Auckland (Tripartite Treaty 1838) | British disaster; ended under Ellenborough
[170:2:4] > Sugauli 1815 (signed) / 1816 (ratified) – exams use both years; Yandabo is **1826**, not 1824 (the year the war began).
[170:2:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.157-158; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.18-19, Part 6 p.19; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.29; Drishti IAS UP PCS Pre 2025 answer key (web, Q114); old app notes row 170
## SUB 3 | Conquest of Sindh (1843)
[170:3:0] - **Governor-General: Lord Ellenborough (1842-44)**; general **Sir Charles Napier** defeated the **Talpur Amirs** at **Miani** and **Dabo** (1843); **Sindh annexed 1843**, Napier its first governor.
[170:3:1] - **Steps:** Treaty of "eternal friendship" (1809, Minto) → **Pottinger's treaty (1832, Bentinck)** – Indus trade → **protectorate (1838, Auckland)** → **subsidiary alliance (Feb 1839)** – force at Shikarpur and Bukkar → **Outram**'s new treaty → war and annexation.
[170:3:2] - **Motives:** recover prestige after the **First Afghan War**, counter **Russia**, control the **Indus** – not the Doctrine of Lapse. Called the **"Tail of the Afghan Storm"**.
[170:3:3] - **Napier:** "We have no right to seize Sindh, yet we shall do so ... a very advantageous, useful, humane piece of rascality".
[170:3:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.141-145; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.1; Spectrum Modern India p.850 (appendix); old app notes row 170
## SUB 4 | Dalhousie (1848-56) – Doctrine of Lapse and Annexations
[170:4:0] - **Doctrine of Lapse:** an **adopted son** could inherit the ruler's private property but **not the state**; a dependent state without a natural heir **lapsed** to the Company. Applied by **Lord Dalhousie** (not its originator – Kittur 1824 is an earlier case).
[170:4:1] TABLE head: State | Year
  [170:4:1.0] Satara | 1848 (first)
  [170:4:1.1] Jaitpur, Sambalpur | 1849
  [170:4:1.2] Baghat | 1850
  [170:4:1.3] Udaipur (Chhattisgarh, not Mewar) | 1852
  [170:4:1.4] Jhansi | 1853
  [170:4:1.5] Nagpur | 1854
[170:4:2] # Four grounds of annexation
[170:4:3] TABLE head: Ground | Cases
  [170:4:3.0] Conquest | Sindh 1843 (Ellenborough), Punjab 1849, Lower Burma / Pegu 1852
  [170:4:3.1] Lapse | Satara to Nagpur; Jhansi
  [170:4:3.2] Misgovernance | Mysore (1831), Coorg + Central Cachar (1834) – Bentinck; Awadh (1856) – Wajid Ali Shah exiled
  [170:4:3.3] Abolition of titles/pensions | Carnatic and Tanjore (1855); Nana Sahib's pension
[170:4:4] - **Sikkim (1850):** Dalhousie annexed parts of Sikkim (Terai, Darjeeling area) on the excuse that its king detained **two English doctors**.
[170:4:5] - **Awadh (1856)** came before the Indigo Revolt (1859-60), the Second Afghan War (1878-80) and the Ilbert Bill (1883).
[170:4:6] - By 1856 British India ran from the **Hindukush to Burma**; lapse, Awadh and lost titles fed the **Revolt of 1857**; Canning **withdrew the Doctrine** after 1857.
[170:4:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.155-157, p.850; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.1-2, p.20; PMF Modern History Part 2 p.97; old app notes row 170
## SUB 5 | Paramountcy – Lord Hastings and the Rajput States
[170:5:0] - **Lord Hastings (1813-23)** turned subsidiary alliances into **paramountcy**: ended non-intervention, crushed the **Pindaris** (Amir Khan, Karim Khan, Chitu) and the Marathas, imposed humiliating treaties on the Peshwa and Sindhia.
[170:5:1] - **Rajputana (1817-18):** Udaipur, Jaipur, Jodhpur, Bundi and others accepted **subordinate alliances**, negotiated by **Charles Metcalfe** – British protection in return for giving up **external relations**.
[170:5:2] - States kept **internal administration** but had **no international life**; the British intervened **to give effect to their international commitments** (and on **misgovernance** – Mysore 1831, Coorg 1834, Awadh 1856).
[170:5:3] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.138, p.154; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.39; old app notes row 170; Charles Metcalfe's role: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 6 | Ranjit Singh and the Anglo-Sikh Wars
[170:6:0] - **Treaty of Amritsar (25 April 1809)** – Ranjit Singh and the Company (**Minto I**, envoy **Charles Metcalfe**): **Sutlej** the boundary. **Tripartite Treaty (June 1838)** with Auckland and Shah Shuja.
[170:6:1] - **Bentinck** met Ranjit Singh at **Ropar (1831)** – treaty of "perpetual friendship".
[170:6:2] - Army trained by **Ventura and Allard**; model brigade **Fauj-i-Khas**. Ranjit Singh died **June 1839** → Kharak Singh, Nau Nihal Singh, Sher Singh, then **Duleep Singh** (regent **Rani Jindan**) – the **last Sikh ruler**.
[170:6:3] TABLE head:  | First War (1845-46) | Second War (1848-49)
  [170:6:3.0] Governor-General | Lord Hardinge I | Lord Dalhousie
  [170:6:3.1] Cause | Sikh army crossed the Sutlej (11 Dec 1845) | Mulraj's revolt at Multan (murder of Vans Agnew and Anderson)
  [170:6:3.2] Battles | Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon (10 Feb 1846) – lost by the treachery of Lal Singh and Teja Singh | Ramnagar, Chillianwala (13 Jan 1849, Gough vs Sher Singh – indecisive), Gujarat (21 Feb 1849) – decisive
  [170:6:3.3] Result | Treaty of Lahore (March 1846): Jalandhar Doab, indemnity, Resident Henry Lawrence; Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh for Rs 75 lakh (Treaty of Amritsar, 16 March 1846); Bhairowal (Dec 1846) – Resident the virtual ruler | Punjab annexed (29 March 1849); Duleep Singh pensioned and sent to England; Kohinoor to Queen Victoria
[170:6:4] - **Order asked:** First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-46) → Santhal revolt (1855-56) → Lytton's Delhi Durbar (1877) → Ilbert Bill (1883).
[170:6:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.145-151; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.18-19, Part 6 p.19-20; old app notes row 170

=== NOTES 1:171 | Governors-general of Bengal and of India – Warren Hastings to Dalhousie: Key Measures
## SUB 0 | William Bentinck (1828-35) – Sati, Thugs and Reforms
[171:0:0] - **Sati declared illegal** by **Regulation XVII of 4 Dec 1829** (the **Bengal Sati Regulation**) – **William Bentinck**, backed by **Raja Rammohan Roy** (a reformer, not the lawmaker); extended to Madras and Bombay in 1830.
[171:0:1] - **Thuggee suppressed (from 1830):** **Captain William Henry Sleeman** (appointed **1835**); Thugs (Hindu and Muslim) worshipped **Kali / Durga / Bhavani**.
[171:0:2] - **Female infanticide** suppressed (earlier regulations 1795, 1802 under Wellesley).
[171:0:3] - **Annexed:** **Mysore taken over (1831) for misgovernance**; **Coorg** and Central Cachar (1834).
[171:0:4] - **Ranjit Singh** received with great honour at **Ropar (1831)** – treaty of "perpetual friendship".
[171:0:5] - **Charter Act 1833:** Bentinck = **last GG of Bengal, first GG of India**; Company's trade ended, Europeans free to settle and hold land – he **eased the entry of British investors and traders** (APPSC key); the Act asked for slavery to be ended.
[171:0:6] - **Education:** Macaulay's Minute and the **English Education Act (1835)**; English the official language – "**Father of Modern Western Education in India**". Revised the **Mahalwari** settlement (Regulation IX, 1833) in the North-Western Provinces.
[171:0:7] TABLE head: Bentinck did NOT | Who did
  [171:0:7.0] Abolish slavery (Act V of 1843) | Ellenborough
  [171:0:7.1] Free the press (1835) | Metcalfe
  [171:0:7.2] Set up the first universities (1857) | Canning
  [171:0:7.3] Remove disabilities on change of religion (1850) | Dalhousie
[171:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.39, Part 6 p.1; Spectrum Modern India p.849; PMF Modern History Part 2 p.41, p.95, Part 3 p.1, p.25-27; old app notes row 171
## SUB 1 | Warren Hastings (1772-85)
[171:1:0] - **Governor of Bengal from 1772**; **first Governor-General of Bengal** under the **Regulating Act, 1773** (in office 1773/74-85).
[171:1:1] - **1772:** ended Clive's **Dual Government**, moved the treasury to Calcutta; **introduced the District Collector** (Diwani Adalats under the collector); **District Diwani and Fauzdari Adalats**; auctioned revenue-collection rights (five-year farming) – the **earliest land revenue settlement for Bengal**.
[171:1:2] - **Wars:** **Rohilla War (1774)** – he **helped Awadh against the Rohillas** (did not encourage them); **First Anglo-Maratha War** (Salbai 1782); **Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84)**; **Ring Fence** policy (Awadh as buffer).
[171:1:3] - **Culture:** **Calcutta Madrasa (1781)** – first Company educational institution; **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784, William Jones)**; **A Code of Gentoo Laws (1776)** – Halhed's English translation of the Manu-based digest *Vivadarnavasetu*; stopped Shah Alam's **Rs 26 lakh** tribute; Supreme Court, Calcutta (1774); Pitt's India Act (1784).
[171:1:4] - **Impeachment:** begun **1787** by **Edmund Burke** in Parliament; trial **1788-95** → **acquitted**. Charges: Rohilla War, **Chait Singh** of Benares, **Begums of Awadh**, judicial murder of **Nand Kumar (1775)**. The **only Governor-General impeached**.
[171:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.39; Spectrum Modern India p.553, p.595, p.848; PMF Modern History Part 2 p.98, p.102-103, Part 3 p.10, p.18, p.54; old app notes row 171
## SUB 2 | Cornwallis (1786-93) – Permanent Settlement and Civil Service
[171:2:0] - **Permanent Settlement (Istamarari) of Bengal, 1793** – zamindars owners; revenue fixed for ever.
[171:2:1] - **Cornwallis Code (1793):** separated **revenue administration from justice**; created the post of **District Judge**; collector left only revenue.
[171:2:2] - **Civil service:** Europeanised the administration, raised salaries, banned private trade – created the **Covenanted Civil Service** (later **ICS**) – "**Father of Civil Services in India**"; Warren Hastings had laid its foundation.
[171:2:3] - **Third Anglo-Mysore War** (Treaty of Seringapatam, 1792).
[171:2:4] - **Second term:** from 30 July 1805; **died 5 Oct 1805 at Ghazipur** (tomb there).
[171:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.39; Spectrum Modern India p.848; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.15; old app notes row 171
## SUB 3 | Dalhousie (1848-56) – the Maker of Modern India
[171:3:0] - **Railways:** **Railway Minute (1853)**; first line **Bombay-Thane (16 April 1853)** – he advocated rapid railway building.
[171:3:1] - **Telegraph** (Calcutta to Bombay, Madras, Peshawar) and the **Post Office Act (1854)**; **Public Works Department** (1854) – before him public works were under the Military Board; **Ganges Canal** (1854).
[171:3:2] - **Education:** **Wood's Despatch (1854)** – so "educational reforms" **were** his; the **Factories Act (1881)** was **Ripon's**, not his.
[171:3:3] - **Social:** Caste Disabilities Removal Act (**1850**); **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)** – listed under Dalhousie by NextGen and Spectrum, though passed on 26 July 1856 after **Canning** took over.
[171:3:4] - **Causes of 1857 from his measures:** Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh, **abolition of titles and pensions** – railways and telegraph alarmed people too; educational reform was not one of them.
[171:3:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.850; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.1; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.66; old app notes row 171
## SUB 4 | Governors-General in Order and the Office
[171:4:0] TABLE head: # | Governor-General | Tenure | Wars / events
  [171:4:0.0] 1 | Warren Hastings | 1773-85 | Rohilla, 1st Maratha, 2nd Mysore
  [171:4:0.1] 2 | Cornwallis | 1786-93 | 3rd Mysore; Permanent Settlement
  [171:4:0.2] 3 | Sir John Shore | 1793-98 | Non-intervention; Kharda (1795, Marathas beat the Nizam); Charter Act 1793
  [171:4:0.3] 4 | Wellesley | 1798-1805 | Subsidiary Alliance; 4th Mysore; 2nd Maratha; College of Fort William (1800)
  [171:4:0.4] 5 | Sir George Barlow | 1805-07 | Vellore Mutiny (1806)
  [171:4:0.5] 6 | Minto I | 1807-13 | Treaty of Amritsar (1809); Charter Act 1813
  [171:4:0.6] 7 | Lord Hastings (Marquess; Francis Rawdon-Hastings, Lord Moira) | 1813-23 | Anglo-Nepal; 3rd Maratha; Pindaris; Mahalwari (1822)
  [171:4:0.7] 8 | Amherst | 1823-28 | 1st Burmese (Yandabo 1826)
  [171:4:0.8] 9 | William Bentinck | 1828-35 | Sati, Thugs, Mysore, Coorg
  [171:4:0.9] 10 | Charles Metcalfe | 1835-36 | Press freed
  [171:4:0.10] 11 | Auckland | 1836-42 | 1st Afghan War; irrigation; famine relief
  [171:4:0.11] 12 | Ellenborough | 1842-44 | Sindh (1843); Gwalior; slavery abolished
  [171:4:0.12] 13 | Hardinge I | 1844-48 | 1st Sikh War, Lahore; preference for English education; human sacrifice banned
  [171:4:0.13] 14 | Dalhousie | 1848-56 | 2nd Sikh War; Lapse; railways
[171:4:1] - **Titles:** Governor of Bengal (first **Clive, 1758**) → **GG of Bengal (Regulating Act 1773: Warren Hastings)** → **GG of India (Charter Act 1833: Bentinck)** → **Viceroy (GoI Act 1858: Canning)**.
[171:4:2] - **Robert Clive** – founder of British rule in Bengal / of the British Empire in India; "heaven-born general"; set up the **Dual Government (1765)**.
[171:4:3] - **Order asked:** Warren Hastings → Cornwallis → Wellesley → William Bentinck.
[171:4:4] - **Not matched trap:** Anglo-Nepal War = **Lord Hastings**, not Sir John Shore.
[171:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 5 p.38-39, Part 6 p.1; Spectrum Modern India p.848-850; PMF Modern History Part 2 p.98-99, p.103, p.106; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.66; old app notes row 171
## SUB 5 | Wellesley, Metcalfe and Ellenborough – Other Measures
[171:5:0] - **Wellesley (1798-1805):** called himself the **"Bengal Tiger"**; Subsidiary Alliance; College of Fort William; took over Tanjore (1799), Surat (1800), Carnatic (1801); **Ceded Districts (1800)**. His administration was dominated by wars; it was **not** confined to Company affairs (statement-type trap).
[171:5:1] - **Charles Metcalfe (1835-36):** **Press Act of 1835 (Metcalfe Act)** repealed the 1823 licensing rules – the "**liberator of the Indian press**" (dated **1835**, at the end of the Bentinck period).
[171:5:2] - **Ellenborough (1842-44):** **ended the First Afghan War (1842)**; **Act V of 1843 abolished slavery** (the Charter Act of 1833 had asked for it); Sindh annexed.
[171:5:3] - **Hardinge I (1844-48):** Anti-Human-Sacrifice Act (**1845**); preference for English education.
[171:5:4] > **Press freed = Metcalfe (1835)**; Vernacular Press Act = Lytton (1878); its repeal = Ripon (1882).
[171:5:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.590, p.849-850; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.1; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.1, p.27; old app notes row 171

=== NOTES 1:172 | Viceroys of India – Canning to Mountbatten: Key Measures, Acts and Events
## SUB 0 | Mayo, Lawrence and Dufferin – Assassination, Census, Shimla, Masterly Inactivity, INC
[172:0:0] # Lord Mayo (1869-72)
[172:0:1] - **Only Viceroy assassinated in office:** **Lord Mayo**, stabbed by the convict **Sher Ali Afridi** at Port Blair (**Andamans**) in **1872** while on tour – not Curzon, Minto, Ripon or Wellesley.
[172:0:2] - **First census:** **1872** under **Mayo** (non-synchronous, not all areas at once); from **1881 (Ripon)** the regular decennial, synchronous census.
[172:0:3]   - ⚠ NextGen Indian History p.3 prints "1871" – a slip; PMF and the Census give **1872**.
[172:0:4] - **Financial decentralisation:** started by **Mayo's Resolution of 1870** (not Ripon, Dalhousie or Metcalfe).
[172:0:5] - Also: **Rajkot College** (Kathiawar) and **Mayo College** (Ajmer) for princes; **Statistical Survey of India**; **Department of Agriculture and Commerce**; state railways; Indian Evidence Act 1872.
[172:0:6] # Sir John Lawrence (1864-69)
[172:0:7] - **Masterly Inactivity:** non-interference in Afghanistan – **John Lawrence** (not Bentinck, Canning or Mayo).
[172:0:8] - **Shimla** officially declared the **summer capital** of British India by **John Lawrence in 1864**.
[172:0:9] - Also: telegraph link with Europe (1865); High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1865); **Indian Forest Department**; Bhutan (Duar) War.
[172:0:10] # Lord Dufferin (1884-88)
[172:0:11] - **INC founded (Dec 1885)** under **Dufferin** – Ripon had left in 1884; Lytton, Lansdowne, Elgin II, Curzon are distractors.
[172:0:12] - In **1887** Dufferin mocked the Congress as representing only a **"microscopic minority"** of the people.
[172:0:13] - **Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885):** Upper Burma annexed (1 Jan 1886) = the **last major extension** of British Indian territory – Dufferin.
[172:0:14] # Canning, Elgin I, Northbrook
[172:0:15] - **Canning (1856-62):** last Company Governor-General and **first Viceroy** (1858); Revolt of 1857; withdrew the Doctrine of Lapse; universities at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857); **Indian Councils Act 1861**, **portfolio system**; 3 Indians nominated (Raja of Benaras, Maharaja of Patiala, Sir Dinkar Rao).
[172:0:16] - **British PM during the Revolt of 1857:** **Palmerston** (1855-58).
[172:0:17] - **Elgin I (1862-63):** Wahabi movement. **Northbrook (1872-76):** abolished income tax; Kuka movement.
[172:0:18] - **Allahabad High Court** came in **1866** – after Canning's term.
[172:0:19] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.184-186; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.1-3; Spectrum Modern India p.850-851, p.162-163; PMF Modern Indian History Part 4 p.7, p.34; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.66; app notes 1:172
## SUB 1 | Lytton and Ripon – VPA, Forward Policy, Ilbert Bill, Factory Act 1881
[172:1:0] # Lord Lytton (1876-80)
[172:1:1] TABLE head: Measure | Year
  [172:1:1.0] Royal Titles Act – Victoria "Kaiser-i-Hind" | 1876
  [172:1:1.1] Delhi Durbar in honour of Queen Victoria (held during famine) | 1 Jan 1877
  [172:1:1.2] Vernacular Press Act, Arms Act | 1878
  [172:1:1.3] Strachey Famine Commission | 1878
  [172:1:1.4] ICS maximum age cut 21 → 19; Statutory Civil Service | 1878-79
  [172:1:1.5] Second Afghan War; Treaty of Gandamak | 1878-80, 1879
[172:1:2] - **Forward / aggressive policy towards Afghanistan ("proud reserve", scientific frontier):** **Lytton** – a Disraeli nominee; not Minto, Dufferin, Elgin or Mayo.
[172:1:3] - **VPA (1878):** magistrates could demand a security bond from vernacular papers without prior government permission – passed by **Lytton**, **not Curzon**; **repealed by Ripon (1882)**.
[172:1:4] - Lytton is **not** linked with the **Ilbert Bill** (that is Ripon).
[172:1:5] # Lord Ripon (1880-84)
[172:1:6] - Sent by **Gladstone's** Liberal government; repealed the **VPA (1882)**; **Local Self-Government Resolution 1882** ("Father of Local Self-Government"); **Hunter Education Commission (1882)**; first synchronous census 1881; revenue heads split into imperial, provincial, divided (1882).
[172:1:7] - **Ilbert Bill (1883):** let Indian judges try Europeans → European agitation = **"White Mutiny"**; exposed racial discrimination in the courts.
[172:1:8] - **Malaviya (Congress 1909):** Ripon "the greatest and most beloved Viceroy whom India has known"; Ripon favoured Indians (not British interests) and undid Lytton's illiberal acts.
[172:1:9] # Factory Acts
[172:1:10] TABLE head: Act | Viceroy | Provisions
  [172:1:10.0] First Factory Act, 1881 | Ripon | Children below 7 barred; children 7-12 max 9 hours; four holidays a month; dangerous machinery fenced
  [172:1:10.1] Second Factory Act, 1891 | Lansdowne | Child age 9-14, 7 hours; women 11 hours with 1½-hour break; weekly holiday
[172:1:11] - The demand came from the **Lancashire** lobby; the **early nationalists (moderates) did NOT support** the Acts of 1881 and 1891 (feared loss of Indian industry's edge).
[172:1:12] # Chronology of the Acts
[172:1:13] - **Indian Civil Service Act 1861 → Royal Titles Act 1876 → VPA 1878 → First Factory Act 1881** → Ilbert Bill 1883 → Councils Act 1892.
[172:1:14] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.851-852, p.163-164, p.566, p.618; PMF Modern Indian History Part 4 p.9, p.34; PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.184-185; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.3-4; iaspoint.com (Malaviya on Ripon); app notes 1:172
## SUB 2 | Lord Curzon – Partition, Archaeology, Tibet, Hostility to Congress
[172:2:0] # Partition of Bengal and "divide and rule"
[172:2:1] - **Partition of Bengal:** decided by **Curzon**; announced 20 July 1905, in force **16 Oct 1905** – the classic example of **"Divide and Rule"** (Hindu–Muslim split).
[172:2:2]   - Minto II's separate electorates (1909) are the other "divide and rule" step – answer **Curzon** when the question is the strategy behind 1905.
[172:2:3] - **Annulled in 1911** (Hardinge II) after the Swadeshi / Vande Mataram agitation.
[172:2:4] # Archaeology
[172:2:5] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [172:2:5.0] 1784 | Asiatic Society (William Jones)
  [172:2:5.1] 1861 | Canning made Alexander Cunningham Archaeological Surveyor – ASI begun
  [172:2:5.2] 1871 | ASI a separate department
  [172:2:5.3] 1902 | Curzon revived it as a central Department of Archaeology; John Marshall Director-General
  [172:2:5.4] 1904 | Ancient Monuments Preservation Act – Curzon
[172:2:6] - **⚠ Disputed:** "Who set up the Department of Archaeology / ASI?" – exam keys (APPSC G1 2012, UPPSC) answer **Curzon**; strictly the ASI dates from **1861 under Canning**. Pick Curzon unless the question says 1861 / Cunningham.
[172:2:7] - **ASI today:** an **attached office of the Ministry of Culture**; motto "Pratnakirti Apavarini"; AMASR Act 1958 protects monuments over 100 years old.
[172:2:8] # Other Curzon measures
[172:2:9] - **Younghusband Mission to Tibet (1903-04)**; **Imperial Cadet Corps (1901)**; NWFP (1901); Police Commission (Frazer, 1902); Universities Commission (Raleigh, 1902) + **Indian Universities Act 1904**; Calcutta Corporation Act 1899; Dept of Commerce and Industry.
[172:2:10] - **On the Congress (1900):** "The Congress is **tottering to its fall**, and one of my great ambitions while in India is to assist it to a **peaceful demise**" – **Curzon** (not Dufferin, Minto or Hamilton).
[172:2:11] - Aloof, bureaucratic "efficiency" rule – credited in keys with the view that government should keep away from the people.
[172:2:12] - **Tenure 1899-1905:** the longest among Curzon, Dufferin, Hardinge, Mayo (overall longest Viceroy: **Linlithgow**, 1936-43).
[172:2:13] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.288, p.852; PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.186-187; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.4; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.67; app notes 1:172
## SUB 3 | Hardinge II and 1911 – Durbar, Capital to Delhi, Bengal Reunited
[172:3:0] # The 12 December 1911 Durbar
[172:3:1] - **Delhi Durbar 1911:** coronation of **George V** and Queen Mary – the **only Durbar attended by the monarch** (1877 = Victoria / Lytton; 1903 = Edward VII / Curzon).
[172:3:2] - Announced: **Partition of Bengal annulled** (Bengal reunited **1911**); **capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi** (formal shift 1912; **New Delhi** by Lutyens and Baker, inaugurated **1931**); **Bihar and Orissa** a separate province (**1912**; Bihar alone from 1936).
[172:3:3] - The Viceroy who **proposed / effected** the transfer of capital = **Lord Hardinge II** (not Minto, Chelmsford, Reading, Curzon, Canning or Mayo).
[172:3:4] - Capital before Delhi = **Calcutta**.
[172:3:5] - **Gateway of India** (Bombay): marks George V's 1911 landing; **foundation stone 31 March 1913**; completed 1924.
[172:3:6] # Hardinge II (1910-16) – other facts
[172:3:7] - **Delhi Conspiracy / Hardinge Bomb Case:** bomb thrown at **Hardinge** on **23 Dec 1912** during his **state entry into Delhi** (Rash Behari Bose, Sachin Sanyal); he was wounded but did not change his attitude towards Indians.
[172:3:8] - Sympathetic to Indians in **South Africa**; **Gokhale's 1912** South Africa visit is linked with him; memoir **"My Indian Years"**; Hindu Mahasabha (1915).
[172:3:9] # Colonial architecture
[172:3:10] - Early 20th century **Indo-Saracenic / Indo-European hybrid** style (New Delhi, public buildings): by integrating Indian and European styles the British sought to show they were **legitimate rulers** of India – both statements true, II explains I.
[172:3:11] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.852; PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.187; PMF Modern Indian History Part 4 p.74; PMF Art & Culture Part 4 (Gateway of India); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.5; app notes 1:172
## SUB 4 | Viceroys 1916–1947 – Rowlatt Act, Irwin, Order of Tenure
[172:4:0] TABLE head: Viceroy | Tenure | Key events
  [172:4:0.0] Chelmsford | 1916-21 | Home Rule; Rowlatt Act 1919; Jallianwala Bagh; GoI Act 1919 (Dyarchy); Sadler Commission
  [172:4:0.1] Reading | 1921-26 | Only Jewish Viceroy (Rufus Isaacs); Chauri Chaura; Swaraj Party; repealed Rowlatt Act (1922)
  [172:4:0.2] Irwin | 1926-31 | Simon Commission; Civil Disobedience (1930); Gandhi–Irwin Pact; Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev hanged 23 Mar 1931
  [172:4:0.3] Willingdon | 1931-36 | Communal Award (MacDonald, 1932); Poona Pact
  [172:4:0.4] Linlithgow | 1936-43 | WWII; August Offer (1940); Cripps; Quit India
  [172:4:0.5] Wavell | 1943-47 | Wavell Plan / Simla 1945; Cabinet Mission 1946 (Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps, A.V. Alexander); Interim Govt (Asaf Ali – Railways); "The Viceroy's Journal"
  [172:4:0.6] Mountbatten | 1947-48 | Last Viceroy, first GG of free India; Independence Act 18 July 1947
[172:4:1] - **Rowlatt Act** = **Chelmsford** (not Irwin, Reading, Wavell, Hardinge II or Minto II).
[172:4:2] - **Match:** MacDonald – Communal Award; Linlithgow – August Offer; Dalhousie – Doctrine of Lapse; Chelmsford – Dyarchy.
[172:4:3] - **Order:** Curzon (1899-1905) → **Hardinge II (1910-16)** → **Chelmsford (1916-21)** → Irwin (1926-31).
[172:4:4] - **Full order:** Canning → Elgin I → Lawrence → Mayo → Northbrook → Lytton → Ripon → Dufferin → Lansdowne → Elgin II → Curzon → Minto II → Hardinge II → Chelmsford → Reading → Irwin → Willingdon → Linlithgow → Wavell → Mountbatten; C. Rajagopalachari = first and last Indian GG.
[172:4:5] - **Other statement facts:** Haripura Congress (1938) = **Subhas Bose** (not C.R. Das); Swami Shraddhanand urged a no-tax protest against the Rowlatt Act.
[172:4:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.852-855; PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.187-188; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.5; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.67; app notes 1:172
## SUB 5 | Commissions, Councils Acts and Financial Decentralisation
[172:5:0] TABLE head: Commission | Year | Subject | Viceroy
  [172:5:0.0] Strachey | 1878-80 | Famine | Lytton
  [172:5:0.1] Hunter | 1882 | Education | Ripon
  [172:5:0.2] Durand | 1893 | Afghan boundary | Lansdowne
  [172:5:0.3] Lyall | 1897 | Famine | Elgin II
  [172:5:0.4] MacDonnell | 1901 | Famine | Curzon
  [172:5:0.5] Scott-Moncrieff | 1901 | Irrigation | Curzon
  [172:5:0.6] Andrew Frazer | 1902 | Police | Curzon
  [172:5:0.7] Raleigh | 1902 | Universities | Curzon
  [172:5:0.8] Royal Commission on Labour | 1929 | Labour | Irwin
[172:5:1] - **Councils Acts:** 1861 Canning (Ordinances up to **6 months**; portfolio system); **1892 Lansdowne**; **1909 Minto II** (separate electorates).
[172:5:2] - **Financial decentralisation:** Mayo 1870 (fixed grants for police, jails, education, medical, roads; local taxes) → Lytton 1877 (wider heads) → Ripon 1882 (imperial, provincial, divided heads).
[172:5:3] - **Elgin II (1894-99):** famine 1896-97, Chapekar brothers killed Rand and Ayerst (1897), Munda uprising (1899). **Lansdowne:** civil services split into imperial, provincial, subordinate.
[172:5:4] - **Minto II (1905-10):** Morley–Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) – **separate electorates** for Muslims; Muslim League 1906; Surat split 1907; 18 July 1908 – **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** and **Bodi Narayana Rao**, first Telugu political prisoners.
[172:5:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern Indian History Part 5 p.184-187; Spectrum Modern India p.851-852; Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 p.29; app notes 1:172

=== NOTES 1:174 | Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853 – Provisions and Significance
## SUB 0 | Charter Act 1813 – End of India Trade Monopoly, Education, Missionaries
[174:0:0] - **Trade:** ended the Company's **monopoly of Indian trade** (thrown open to all British merchants) **except tea, opium and the China trade** – a statement "abolished the monopoly **including its tea trade**" is false.
[174:0:1] - **Sovereignty:** asserted the **sovereignty of the British Crown** over the Company's Indian territories; charter renewed for **20 years**.
[174:0:2] - **Education:** at least **Rs 1 lakh a year** for the revival of literature and promotion of science among Indians – first State responsibility for education (the chief reason the Act is called important).
[174:0:3] - **Missionaries** allowed to come to India and preach (Wilberforce, Charles Grant).
[174:0:4] - Courts in India got more power over European British subjects; local governments could tax persons; separate commercial and territorial accounts.
[174:0:5] - **UPSC 2019:** (1) monopoly ended except tea and China ✓ (2) Crown sovereignty ✓ (3) "revenues now controlled by Parliament" ✗ → **1 and 2 only**.
[174:0:6] > Which Act ended the Company's India trade monopoly? **1813** (1833 ended the tea/China monopoly).
[174:0:7] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 p.27; PMF Modern Indian History Part 2 p.105-106; Spectrum Modern India p.537; testbook.com (CGPSC 2023 key); app notes 1:174
## SUB 1 | Charter Act 1833 – Governor-General of India and Centralisation
[174:1:0] - **GG of Bengal → Governor-General of India** (first: **Lord William Bentinck**) – the **final step towards centralisation**; GG-in-Council got exclusive law-making for all British India; laws called **Acts** (earlier Regulations).
[174:1:1] - **Trade:** ended the remaining monopoly in **tea and the China trade**; Company became a purely **administrative** body; Europeans free to settle.
[174:1:2] - **Law Member** added as **4th member**: **T.B. Macaulay** (a Briton) – **no Indian Law Member** was provided; **First Law Commission (1834)** under **Macaulay** to codify Indian laws (IPC). The Law Member post is the origin of the **Ministry of Law and Justice**.
[174:1:3] - **Section 87:** no Indian to be barred from office by religion, birth, descent or colour; slavery to be abolished (done 1843).
[174:1:4] - Territories held **"in trust for His Majesty"** (Laxmikanth); the 1853 Act repeated it without a term.
[174:1:5] - **Agra Presidency:** almost all of present UP separated from Bengal Presidency in **1834** → North-Western Provinces (1836).
[174:1:6] - **Macaulay** (Commons, 1833 Bill): "The Company is an **anomaly** but it is part of a system where everything is an anomaly".
[174:1:7] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 p.28; PMF Modern Indian History Part 2 p.106; PMF Modern Indian History Part 3 p.1; Spectrum Modern India p.537-538; app notes 1:174
## SUB 2 | Charter Act 1853 – Legislative Council and Open Competition
[174:2:0] - **Last** Charter Act; Company's rule renewed **with no fixed term** ("in trust" for the Crown till Parliament provides otherwise).
[174:2:1] - **First functioning Legislative Council:** legislative and executive functions separated; **6 new legislative members** (4 from **Madras, Bombay, Bengal, Agra** + **Chief Justice** + one Calcutta judge) → Central Legislative Council of 12, a **"mini-Parliament"**.
[174:2:2] - **Civil services:** Directors' patronage ended → **open competitive examination** (the Act of **1853**; not 1833, 1858 or 1882); **Macaulay Committee 1854**.
[174:2:3] - **Imperial Legislative Council** (under the Indian Councils Act) was British India's legislature from **1861** to 1947.
[174:2:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 p.28-29; PMF Modern Indian History Part 3 p.2; Spectrum Modern India p.538-539; app notes 1:174
## SUB 3 | Charter Act 1793, Centralisation Trend and Persons
[174:3:0] - **1793:** charter and trade monopoly renewed **20 years**; override power to all GGs and Governors; Board of Control paid from **Indian revenues**.
[174:3:1] TABLE head: Act | Step
  [174:3:1.0] Regulating Act 1773 | GG of Bengal; presidencies subordinated
  [174:3:1.1] Pitt's India Act 1784 | Board of Control
  [174:3:1.2] Charter Act 1833 | GG of India – peak of centralisation
  [174:3:1.3] Charter Act 1853 | Legislative Council with provincial members
  [174:3:1.4] Indian Councils Act 1861 | Legislative power restored to Bombay and Madras
[174:3:2] - **Persons:** Raja Ram Mohan Roy – first demand for Indians in services (1832); Fort William College (Wellesley, 1800) → Haileybury (1806); Macaulay's Minute (1835); Law Commission 1834-38.
[174:3:3] - **Chronology:** Plassey 1757 → Buxar 1764 → Diwani 1765 → 1773 → 1784 → 1813 → 1858.
[174:3:4] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 p.27-29; Spectrum Modern India p.536; app notes 1:174

=== NOTES 1:175 | Land Revenue Systems – Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari; Areas and Effects
## SUB 0 | Ryotwari System – Read, Munro, Baramahal; Features and Areas
[175:0:0] # Origin and First Areas
[175:0:1] - **Devised by:** **Captain Alexander Read** (first experiment) and **Thomas Munro** – not Cornwallis, Elphinstone or Holt Mackenzie; also called the **"Munro system"**.
[175:0:2] - **First experiment:** **Baramahal (1792)** – territory ceded by Tipu after the Third Mysore War (Treaty of Srirangapatnam, 1792); Read was Superintendent of Revenue, Munro his assistant (1792-99).
[175:0:3]   - Baramahal = present **Salem** and environs (Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri, Tiruvannamalai) – not Anantapur.
[175:0:4] - **First in Andhra:** the **Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema)** by Munro, after his survey (1802-07); old notes date it **1802** (one APPSC stem says 1808 – still Munro).
[175:0:5] - **Whole Madras Presidency:** officially enforced by Munro as **Governor (1820)**; approved by Lord Hastings.
[175:0:6] - **Bombay:** extended by Munro's disciple **Mountstuart Elphinstone** after 1818 (Pringle's Ricardo-based survey; later Wingate and Goldsmid).
[175:0:7] - **Areas:** **Madras**, **Bombay**, **Assam**, Coorg, Burma – about **51%** of British India; so Ryotwari = **South India** first, West India (Bombay) second.
[175:0:8] > "First in Madras Presidency" = Baramahal; "first in Andhra" = Rayalaseema; "prevalent in" = South India (Madras).
[175:0:9] # Features
[175:0:10] - **Settlement directly with the ryot**, who paid revenue **directly to the Government** – no intermediary; peasant recognised as **owner (proprietor)**.
[175:0:11] - Ryots **registered and given pattas**; land **surveyed and assessed before being taxed** (UPSC 2012: all three statements correct).
[175:0:12] - Ryot could **sell, mortgage, gift, lease or sublet**; not evicted while the assessment was paid.
[175:0:13] - Assessment fixed on the **land, not the crop**; **revised periodically – about every 30 years** (20-30).
[175:0:14] - First demand **50%** of estimated produce (not 30%); **no automatic remission** after a bad harvest – only occasional reduction.
[175:0:15] - Munro: **"The Ryotwari is a system which has always prevailed in India."**
[175:0:16] # In Practice – Criticism
[175:0:17] - "Many zamindars replaced by **one giant zamindar**" – the State as **ultimate landlord**; revenue very high, enhanced at will, payable even in drought.
[175:0:18] - Arbitrary **'putcut'** assessment where no survey; over-assessment, poor records, unclear boundaries.
[175:0:19] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.60-64; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.25; NextGen AP History Part 21 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-21.txt) p.7; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.179; app notes 1:175
## SUB 1 | Thomas Munro and the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema)
[175:1:0] TABLE head: Years | Munro's post
  [175:1:0.0] 1761 | Born 27 May, Glasgow; reached Madras as a military cadet 15 Jan 1780
  [175:1:0.1] 1792-99 | Assistant to Read in Baramahal
  [175:1:0.2] 1800-07 | First Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, HQ Anantapur, four sub-collectors
  [175:1:0.3] 1802-07 | Field survey of the Ceded Districts; Ryotwari introduced
  [175:1:0.4] 1814-18 | President of the Judicial Commission
  [175:1:0.5] 1820-27 | Governor of Madras – "Father of Ryotwari"
[175:1:1] - **Ceded Districts (1800):** Bellary, Anantapur, Cuddapah, Kurnool – ceded by the Nizam under the Subsidiary Alliance.
[175:1:2] - **Palegars (poligars) suppressed** by Munro with **General Campbell** in **18 months** – 80 palegars removed (49 Cuddapah, 31 Bellary-Kurnool); not Wellesley, Metcalfe or the French (Dupleix, Bussy).
[175:1:3] - **Why Rayalaseema:** no strong zamindars; he distrusted palegars and big intermediaries – **direct contact with cultivators**.
[175:1:4] - **Spoke Telugu fluently** and ran the administration without interpreters (unlike other collectors); revered as **"Mandava Rishi"**.
[175:1:5] - **Died of cholera at Pattikonda (Kurnool), 6 July 1827**; buried at **Gooty**.
[175:1:6] - After Munro left (1807-08), **village-lease settlements** replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts until ryotwari was restored (about 1820).
[175:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 21 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-21.txt) p.4, p.7-9; NextGen AP History Part 16 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-16.txt) p.3; NextGen AP History Part 17 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-17.txt) p.22-25; NextGen AP History Part 7 p.3; app notes 1:175
## SUB 2 | Permanent Settlement (Zamindari) – Cornwallis 1793
[175:2:0] # Origin
[175:2:1] - Warren Hastings' five-year farming (1772) → annual leases → Cornwallis' **decennial (10-year) settlement, 1789** → declared **permanent in 1793**.
[175:2:2] - **Introduced by Lord Cornwallis, 1793**, in **Bengal and Bihar**, then Orissa, the northern districts of Madras (Circars, 1802) and Varanasi – about **19%** of British India; **planned by John Shore** (with James Grant).
[175:2:3] - "Introduced in **1795**" is wrong; Madras and Coorg were **not** under it.
[175:2:4] # Features
[175:2:5] - Made with **zamindars**, recognised as **owners (proprietors)**; rights **hereditary, transferable, saleable** (alienable, rentable, heritable).
[175:2:6] - Revenue **fixed for ever**; zamindar paid **10/11** of the rental, kept **1/11**.
[175:2:7] - **Sunset Law:** revenue due by sunset of the date, else the estate was sold.
[175:2:8] - Cultivators reduced to **tenants-at-will**; many zamindars **did not issue pattas** because there was **no official check** on them.
[175:2:9] - **Regulations of 1799 (Haftam) and 1812 (Panjam)** let zamindars seize tenants' property without a court.
[175:2:10] # Why a fixed, high demand
[175:2:11] - Stable income for the Company, cheap collection through few zamindars, a **loyal landlord class (political allies)**; officials hoped that with ownership and a fixed demand **zamindars would invest in land** so that area and yield rose.
[175:2:12] - Drawback for the Company: after **1810 prices rose**, the zamindars gained, the Company could not raise its share → it was **rarely extended beyond Bengal** (UPSC-type: Statement I true, II false).
[175:2:13] # Results
[175:2:14] - **Ryots at the mercy of zamindars**; stable income for the Company; zamindars **allies of the Company** (not deprived of ownership).
[175:2:15] - By 1815 about half of Bengal's estates sold for arrears → new landlords: **urban merchants and moneylenders**; **absentee landlordism, sub-infeudation, rack-renting**.
[175:2:16] - **Litigation rose after 1793** because of Cornwallis' **judicial reforms (abolition of court fees, separate civil courts)** – not the land provisions (UPSC 2011 key: none of the three).
[175:2:17] - Profits of agriculture went to the **zamindars**, not the cultivators or the Company.
[175:2:18] - **Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885:** tenants' (occupancy) rights in **Bengal and Bihar**.
[175:2:19] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.55-60, p.83-84; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.24; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.576; https://www.pmfias.com/cornwallis-permanent-settlement-litigation-pyq-2011/; app notes 1:175
[175:2:20] - **Chronology:** Permanent Settlement 1793 → Subsidiary Alliance 1798 → Doctrine of Lapse 1848 → Partition of Bengal 1905.
## SUB 3 | Mahalwari and Taluqdari; the Three Systems Compared
[175:3:0] # Mahalwari
[175:3:1] - **Devised by Holt Mackenzie, 1822** (Regulation VII of 1822) in the **North-Western Provinces of the Bengal Presidency** – the "father" of Mahalwari and the first officer to try it.
[175:3:2] - **1833:** revised under **William Bentinck** by **R.M. Bird** (Regulation IX of 1833, "father of land settlement in north India"), carried on by **James Thomason**.
[175:3:3] - **Areas:** **North-Western Provinces (Agra-Oudh), Punjab**, Gangetic valley, parts of Central India – about **30%**.
[175:3:4] - **Unit:** the **mahal** (village or group of villages); land owned **jointly by the village community** (not the government); common ownership = **"Bhai Chara" / "Mahali"**.
[175:3:5] - Revenue fixed per village, collected by the **village headman (lambardar)**; each cultivator paid his share, **village collectively liable**; **periodically revised** (not fixed).
[175:3:6] # Taluqdari
[175:3:7] - **Taluqdari = Awadh (Oudh)** – "Taluqdari – Bombay" is the wrong pair; taluqdar = landlord-middleman.
[175:3:8] # Comparison
[175:3:9] TABLE head: Basis | Permanent | Ryotwari | Mahalwari
  [175:3:9.0] Settled with | Zamindar | Individual ryot | Village (mahal)
  [175:3:9.1] Owner | Zamindar | Ryot | Village community
  [175:3:9.2] Revenue | Fixed for ever | Revised ~30 years | Revised periodically
  [175:3:9.3] Area | Bengal, Bihar, Orissa | Madras, Bombay, Assam | NWP, Punjab
  [175:3:9.4] Man | Cornwallis, John Shore | Read, Munro | Holt Mackenzie, Bird
[175:3:10] - All three made land **saleable, mortgageable and alienable** – a commodity.
[175:3:11] - Different systems in different regions created **different classes** in the peasantry.
[175:3:12] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.64-65; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.26; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.180; app notes 1:175
## SUB 4 | Effects of the Land Systems; Revenue in Andhra
[175:4:0] # Effects
[175:4:1] - Rigid **cash revenue**, payable even when crops failed → loans from **moneylenders** → mortgage and **loss of land**; the moneylender became the **greatest evil** of the village economy.
[175:4:2] - Cash revenue pushed **commercial crops** (indigo, cotton, opium, jute); the **American Civil War** cotton slump (1866) → defaults → land to moneylenders.
[175:4:3] - New classes: **merchant-landlords** in Zamindari areas; **moneylender-landlords** in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas.
[175:4:4] - **Alice Thorner:** Ryotwari destroyed the village system and isolated farmers from the government.
[175:4:5] # Andhra
[175:4:6] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [175:4:6.0] 1765-66 | Northern Circars (Sarkars) obtained – Mughal farman and treaty with the Nizam
  [175:4:6.1] 1788 | Guntur acquired
  [175:4:6.2] 1794 | Battle of Padmanabham – Vijayarama Gajapati Raju of Vizianagaram killed
  [175:4:6.3] 1800 | Ceded Districts given by the Nizam
  [175:4:6.4] 1802 | Permanent Settlement in the Circars (Vizianagaram peshcush Rs 6 lakh); Munro's survey and Ryotwari in Rayalaseema
  [175:4:6.5] 1846 | Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt – attacked the Koilkuntla (Kovela Kuntla) treasury
  [175:4:6.6] 1858 | Madras Inam Commission – checked rent-free inam titles
  [175:4:6.7] 1948 | Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act – zamindari abolished
[175:4:7] - **Pattern:** **Zamindari** in the coastal Circars (zamindars paid **peshcush**); **Ryotwari** in **Rayalaseema** (Ceded Districts); Mahalwari-type (headmen) in **Nellore**.
[175:4:8] - **Haveli** = land under direct Company control; grouped into **mootahs** and auctioned (1802) – held as proprietary estates, many fell into arrears; **Moturpha** = tax on professions, trades and looms; **Inam** = rent-free title.
[175:4:9] - Permanent Settlement in Andhra (1802): **auction system abolished, tax fixed**.
[175:4:10] - **Mirasidar** (Madras) = holder of mirasi rights, the designated revenue payer; **Banian** = Indian agent of the Company; **Aurang** = warehouse/workshop (not the treasury) – UPSC 2020.
[175:4:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 21 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-21.txt) p.3-5; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.25-27; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.65-67; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.577; app notes 1:175

=== NOTES 1:176 | Economic Impact of Colonial Rule – Drain of Wealth, Deindustrialisation, Commercialisation of Agriculture
## SUB 0 | Drain of Wealth and the Economic Nationalists
[176:0:0] # Meaning
[176:0:1] - **Drain of wealth:** the part of India's wealth carried to **Britain** without **adequate economic or material return** – peculiar to **British** rule (not Portuguese, Dutch or French).
[176:0:2] - **Began** with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)** – Bengal's revenue bought the Company's export "investments".
[176:0:3] - India usually had a **favourable balance of trade**; the drain took the form of **unrequited exports** (export surplus paid for Home Charges, British office and war expenses) – NOT an excess of imports.
[176:0:4] - In the 18th century the drain was about **2-3% of Britain's national income** (Spectrum) and nearly 9% of India's income (PMF) – it helped finance Britain's industrial revolution.
[176:0:5] # Components (Home Charges and more)
[176:0:6] TABLE head: Component | What it covered
  [176:0:6.0] Salaries, pensions | Of British civil and military officials, remitted home
  [176:0:6.1] Interest | On the public debt raised in Britain
  [176:0:6.2] Railway guarantee | 5% assured return to British investors, paid from Indian revenue
  [176:0:6.3] Military | British Indian Army and wars abroad – the largest budget head
  [176:0:6.4] Profits | Of British capitalists, merchants, banks, shipping and insurance
[176:0:7] - **Reason per Naoroji's theory (APPSC FRO):** profits taken by British capitalists from India.
[176:0:8] - Naoroji: what was drained was a **"potential surplus"** that could have developed India; imperialists claimed linking India to the world capitalist market was itself modernisation (both true, II does not explain I).
[176:0:9] # Dadabhai Naoroji
[176:0:10] - **"Grand Old Man of India"**; propounded and popularised the **drain theory**; first stated in **"England's Debt to India" / "England's Duties to India" (1867)**; coined **"moral drain"**.
[176:0:11] - Book: ***Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (1901)**; also ***Poverty of India: Papers and Statistics*** (from his 1876 paper "The Poverty of India"); he used the phrase **"Un-British"**.
[176:0:12] - **First estimate of per capita income: Rs 20 (1867-68)** – not Ranade, Hunter or R.C. Dutt.
[176:0:13] - Showed (1880) that a **jail convict's food and clothing cost about 50% more** than the average Indian's income (old app key; not checked).
[176:0:14] - First Indian elected to the **House of Commons (1892, Finsbury Central)**; first to make **Swaraj** the national demand (Calcutta Congress, 1906).
[176:0:15] # Other Economic Critics
[176:0:16] TABLE head: Writer | Work
  [176:0:16.0] R.C. Dutt | *Economic History of India* (2 vols, 1901-03) – economic record of colonial rule; *Open Letters to Lord Curzon* (1900)
  [176:0:16.1] G. Subramania Iyer | *Some Economic Aspects of British Rule in India* (1903)
  [176:0:16.2] William Digby | *'Prosperous' British India* (1901)
  [176:0:16.3] M.G. Ranade | *Essays on Indian Economics*
  [176:0:16.4] R.P. (Rajani Palme) Dutt | *India Today* – stages of colonialism (not R.C. Dutt)
  [176:0:16.5] Ramkrishna Vishwanath | First Marathi economics book (1843) on the drain
[176:0:17] - Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer and R.C. Dutt were **all** economic critics of colonialism (UPSC 2015).
[176:0:18] - The economic critique was the Moderates' greatest contribution and a base of **Swadeshi**; Moderates demanded cuts in **military spending**, lower land revenue, protective tariffs.
[176:0:19] - Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti: paper ***The Crescent*** (reported Andhra famines); Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam.
[176:0:20] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.73-76; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.580-585; NextGen AP History Part 17 p.23; app notes 1:176
## SUB 1 | Stages of Colonialism; One-way Free Trade and Deindustrialisation
[176:1:0] # Stages (R.P. Dutt, *India Today*)
[176:1:1] TABLE head: Stage | Period | Feature
  [176:1:1.0] Mercantilist (merchant capital) | 1757-1813 | Company monopoly; mostly purchase of Indian goods for export, paid from Bengal revenue
  [176:1:1.1] Free trade (industrial capital) | 1813-1858 | India a market for British goods and supplier of raw materials
  [176:1:1.2] Finance capital | 1858 onwards | British capital in railways, plantations, banks
[176:1:2] - India changed from a **leading exporter of manufactures** to a **supplier of raw materials** – an **agricultural colony of manufacturing Britain**.
[176:1:3] # One-way Free Trade
[176:1:4] - **Charter Act of 1813** ended the Company's trade monopoly → **one-way free trade**: British goods entered India **duty-free / nominal duty**; Indian textiles paid **heavy duties in Britain** (already from the 1720 laws) – so "tax-free import of Indian textiles into the UK" is false.
[176:1:5] - **Imperial preference:** special privileges (lower duties) for **British imports in India**.
[176:1:6] - **Cotton excise (1894-96)** on Indian mill cloth to offset the import duty on British goods; **Suez Canal (1869)**.
[176:1:7] - **Railways:** built by private British companies with a **5% guarantee from Indian revenue** (not financed by the British government); they carried British goods inland and raw materials out – **accelerated the decay of handicrafts**.
[176:1:8] - Karl Marx: British economic policy in India "disgusting"; the British **"inundated the very mother country of cotton with cottons"**.
[176:1:9] # Deindustrialisation
[176:1:10] - Weavers coerced (1769 directive on silk; Bolt 1772); Lancashire cloth in Bengal **1786**; by **1850** India took **one-fourth** of British cotton exports.
[176:1:11] - **Industrial Revolution (first half of the 19th century):** **Indian handicrafts were ruined**; **raw cotton** exports rose (not textile exports).
[176:1:12] - Process intensified **after 1813**, aggravated by the end of the Company's monopoly (UPPSC key: both statements).
[176:1:13] - Other causes: loss of princely patrons, export of raw materials, transit duties, British privileges (**B.D. Basu**); shipbuilding crushed by the 1813-14 laws.
[176:1:14] - **Share of world manufactures:** about **24.5% (1750)** → under **2% (1900)** (Paul Bairoch).
[176:1:15] - **Results:** urban handicrafts' sudden collapse; **artisans crowded into agriculture**; **Dhaka** (muslin) declined while Calcutta, Madras, Bombay grew.
[176:1:16] - **No independent industrial development:** **absence of heavy (capital-goods) industries**; laissez-faire did **not** promote indigenous capitalism.
[176:1:17] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.69-72, p.78, p.80-81; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.577-579, p.583; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 p.25; app notes 1:176
## SUB 2 | Commercialisation of Agriculture; Opium and Peasant Laws
[176:2:0] - **Commercialisation of Indian agriculture** = a main 19th-century economic result of British rule (UPSC 2018) – not more handicraft exports, Indian factories or rapid urban growth.
[176:2:1] - Forced by **cash revenue**; cash crops replaced food crops → less food security, **famines**.
[176:2:2] - Poorer peasants because they were **exploited by merchants and middlemen** (sold at any price after harvest to the grain merchant-moneylender).
[176:2:3] - **Ganjam / Deccan:** American Civil War cotton boom, slump in 1866 → debt, famine, Deccan riots.
[176:2:4] TABLE head: Crop | Main region
  [176:2:4.0] Indigo | Bengal, Bihar – Tinkathiya (3/20 of holding); Indigo Revolt 1859-60
  [176:2:4.1] Cotton | Deccan, Gujarat, Berar
  [176:2:4.2] Jute | Bengal
  [176:2:4.3] Opium | Bihar (and Bengal, Malwa)
  [176:2:4.4] Tea | Assam
[176:2:5] - **Triangular trade** India–China–England rested on **opium**: Indian opium → China; Chinese tea and silver → Britain; British goods → India. **Opium Wars: Britain v. China** (1839-42, 1856-60).
[176:2:6] - By the late 19th century India was a large exporter of **cotton yarn and wheat** (NDA 2014 key).
[176:2:7] TABLE head: Law | Protected peasants against
  [176:2:7.0] Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1879 | Moneylenders, after the Deccan riots (1875)
  [176:2:7.1] Punjab Land Alienation Act, 1900 | Transfer of land to non-agriculturists (moneylenders)
[176:2:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.82-83, p.87; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.576-577; NextGen AP History Part 16 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-16.txt) p.5; app notes 1:176
## SUB 3 | Andhra Crafts and Industries Under British Rule
[176:3:0] - **Textiles = second-largest employer after agriculture** in British-period Andhra.
[176:3:1] - **Decline:** machine cloth from England + Company duties and loom tax (moturpha) → exports from Visakhapatnam fell from Rs 7 lakh to Rs 1 lakh (1830s), Machilipatnam Rs 30 lakh → Rs 2,750 (1843-44), Nellore Rs 1.8 lakh → Rs 360 (1842-43); the industry **lost foreign and local markets** (only "declined" is correct); weavers migrated to Burma, Sri Lanka, Mauritius.
[176:3:2] # Carpets
[176:3:3] - **Eluru carpets** and **Kurnool rugs** were known in the international market; the Eluru craft grew under **Persian immigrants during Muslim rule**; shown at the **London Exhibition, 1851**; declined by the mid-19th century.
[176:3:4] TABLE head: Place | Product
  [176:3:4.0] Srikakulam | Muslin
  [176:3:4.1] Machilipatnam | Dyed cloth; chintz (16th-17th c.); first Dutch factory
  [176:3:4.2] Nellore | Towels
  [176:3:4.3] Eluru | Carpets
  [176:3:4.4] Kurnool | Rugs, blankets
  [176:3:4.5] Peddapuram, Dharmavaram, Berhampur | Silk
  [176:3:4.6] Uppada | Jamdani silk
  [176:3:4.7] Ponduru (Srikakulam) | Fine hand-spun khadi
[176:3:5] - **Kamsalis** = goldsmiths (Viswabrahmin artisans) in Andhra records.
[176:3:6] # Minerals and Industry
[176:3:7] - **Manganese:** **Visakhapatnam** district (Vizianagaram mines) stood **first in the world, 1892-1929** – not Nellore; **Nellore = mica**.
[176:3:8] - Jute mills Chittivalasa and Nellimarla; first railway in Andhra **Puttur–Renigunta (1862)**.
[176:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 21 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-21.txt) p.5-6; NextGen AP History Part 16 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-16.txt) p.4-5; NextGen AP History Part 7 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-07.txt) p.3; NextGen AP History Part 6 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-06.txt) p.7; app notes 1:176; general knowledge, not checked (Kamsalis)
## SUB 4 | Modern Industry, Currency and the Economy at Independence
[176:4:0] TABLE head: Industry | First / key fact
  [176:4:0.0] Cotton mill | Fort Gloster (Calcutta) 1818 failed; Bombay, 1854 – Cowasji Nanabhai Davar (Spectrum: set up 1853)
  [176:4:0.1] Jute mill | Rishra (Bengal), 1855
  [176:4:0.2] Tea company | Assam Company, 1839 – formed in England; HQ Nazira
  [176:4:0.3] Iron and steel | TISCO, 1907
[176:4:1] - **Cotton mills Indian-owned; jute mills foreign-owned (Bengal)**; capital goods only about one-fourth of output.
[176:4:2] - **Hilton Young Commission (1926):** rupee at **1s 6d** (Indian business, Purshottamdas Thakurdas, wanted 1s 4d) – to aid **remittances from India and keep India's creditworthiness**; made Indian goods dearer abroad; recommended a central bank → **RBI 1935**.
[176:4:3] - Bombay mill workers lived in **chawls** (one-room tenements).
[176:4:4] # On the Eve of Independence
[176:4:5] TABLE head: Indicator | Value
  [176:4:5.0] World income share (Angus Maddison) | 27% (1700) → 3% (1950)
  [176:4:5.1] Per capita income | about Rs 265
  [176:4:5.2] Life expectancy | 32 years
  [176:4:5.3] Literacy | under 16%
  [176:4:5.4] Agriculture | over 75% of workers, about 50% of GDP
[176:4:6] - India had a **strong pre-British industrial base**; British policy caused **deindustrialisation**; agriculture **stagnant, low-productivity, monsoon-dependent**; trade = raw materials out, finished goods in; infrastructure served British interests.
[176:4:7] - Slow industrialisation for want of **capital goods industries**; public sector only railways, power, ports, communications.
[176:4:8] - Under zamindari the **profit from agriculture went to the zamindars**; fertiliser use was negligible.
[176:4:9] - Ruined: Indian industries and trade, agriculture stagnated – **not** "ruin of feudalism".
[176:4:10] - First Plan priority: agriculture, irrigation, power.
[176:4:11] - **Imperial Gazetteer of India:** compiled by **W.W. Hunter**; **James Mill** (*History of British India*, 1817) divided Indian history into **Hindu, Muslim and British** periods.

  1 only | 2 only | *Both 1 and 2 | Neither 1 nor 2
  x: India had a strong industrial base before British rule, and British trade policy caused its deindustrialisation.

=== NOTES 1:178 | Education Policy – Orientalist-anglicist Debate, Macaulay's Minute, Wood's Despatch 1854, Hunter Commission
## SUB 0 | Early Institutions and Orientalist Scholars
[178:0:0] # Institutions before 1835 – founder and year
[178:0:1] TABLE head: Institution | Year | Founder | Exam fact
  [178:0:1.0] Calcutta Madrasa | 1781 | Warren Hastings | Muslim law; first Madrasa set up by the British (UPPSC 2006 ×2)
  [178:0:1.1] Asiatic Society of Bengal | 15 Jan 1784 | Sir William Jones | Oriental research – manuscripts, translations; journal *Asiatick Researches*
  [178:0:1.2] Sanskrit College, Benaras | 1791 | Jonathan Duncan (Resident) | First Sanskrit Mahavidyalaya at Varanasi; Hindu law and philosophy
  [178:0:1.3] Fort William College | 10 July 1800 | Lord Richard Wellesley | To train Company civil servants in Indian languages and customs; Directors replaced it with Haileybury (England) in 1806
  [178:0:1.4] Hindu College, Calcutta | 1817 | Ram Mohan Roy (UPSC key) with David Hare | First Western-style secular college; later Presidency College
  [178:0:1.5] Delhi College | 1824 | Grew out of Ghazi-ud-din Khan's Madrasa | After Hindu College
  [178:0:1.6] Vedanta College | 1825 | Ram Mohan Roy | 
  [178:0:1.7] Mayo College, Ajmer | 1875 | Named after Lord Mayo (Richard Bourke) | School for Indian princes and nobility – the odd one out among missionary colleges
  [178:0:1.8] MAO College, Aligarh | 1875 | Sir Syed Ahmad Khan | AMU from 1920
  [178:0:1.9] Central Hindu School, Banaras | 7 July 1898 | Annie Besant | Nucleus of BHU (1916)
[178:0:2] - **Order:** Hindu College (1817) → Delhi College (1824) → Mayo / MAO (1875) (UPPCS 2012).
[178:0:3] - **⚠ Disputed:** Hindu College was founded by **David Hare and Bengali notables**; keys add Ram Mohan Roy, and **Alexander Duff** only reached India in 1830.
[178:0:4] - **Royal Asiatic Society:** keys answer **William Jones** (the Asiatic Society, 1784); strictly the London **Royal Asiatic Society (1823)** was founded by **H.T. Colebrooke**.
[178:0:5] # Orientalist scholars and their works
[178:0:6] TABLE head: Scholar | Known for
  [178:0:6.0] Sir William Jones | Asiatic Society (1784); translated Abhijnana Shakuntalam (1789) and Manusmriti; identified Sandrokottos = Chandragupta Maurya
  [178:0:6.1] Charles Wilkins | First English translation of the Bhagavad Gita (1785)
  [178:0:6.2] H.T. Colebrooke | Professor of Hindu law and Sanskrit at Fort William College (1805, Wellesley); *Digest of Hindu Law*; "Essay on the Vedas"
  [178:0:6.3] N.B. Halhed | *A Code of Gentoo Laws* (1776); Bengali grammar (1778)
  [178:0:6.4] James Mill (Anglicist) | *The History of British India* (1817) – Hindu, Muslim, British periods; not J.S. Mill (his son)
[178:0:7] > Recall angle: founder ↔ institution, translator ↔ text; Hastings = Madrasa, Duncan = Sanskrit College, Jones = Asiatic Society, Wellesley = Fort William.
[178:0:8] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.595; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.4, p.17-20, p.33; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.60-61; app notes 1:178 (sub 1)
## SUB 1 | Charter Act 1813, the Orientalist–Anglicist Debate and Macaulay's Minute
[178:1:0] # Steps that led to English education
[178:1:1] - **Charter Act 1813:** **Rs 1 lakh a year** for reviving literature, encouraging learned Indians and promoting **modern sciences**; also admitted **missionaries** and ended the Company's India trade monopoly.
[178:1:2]   - The grant was **not made available till 1823** – delayed by the debate over how to spend it.
[178:1:3] - **General Committee of Public Instruction (GCPI), 1823:** set up to **manage the education grant**; it split into Orientalists and Anglicists.
[178:1:4] - Led to English education: **Charter Act 1813 + GCPI 1823 + Orientalist–Anglicist controversy** – all three (UPSC 2018).
[178:1:5] # The two camps
[178:1:6] TABLE head: Orientalists | Anglicists
  [178:1:6.0] Grant for Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian (classical) learning, alongside some Western subjects | Spend exclusively on Western science and literature
  [178:1:6.1] Warren Hastings, William Jones, Jonathan Duncan, H.T. Colebrooke, H.H. Wilson, Halhed | T.B. Macaulay (leader), Bentinck, Charles Trevelyan, James Mill
  [178:1:6.2] In Madras Thomas Munro backed pathashalas and vernacular schooling | Anglicists were split on the medium: English vs vernaculars
[178:1:7] - **Munro's Survey of Indigenous Education (1826):** a wide network of **vernacular village schools** in the Madras Presidency; his collectorate and tahsildari schools were **closed in 1836** after the 1835 resolution.
[178:1:8] # Macaulay's Minute, 2 February 1835
[178:1:9] - Written by **Macaulay** as **Law Member** and **President of the GCPI**; approved by **William Bentinck** – "Father of Modern Western Education in India".
[178:1:10] - **Settled the row for the Anglicists:** funds for **Western science and literature through English alone**.
[178:1:11] - **Remarks:** "**a single shelf of a good European library** was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia"; all the history in Sanskrit books "less valuable than ... the most paltry abridgement used at preparatory schools in England" (1835).
[178:1:12] - **Aim:** a class "**Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals and in intellect**" – **interpreters** between rulers and ruled.
[178:1:13] - **Downward Filtration Theory:** educate a few of the upper and middle classes; learning would **filter down** to the masses – an **education** policy (not railways, irrigation or poverty), credited to **Macaulay**; criticised for neglecting mass literacy.
[178:1:14] - **English Education Act 1835 (Bentinck):** English the medium of higher education; promotion of oriental institutions **stopped** – so "stipends and printing of classics were to continue" is the **incorrect** statement.
[178:1:15] - Called the **foundation of modern education** in India (IAS 1993); English education came in **Bentinck's** reign.
[178:1:16] - **Follow-up:** 1837 English replaced Persian as official language; 1844 Hardinge made English knowledge a condition for government jobs.
[178:1:17] > Trap: 1835 = **Bentinck + Macaulay**; 1854 = **Charles Wood + Dalhousie**; downward filtration = Macaulay, rejected by Wood.
[178:1:18] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.596-597; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.17, p.20, p.31-32; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.69; app notes 1:178 (sub 2-4)
## SUB 2 | Wood's Despatch 1854 and the Universities of 1857
[178:2:0] # The Despatch
[178:2:1] - Issued **19 July 1854** by **Sir Charles Wood**, **President of the Board of Control**, under Governor-General **Dalhousie**.
[178:2:2] - **"Magna Carta of English Education in India"** – the **first comprehensive plan** and the **most important education document** of British India (APPSC G1 2002; G1 PYQ).
[178:2:3] - **Aim:** spread of **European (Western) learning and culture**, with practical benefits over oriental knowledge (UPSC 2003).
[178:2:4] # Provisions
[178:2:5] - State to take responsibility for **education of the masses** – **rejected downward filtration** (on paper).
[178:2:6] - **Graded hierarchy:** vernacular primary schools → Anglo-vernacular high schools → affiliated colleges (district) → **universities** in the presidency towns.
[178:2:7] - **Medium:** **English for higher studies**, **vernaculars at school level** – not English at all levels (UPSC 2018: "A and B only").
[178:2:8] - **Grants-in-aid** to encourage private (mostly missionary) enterprise.
[178:2:9] - Stress on **female education**, **vocational** training and **teachers' training**; education departments in every province; secular education in government institutions.
[178:2:10] # Universities of 1857
[178:2:11] TABLE head: University | Year | Note
  [178:2:11.0] Calcutta | 1857 | Under Lord Canning
  [178:2:11.1] Bombay | 1857 | 
  [178:2:11.2] Madras | 1857 | 5 September 1857
[178:2:12] - **Model:** **University of London** – affiliating and examining universities; Calcutta University came from **Wood's Despatch**, not Hunter or Macaulay.
[178:2:13] - Bankim Chandra Chatterjee was among Calcutta's first two graduates (1858).
[178:2:14] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.597-598; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.34-35; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.61; app notes 1:178 (sub 5)
[178:2:15] - **Dalhousie's Minute (1853):** backed **vernacular education**; the Despatch followed in 1854.
## SUB 3 | Hunter to Sargent – Later Commissions and Plans
[178:3:0] # Education bodies after 1857
[178:3:1] TABLE head: Body | Year | Viceroy / head | Focus
  [178:3:1.0] Hunter Commission (first Indian Education Commission) | 1882 | Lord Ripon; W.W. Hunter | Reviewed progress since 1854; primary education through vernacular; primary schools to district and municipal boards; secondary in literary + vocational streams; female education
  [178:3:1.1] Raleigh (Universities) Commission | 1902 | Curzon; Sir Thomas Raleigh; Indian members Syed Hussain Bilgrami and Justice Gurudas Banerjee | → Indian Universities Act 1904 – more government control
  [178:3:1.2] Resolution on Education Policy | 1913 | Hardinge II | Answer to Gokhale's demand for compulsory primary education
  [178:3:1.3] Sadler (Calcutta University) Commission | 1917–19 | Dr M.E. Sadler (VC, Leeds); members Ashutosh Mukherjee, Zia-ud-din Ahmad | 12-year school, intermediate stage, 3-year degree
  [178:3:1.4] Hartog Committee | 1929 | Sir Philip Hartog; Simon Commission sub-committee; Irwin (not Wavell) | Growth of education; wastage and stagnation in primary schooling
  [178:3:1.5] Sargent Plan | 1944 | Central Advisory Board of Education; Sir John Sargent; Wavell | Free compulsory education 6–14; target: England's level in 40 years
  [178:3:1.6] University Education Commission | 1948–49 | S. Radhakrishnan | Moral education – start the day with silent meditation
[178:3:2] - **Chronology:** Wood (1854) → Hunter (1882) → Sadler (1917) → Sargent (1944) = "C A B D" (UPPCS 2018).
[178:3:3] - **First decentralisation of primary education:** Hunter Commission (control to local boards).
[178:3:4] - **Wastage** = leaving school before finishing the primary course; **stagnation** = repeating a class; first described by **Hartog**.
[178:3:5] - **3H (Head, Heart, Hand):** keys say **Gandhi** (Nai Talim / basic education); the idea comes from **Pestalozzi**.
[178:3:6] - **Madan Mohan Malaviya** (BHU 1916) pressed for **religious education** in Indian universities.
[178:3:7] # Other colonial commissions (distractors)
[178:3:8] TABLE head: Body | Year | Subject
  [178:3:8.0] Campbell | 1866 | Orissa famine (John Lawrence era)
  [178:3:8.1] Strachey | 1878 | Famine policy → Famine Code
  [178:3:8.2] Hunter Committee (Lord William Hunter) | 1919 | Jallianwala Bagh / Punjab disorders
  [178:3:8.3] Lee | 1924 | Civil services
  [178:3:8.4] Muddiman | 1924 | Working of dyarchy
  [178:3:8.5] Royal Commission on Agriculture | 1926 | Agriculture – Lord Linlithgow
  [178:3:8.6] Butler | 1927 | Indian States and Paramount Power
  [178:3:8.7] Simon | 1927 | Constitutional reforms
  [178:3:8.8] Whitley | 1929 | Labour conditions – J.H. Whitley
[178:3:9] > Match angle (UPSC 1997): Butler – States; Hartog – education; Hunter Inquiry – Jallianwala; Muddiman – dyarchy.
[178:3:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.598-604; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.37, p.39-41; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.62; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.69, p.95; app notes 1:178 (sub 6, 7)
## SUB 4 | Education in Andhra and Hyderabad
[178:4:0] # Missionaries – the first spreaders of Western education
[178:4:1] - Western education in Andhra was **first spread by Christian missionaries** – they contributed most (APPSC G2 2011; AP History).
[178:4:2] TABLE head: Mission | Andhra centre
  [178:4:2.0] London Missionary Society | First (1805, Jammalamadugu); Kadapa centre (1824)
  [178:4:2.1] North German Society | Rajahmundry and Eluru (1843)
  [178:4:2.2] Lutherans (Father Heyer) | Guntur
  [178:4:2.3] American Baptists | Ongole (1866), Nellore, Rayalaseema
  [178:4:2.4] Church Missionary Society | Machilipatnam – Rev. Robert Turlington Noble
[178:4:3] # Coastal Andhra
[178:4:4] - **Noble School, Machilipatnam (1843):** Rev. **Robert Noble** (CMS; arrived 1841); college by **1864** – today **Noble College** (not Rajahmundry).
[178:4:5] - Central Collegiate Institute, Madras (1841) → forerunner of **Presidency College**.
[178:4:6] - **G.N. Taylor** (Sub-Collector, Godavari): Anglo-Vernacular School, **Narsapur (1852)**, branches Palakollu, Penugonda, Achanta; **Godavari District Education Scheme (1854)**.
[178:4:7] - **Rajahmundry:** second-grade college **1873** → degree college **1877**; result-based grants-in-aid from **1877–78**.
[178:4:8] - Order: Central Collegiate Institute (1841) → Noble School (1843) → Madras University (1857) → result grants (1877–78).
[178:4:9] - English education created a **reformist middle class** (e.g. **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** at Rajahmundry; Vivekavardhini 1874).
[178:4:10] - Early centres of English education in Andhra: **Machilipatnam and Rajahmundry**.
[178:4:11] # Andhra and Hyderabad institutions
[178:4:12] TABLE head: Institution | Founder | Year | Note
  [178:4:12.0] City High School / Chaderghat High School | Salar Jung I | 1870 / 1872 | General schools
  [178:4:12.1] Madrasa-e-Aliya | Salar Jung I | 1873 | Hyderabad; for sons of nobles (Madrasa-e-Aizza 1878 – royal family)
  [178:4:12.2] Nizam College | Merger of Chaderghat High School and Madrasa-e-Aliya | 1887 | Principal Aghorenath Chattopadhyaya
  [178:4:12.3] Deccan Education Society | Agarkar, Tilak, Chiplunkar, Namjoshi | 1884 | → Fergusson College (1885)
  [178:4:12.4] Andhra Jatheeya Kalasala (National College) | Hanumanta Rao, Krishna Rao, Pattabhi | 1910 | Machilipatnam; Home Rule protests (1917)
  [178:4:12.5] Osmania University | Mir Osman Ali Khan | 1918 | First Indian university with an Indian language (Urdu) medium
  [178:4:12.6] Andhra University | Act 1925 | 1926 | Opened at Bezawada; to Waltair 1930; first VC C.R. Reddy
  [178:4:12.7] Sri Venkateswara University | Andhra State (CM T. Prakasam) | 1954 | Tirupati
  [178:4:12.8] Vijayarama Gana Pathasala | Vizianagaram | Music college from 1953 | Playback singer P. Susheela studied here
[178:4:13] - **⚠ Disputed:** Osmania – most books **1918**; the Nizam's founding firman was issued in **1917**.
[178:4:14] - **Mir Osman Ali Khan (Asaf Jah VII):** named **world's richest man by TIME** (about US$2 billion, early 1940s); large donations to **AMU and BHU**; he did **not** set up Santiniketan (Tagore's, Bengal).

## SUB 5 | Aims and Effects of British Education Policy
[178:5:0] # Why the British spread modern education
[178:5:1] - **Main reason:** a **cheap supply of educated Indians for subordinate posts** in administration and British firms – hence English as the medium.
[178:5:2] - Also: pressure from enlightened Indians, missionaries, humanitarian officials; a market for British goods; reconciling Indians to British rule.
[178:5:3] # Effects
[178:5:4] - English education brought Indians **into contact with Western thought** – science, reason, liberty – which fed the socio-cultural renaissance and nationalism.
[178:5:5] - Mass education neglected (illiteracy 84% in 1911); women's and technical education neglected; education a monopoly of upper classes.
[178:5:6] # Technical education
[178:5:7] - **Engineering College, Roorkee (1847)** – later **Thomason College** – India's **first engineering college**; Calcutta College of Engineering 1856; Poona 1858.
[178:5:8] - First medical college: Calcutta, 1835; Curzon set up the agriculture college at **Pusa**.
[178:5:9] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.597, p.604-605; app notes 1:178
