## SUB 0 | Railways – First Lines, Purpose and the Guarantee System
[179:0:0] # Firsts
[179:0:1] TABLE head: Milestone | Year | Fact
  [179:0:1.0] First passenger train | 16 April 1853 | Bori Bunder (Bombay) → Thane, 34 km, 14 coaches, 3 locomotives; built by the Great Indian Peninsula Railway Company
  [179:0:1.1] Dalhousie's Railway Minute | 1853 | Trunk-line network for military, commercial and administrative purposes
  [179:0:1.2] First line in Eastern India / West Bengal | 1854 | Howrah → Hooghly
  [179:0:1.3] First line in North India | – | Delhi → Agra
  [179:0:1.4] First line in South India | 1 July 1856 | Royapuram (Madras) → Wallajah Road (Arcot); Madras Railway Company
  [179:0:1.5] First railway in Andhra | 1862 | Puttur–Renigunta
  [179:0:1.6] Passenger trains in England | 1825 | Stockton and Darlington Railway
[179:0:2] - **Governor-General:** **Lord Dalhousie** – railways laid in his time; he is linked with the first train (not Bentinck, Ripon, Curzon).
[179:0:3] - **Credit:** railways, post and telegraph = **Dalhousie**; **state railways = Mayo**.
[179:0:4] # Who built them and why
[179:0:5] - **Initially built and run by private British companies** under the **guarantee system** – a **5% minimum return** on capital, **paid from Indian revenues** whether or not the lines made a profit; the state built lines itself from **1869**.
[179:0:6] - **Official reasons:** faster movement, communication, administration, **troop movement**.
[179:0:7] - **Colonial economic purpose:** carry **raw materials to the ports** and **British goods into Indian markets**; market for British capital goods.
[179:0:8] - **Unintended effects:** a **national market**, shared travel across castes, faster nationalist mobilisation.
[179:0:9] - **Karl Marx (1853):** the railway system would become in India "truly the **forerunner of modern industry**".
[179:0:10] - **Indian Railways** – the **biggest enterprise of the Government of India** today.
[179:0:11] - Nationalist economic critique: **Indian capitalists** demanded "**Indian domination of Indian markets**".
[179:0:12] # Railways in Hyderabad State
[179:0:13] - **Wadi–Secunderabad line** (Nizam's Guaranteed State Railway): built **1871–74**, opened **9 October 1874** (NextGen says 1878; printed key 1872 – both wrong).
[179:0:14] - **Chanda Railway agitation (1883):** protest against extending the **Nizam's State Railway** to Chanda (Chandrapur) on terms favouring a London company; led by **Dr Aghorenath Chattopadhyaya** (Principal) – deported **20 May 1883**; the first public political agitation in Hyderabad.
[179:0:15] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.107; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.77-78, p.180; NextGen Modern L3 Part 4 p.3, p.5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nizam%27s_Guaranteed_State_Railway; app notes 1:179 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 1 | Early Newspapers and Raja Ram Mohan Roy
[179:1:0] # First papers
[179:1:1] - **First printing press:** **Goa, 1556**, Portuguese **Jesuits**; movable-type press invented by **Johannes Gutenberg** (c. 1440).
[179:1:2] TABLE head: Paper | Year | Founder / editor | Note
  [179:1:2.0] Bengal Gazette (Calcutta General Advertiser) | 1780 | James Augustus Hicky (Irishman) | First newspaper in India, English weekly; seized for criticising the government
  [179:1:2.1] Digdarshan | 1818 | Serampore | First Bengali monthly
  [179:1:2.2] Sambad Kaumudi | 1821 | Ram Mohan Roy | Bengali weekly
  [179:1:2.3] Mirat-ul-Akhbar | 1822 | Ram Mohan Roy | First journal in Persian
  [179:1:2.4] Jam-i-Jahan Numa | 1822 | An English firm | First Urdu paper
  [179:1:2.5] Bombay Samachar | 1822 | – | First Gujarati paper
  [179:1:2.6] Samachar Chandrika | 1822 | Bhavani Charan Bandyopadhyay | Opposed Roy's religious and social ideas
  [179:1:2.7] Udant Martand | 1826 | Jugal Kishore Shukla | First Hindi newspaper
  [179:1:2.8] Hindoo Patriot | 1853 | Girish Chandra Ghosh; later Harish Chandra Mukherjee | First English paper by Indians; Mukherjee backed the Indigo Movement
  [179:1:2.9] Som Prakash | 1858 | Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (Dwarkanath Vidyabhushan, editor) | Indigo farmers
  [179:1:2.10] Indian Mirror | 1861–62 | Debendranath Tagore, Manmohan Ghosh | Calcutta; first Indian daily in English
  [179:1:2.11] The Bengalee | 1862 | Girish Chandra Ghosh; from 1879 Surendranath Banerjea | English
  [179:1:2.12] The Pioneer | 1865 | George Allen | Allahabad – not Gandhi
  [179:1:2.13] Amrita Bazar Patrika | 1868 | Sisir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh | Jessore, Bengali; turned English overnight (1878)
  [179:1:2.14] Tahzeeb-ul-Akhlaq | 1870 | Sir Syed Ahmad Khan | Urdu
  [179:1:2.15] The Hindu | 1878 | G. Subramania Iyer, M. Veeraraghavachariar and others | Madras, English
  [179:1:2.16] Kesari / Maharatta | 1881 | Tilak | Marathi / English
[179:1:3] # Raja Ram Mohan Roy
[179:1:4] - Opposed the **Jury Act of 1826** (non-Christians could not sit on juries trying Christians).
[179:1:5] - Closed **Mirat-ul-Akhbar** in protest against the **1823 Licensing Regulations**.
[179:1:6] - Also founded Hindu College (1817, with David Hare), Vedanta College (1825).
[179:1:7] > Trap: Mirat = **Persian**; Sambad Kaumudi = **Bengali**; Tahzeeb-ul-Akhlaq = **Urdu**; first English paper of Indians = **Hindoo Patriot**, not The Hindu.

## SUB 3 | Press Laws and the Vernacular Press Act, 1878
[179:3:0] # Press laws in sequence
[179:3:1] TABLE head: Law | Year | Governor-General | Provision
  [179:3:1.0] Censorship of Press Act | 1799 | Wellesley | Wartime pre-censorship; papers to print names of printer, editor and proprietor (the first press regulations)
  [179:3:1.1] Licensing Regulations | 1823 | John Adams (acting) | Press without licence a penal offence; Mirat-ul-Akhbar stopped
  [179:3:1.2] Press Act (Metcalfe Act) | 1835 | Charles Metcalfe | Repealed 1823 rules – "liberator of the Indian press"
  [179:3:1.3] Licensing Act | 1857 | Canning | Emergency of the revolt
  [179:3:1.4] Registration Act | 1867 | John Lawrence | Printer, publisher and place on every book/paper; copy to government
  [179:3:1.5] Sedition, Sec. 124A IPC | 1870 | Mayo | "Exciting disaffection"
  [179:3:1.6] Vernacular Press Act | 1878 | Lytton | Gagging Act
  [179:3:1.7] Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act | 1908 | Minto II | Magistrates could seize presses
  [179:3:1.8] Indian Press Act | 1910 | Minto II | Revived the worst VPA features – security deposits
[179:3:2] - **Acts to control the press:** **1835, 1867, 1878, 1908**.
[179:3:3] - Press censorship was **primarily implemented** by **Wellesley** (1799); Hastings relaxed it in 1818.
[179:3:4] - 1908 and 1910 Acts are both Minto II era but **not cause and effect**.
[179:3:5] - Annie Besant's papers had to deposit Rs 2,000, then Rs 10,000 under the Press Act (1916–17).
[179:3:6] # Vernacular Press Act, 1878
[179:3:7] - Passed **14 March 1878** under **Lord Lytton**, **modelled on the Irish Press Laws**, to **control Indian-language newspapers** (not to encourage them).
[179:3:8] - **Background:** criticism of Lytton over the **1876–77 famine** and the costly **Delhi Durbar (1877)**.
[179:3:9] - **Provisions:** the **district magistrate** (without prior government permission) could make printers/publishers sign a **bond**, demand **forfeitable security**, **seize presses** for repeat offences; **no appeal** to a court; exemption only by **submitting proofs to a government censor**.
[179:3:10] - **Discriminatory:** applied **only to vernacular papers**, not English ones; about 20 English and 200 vernacular papers in 1878 (textbook figure).
[179:3:11] - **Evasion:** **Amrita Bazar Patrika** turned into an **English paper overnight**.
[179:3:12] - Proceedings under it: Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash, Samachar.
[179:3:13] - **Repeal:** **1882** by **Lord Ripon**; pre-censorship dropped, a **press commissioner** appointed.
[179:3:14] # Year matching and chronology
[179:3:15] TABLE head: Act / policy | Year | Viceroy
  [179:3:15.0] Wood's Despatch | 1854 | Dalhousie
  [179:3:15.1] Vernacular Press Act | 1878 | Lytton
  [179:3:15.2] First Factory Act | 1881 | Ripon
  [179:3:15.3] Repeal of VPA; Hunter Commission | 1882 | Ripon
  [179:3:15.4] Famine Code; Ilbert Bill | 1883 | Ripon
[179:3:16] - **APPSC G1 2023:** Famine Code 1883, VPA 1878, Wood 1854, Factory Act 1881.
[179:3:17] - **Order:** Dramatic Performances Act (1876) → **VPA (1878)** → Bengal Tenancy Act (1885) → NWP and Oudh Act (1890).
[179:3:18] - **Order:** Ban on Sati (1829) → Wood's Despatch (1854) → VPA (1878) → Rowlatt Act (1919).
[179:3:19] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.589-594; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.163, p.167; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.66; app notes 1:179 (sub 5-7)

## SUB 5 | Telegraph, Post and the Press Today
[179:5:0] # Telegraph and post
[179:5:1] - **First telegraph line:** Calcutta → **Diamond Harbour**, **W.B. O'Shaughnessy** (experimental 1850; opened **1851**); Calcutta–Agra 1853.
[179:5:2] - Telegraph trunk lines linked Calcutta, Bombay, Madras and Peshawar (Dalhousie); **India–Europe telegraph 1865** (John Lawrence, 1864–69).
[179:5:3] - **Post Office Act 1854 (Dalhousie):** **postage stamps** and a **uniform rate** (half anna a letter) regardless of distance.
[179:5:4] - **First stamps:** **Scinde Dawk (1852)**, Karachi; the first all-India stamps (1854) were printed at the **Survey of India** (Surveyor General's) office, Calcutta.
[179:5:5] # Press today (as of 2026)
[179:5:6] - **Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023** replaced the **1867** Act (in force 1 March 2024); the RNI is now the **Press Registrar General of India**.
[179:5:7] - **World Press Freedom Index 2026 (RSF, 30 April 2026):** India **157th of 180**.
[179:5:8] - **Press Council** (Press Council Act, **1978**) has no punitive powers.
[179:5:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.78-79; Oct Latest Daily CA 22 Oct 2026 p.6; https://scroll.in/latest/1092488/india-ranks-157-out-of-180-countries-in-2026-world-press-freedom-index; app notes 1:179 (sub 0, 11)

=== NOTES 1:180 | Administrative Changes – Civil Services, Army, Police, Judiciary, Local Self-government
## SUB 0 | Local Self-Government – Madras 1688, Mayo 1870, Ripon 1882
[180:0:0] # Milestones
[180:0:1] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [180:0:1.0] 29 Sep 1688 | Madras – first Municipal Corporation in India (charter 30 Dec 1687); now Greater Chennai Corporation, the oldest
  [180:0:1.1] 1726 | Corporations at Bombay and Calcutta
  [180:0:1.2] 1817 | Lottery Committee, Calcutta – town planning with lottery funds (Strand Road, Dalhousie Square)
  [180:0:1.3] 1864-68 | First local bodies – nominated members, headed by District Magistrates; seen as tax tools
  [180:0:1.4] 1870 | Mayo's Resolution – financial decentralisation
  [180:0:1.5] 1882 | Ripon's Resolution (18 May 1882) – "Magna Carta" of LSG
  [180:0:1.6] 1872 | Bombay Municipal Act – half the Corporation members elected by ratepayers; drafted and backed by citizens led by Pherozeshah Mehta
  [180:0:1.7] 1899 | Calcutta Corporation (Municipal) Act – Curzon: reduced the elected members, increased nominated ones; 28 members resigned in protest
  [180:0:1.8] 1907-09 | Royal Commission on Decentralisation (chairman C.E.H. Hobhouse) – stressed village panchayats; only recommendations
  [180:0:1.9] 1919 | LSG a transferred subject under dyarchy (finance stayed reserved)
  [180:0:1.10] 1924 | Cantonments Act – passed by the Central legislature
  [180:0:1.11] 1935 | LSG a provincial subject
[180:0:2] - **Father of Local Self-Government in India = Lord Ripon** (Viceroy 1880-84) – not Mayo, Lytton, Curzon, Canning, Dalhousie, Cornwallis or Macaulay.
[180:0:3] - **Not correctly matched (UPRO 2017):** Local self-government – **Lytton** ✘ (it is Ripon); Doctrine of Lapse – Dalhousie ✔; Permanent Settlement – Cornwallis ✔.
[180:0:4] - **APPSC G2 2025 statements:** Cantonments Act 1924 by the Central legislature, Madras corporation 1688, Ripon father of LSG – **all three correct**.
[180:0:5] # Mayo vs Ripon
[180:0:6] TABLE head: Mayo (1869-72) | Ripon (1880-84)
  [180:0:6.0] Resolution 1870 | Resolution 1882
  [180:0:6.1] First step to bifurcate Central and Provincial finances: provinces got fixed grants for police, jails, education, medical services, roads, to run as they liked, and were told to raise local taxes | Local boards with non-official majority, elected where possible; non-official chairmen; official control only to revise, not dictate
  [180:0:6.2] "Local interest, supervision and care are necessary" for funds on education, sanitation, medical relief, local works | Local bodies as an instrument of political and popular education
  [180:0:6.3] Also statistical survey and first census (1872) | Father of LSG; also repealed Vernacular Press Act, Hunter Commission (1882), Ilbert Bill
[180:0:7] - **Mayo's Resolution 1870 statements (State PSC):** first step bifurcating central/provincial finances; provinces empowered to administer certain services; meant to correct the imbalance and meet the actual needs of provinces → **all four correct**.
[180:0:8] - **After Ripon:** elected members stayed a **minority** in district boards, franchise narrow, bodies **short of money and under official control** (could be suspended or superseded).
[180:0:9] - **Curzon and LSG (UPRO 2023):** Curzon's **Calcutta Municipal Act 1899** is the safe statement; he spoke of British rule as a message "carved in granite" (1904).
[180:0:10] > Madras 1688 → Bombay/Calcutta 1726 → Mayo 1870 → Ripon 1882 → Hobhouse 1907-09 → 1919 transferred → 1924 Cantonments → 1935 provincial.
[180:0:11] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. ch.40 p.569 (file p.117); PMF Modern History Part 3 p.212-213; Spectrum Modern India p.559-561; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.4; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.96; Rocket Polity p.5, p.94; old app notes row 180
## SUB 1 | ICS Indianisation – First Indians, Age Limits, Commissions, Simultaneous Exam
[180:1:0] # Chronology
[180:1:1] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [180:1:1.0] 1853 | Charter Act – open competition ends Directors' patronage
  [180:1:1.1] 1854 | Macaulay Committee – exam in London; preference for Oxford/Cambridge graduates
  [180:1:1.2] 1861 | Indian Civil Service Act – posts reserved for covenanted servants; limited Indian entry, mainly uncovenanted posts (7 years' residence, local-language exam)
  [180:1:1.3] 1863/1864 | Satyendranath Tagore – first Indian in the ICS (qualified 1863, joined 1864; posted to the Bombay Presidency)
  [180:1:1.4] 1869 | Surendranath Banerjea selected; disqualified over age, restored by court, then dismissed for a minor judicial error
  [180:1:1.5] 1878 | Lytton cut the maximum age to 19
  [180:1:1.6] 1878-79 | Statutory Civil Service (Lytton) – one-sixth of covenanted posts for Indians of high families by nomination; abolished
  [180:1:1.7] 1885 | INC demands higher age and simultaneous exams from its first session
  [180:1:1.8] 1886-87 | Aitchison Commission (Dufferin)
  [180:1:1.9] 1892 | Age raised to 23 (21-23) after Aitchison
  [180:1:1.10] 1906 | Age limits raised to 22-24
  [180:1:1.11] 1912-15 | Islington Commission (Hardinge II) – Indianisation of higher posts
  [180:1:1.12] 1919 | Montford Report / GoI Act 1919 – separate ICS exam in India
  [180:1:1.13] 1922 | Exam held simultaneously in India (Allahabad, Feb 1922) and England
  [180:1:1.14] 1923-24 | Lee Commission (Reading)
  [180:1:1.15] 1 Oct 1926 | Public Service Commission set up (chairman Sir Ross Barker)
  [180:1:1.16] 1935 | GoI Act 1935 – Federal PSC + Provincial PSCs
  [180:1:1.17] 1 Jan 1941 | Indians (617) outnumbered Europeans (585) in the ICS
  [180:1:1.18] 1947 / 1950 | ICS → IAS; UPSC
[180:1:2] - **Age ladder:** **23** (1859) → 22 (1860) → 21 (1866) → **19** (1878) → **23** (1892) → **24** (22-24, 1906). "Raised to 24" = **1906**, not 1892.
[180:1:3] - **Dismissed / "unjustly turned out" of the ICS:** **Surendranath Banerjea** – not Satyendranath Tagore, R.C. Dutt or Subhas Bose (Bose resigned in 1921).
[180:1:4] - **Sardar Patel** called the civil service the **"Steel Frame"** of India.
[180:1:5] # Commissions
[180:1:6] TABLE head: Commission | Year | Viceroy | Main point
  [180:1:6.0] Aitchison | 1886 | Dufferin | Dropped covenanted/uncovenanted; Imperial, Provincial, Subordinate services; strengthened the provincial service; abolished Statutory Civil Service; age 23; opposed simultaneous exams
  [180:1:6.1] Islington | 1912-15 | Hardinge II | Indianisation of higher posts (25% reserved)
  [180:1:6.2] Lee | 1923-24 | Reading | 50:50 Indian-European parity in ICS within 15 years; independent Public Service Commission
[180:1:7] - **Aitchison suggested (APPSC AEE):** **c** (strengthen provincial services) and **d** (Imperial, Provincial, Subordinate) – not **a** (high-family nominees = Lytton's Statutory Civil Service, which it abolished) or **b** (it rejected simultaneous exams) → **"c and d"**.
[180:1:8] - **Formation of the "Civil Service of India" (Imperial/Provincial/Subordinate):** the **Aitchison** Commission – not Whitley (labour), Butler (princely states) or Sapru.
[180:1:9] - **Equalisation of Indians and Europeans in the ICS:** **Lee Commission** – not Simon, Cabinet Mission or the Queen's Proclamation.
[180:1:10] - **Simultaneous exam recommended by:** the **Montagu-Chelmsford Report** – Aitchison opposed it; Hobhouse was on decentralisation.
[180:1:11] > Aitchison = three-tier services; Islington = Indianisation; Lee = 50:50 + PSC. PSC 1926 came after Lee (1924). Simultaneous exam: demanded 1885, provided by 1919 Act, held 1922.
[180:1:12] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.546-549; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.2-5; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.68 (Sheet #107), p.95; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.3, p.45; GKToday "Public Service Commission in Colonial India"; old app notes row 180
## SUB 2 | Ilbert Bill, 1883 – Indian Judges and European Offenders
[180:2:0] - **Viceroy:** **Ripon**; drafted by **Law Member C.P. Ilbert**.
[180:2:1] - **Aim:** remove the **disqualification of Indian magistrates** – let Indian **district magistrates and sessions judges** try **European British subjects** in **criminal cases**; Indians and Europeans **on par in criminal jurisdiction**.
[180:2:2] - **Not:** restrictions on carrying arms (Arms Act 1878), on vernacular newspapers (Vernacular Press Act 1878), civil service exams in India, or the cotton import duty.
[180:2:3] - **Opposition:** fierce European agitation = the **"White Mutiny"**.
[180:2:4] - **Outcome (1884):** diluted – a European tried by an Indian judge could demand a **jury of at least half Europeans**.
[180:2:5] - **Indian Association** **backed** the Bill; Indians learnt the value of organised all-India agitation.
[180:2:6] > Ilbert Bill = racial equality in **criminal** jurisdiction; asked by UPSC 2003 and 2013.
[180:2:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.19; Spectrum Modern India p.275, p.278; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.4, p.43; old app notes row 180
## SUB 3 | Judiciary – Hastings, Cornwallis Code, High Courts
[180:3:0] TABLE head: Governor-General / Act | Reform
  [180:3:0.0] Warren Hastings (1772) | District Diwani Adalat (civil, under the Collector) and Faujdari Adalat (criminal); Sadar Diwani and Sadar Nizamat Adalats
  [180:3:0.1] Regulating Act 1773 | Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774); first Chief Justice Sir Elijah Impey
  [180:3:0.2] Cornwallis Code 1793 | Collector lost judicial powers (only revenue collector); post of District Judge; separation of revenue and justice; 4 provincial courts of appeal at Calcutta, Dacca, Murshidabad, Patna
  [180:3:0.3] Bentinck | Abolished provincial courts of appeal and circuit (work to Commissioners); separate Sadar courts at Allahabad; vernacular/English replaced Persian
[180:3:1] - **Why 1793:** Cornwallis was **alarmed at the power concentrated in the Collector** and kept judicial and revenue work apart (UPSC 2010).
[180:3:2] - **Established the judicial organisation in India:** **Lord Cornwallis** (Cornwallis Code) – not Mayo, Curzon or Attlee.
[180:3:3] TABLE head: Code / Act | Year
  [180:3:3.0] Judicial Committee of the Privy Council | 1833
  [180:3:3.1] Code of Civil Procedure | 1859
  [180:3:3.2] Indian Penal Code | 1860
  [180:3:3.3] Code of Criminal Procedure | 1861
  [180:3:3.4] Indian High Courts Act | 1861 – High Courts replaced the Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats
  [180:3:3.5] High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras | 1862, by Letters Patent under Crown authority (Canning)
  [180:3:3.6] Allahabad High Court | 1866
  [180:3:3.7] Federal Court | GoI Act 1935 (set up 1937)
[180:3:4] - **⚠ Year of the first High Courts:** **1862** (NextGen Rocket, PMF); Spectrum prints **1865** – a PYQ offering only 1853/1856/1858/1865 needs **1862** added.
[180:3:5] - **AP angle:** the **Andhra petitions** of the 1850s asked for trained judges, police separate from revenue officials and Indians in higher posts. Jun 2026: AP approved **Rs 130.38 crore** for phase-1 of the **AP Judicial Academy**.
[180:3:6] > Hastings = Collector **gets** the civil adalat; Cornwallis = Collector **loses** judicial powers; Bentinck = **abolishes** appeal courts.
[180:3:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.553-555; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.106 (Sheet #134); PMF Modern History Part 3 p.11-13; old app notes row 180
## SUB 4 | Madras Presidency Rural Local Boards – Cesses and Taluk Boards
[180:4:0] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [180:4:0.0] 1863 | Madras Education Cess Act (Act VI of 1863) – school cess; the first enactment for rural local purposes
  [180:4:0.1] 1864 / 1866 | Village cess (village establishment) / District Roads Cess Act
  [180:4:0.2] 1871 | Madras Local Funds Act – Local Fund Boards first constituted; cess of one anna per rupee of land revenue for roads, schools, hospitals; repealed the 1863 and 1866 cesses; two-thirds of the land cess for roads
  [180:4:0.3] 1878 | Madras Act I of 1878 – local cess raised from one to two annas (Malabar)
  [180:4:0.4] 1884 | Madras Local Boards Act – three tiers: district board, taluk board, union
  [180:4:0.5] 1920 | Madras Local Boards Act + Madras Village Panchayats Act – three tiers kept
  [180:4:0.6] 1934 | Madras Local Boards (Amendment) – taluk boards abolished; reason usually given: serious financial problems (too weak beside the district boards); elementary schools went back to district boards
[180:4:1] > AP Panchayat Secretary angle: 1863 education cess → 1871 one anna → 1884 three tiers → 1934 taluk boards abolished.
[180:4:2] ~~ Sources: M. Venkatarangaiya, "Functions of Local Boards", Triveni Jul-Aug 1929 (wisdomlib.org); HC Deb 24 May 1880 (Malabar local cess, api.parliament.uk); web search summaries on 1934 (scribd chapter, not verified); old app notes row 180
## SUB 5 | Company-era Civil Service – Cornwallis and Fort William College
[180:5:0] - **Lord Cornwallis** (1786-93) = **"Father of Civil Services in India"**: created the **Covenanted Civil Service**; **raised salaries**, banned **private trade and gifts**, promotion by **seniority**.
[180:5:1] - **Wellesley** ("Bengal Tiger") set up the **College of Fort William, Calcutta, in 1800** (minute of 10 July 1800; PMF gives 24 Nov 1800) **to train British civilians (Company recruits) for administration** – languages (Persian, Hindustani), law, literature.
[180:5:2]   - **UPSC 2020:** purpose = **train British civilians for administrative purposes** – not a Directors' order (they **disapproved**), not oriental revival, not jobs for William Carey (who taught Bengali there).
[180:5:3]   - **UPRO 2021:** "founded 10 **June** 1800" ✘; "to teach Indian languages to British officers" ✔ → **only 2**.
[180:5:4] - **1806:** replaced by the **East India College, Haileybury** (England) – law, political economy, Indian languages.
[180:5:5] - **1833:** Charter Act – Law Commission under **T.B. Macaulay**; codification. **1853:** Charter Act ended Directors' **patronage** (open competition; Trevelyan, Robert Lowe); power passed to the Crown only in 1858.
[180:5:6] - **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** (1832, evidence before Parliament) = first Indian to **demand** Indians in higher posts. Bentinck = modern Western education.
[180:5:7] - ICS → **IAS** (direct successor).
[180:5:8] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.545-546, p.595; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.4, p.29; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.66; old app notes row 180
## SUB 6 | Police and Army
[180:6:0] # Police
[180:6:1] TABLE head: Introducer | Reform
  [180:6:1.0] Cornwallis (1791-93) | Took police duties from zamindars; thanas (circles of 20-30 sq miles) under an Indian daroga; kotwal kept in towns
  [180:6:1.1] Munro – Judicial Commission 1814-18 | Police under the Collector; minor crimes tried by village officers (village munsif)
  [180:6:1.2] Police Commission 1860 → Police Act 1861 (Canning) | Royal Irish Constabulary model; IG (province), DIG (range), SP (district); meant to crush dissent
  [180:6:1.3] Curzon – Police Commission 1902-03 | Chairman Sir Andrew Fraser; CID in provinces, Central Intelligence Bureau
[180:6:2] - **Daroga** = the local face of the **"aura and authority of Company Bahadur"** (UPRO 2021); appointed and supervised by the Magistrate; notorious for misuse of power – not the kotwal, amala or zamindar.
[180:6:3] - **Thomas Munro:** President of the Judicial Commission (1814-18); **Governor of Madras 1820-27**; extended **Ryotwari**. Madras Presidency governed Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema.
[180:6:4] # Army after 1857
[180:6:5] TABLE head: Body | Year | Point
  [180:6:5.0] Peel Commission | 1859 | More European troops: Bengal 1 European : 2 Indians; Madras/Bombay 1 : 3 (ratio finally fixed at 2 : 5 there); artillery with Europeans
  [180:6:5.1] Eden Commission | 1879 (Lytton) | Amalgamate the three presidency armies
  [180:6:5.2] Presidency armies abolished | 1 April 1895 | One Indian Army under four commands
[180:6:6] - **Policy:** "balance and counterpoise", martial-race theory (Sikhs, Gurkhas, Pathans); no Indian officers till 1918.
[180:6:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.549-552; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.8; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.5-6; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.4; old app notes row 180

=== NOTES 1:181 | Revolt of 1857 – Political Causes
## SUB 0 | Doctrine of Lapse – Dalhousie's Annexations (1848-56)
[181:0:0] - **Rule:** a dependent state whose ruler died **without a natural male heir** lapsed to the Company; an **adopted son** could inherit the ruler's **private property only**, not the throne.
[181:0:1] - **Lord Dalhousie** (1848-56) applied it with zeal, but he was **not its originator** (earlier cases existed). Announced/first applied **1848**.
[181:0:2] TABLE head: State | Year
  [181:0:2.0] Satara (FIRST) | 1848
  [181:0:2.1] Jaitpur (Bundelkhand) | 1849
  [181:0:2.2] Sambalpur (Orissa) | 1849
  [181:0:2.3] Baghat | 1850
  [181:0:2.4] Udaipur (Chhattisgarh) | 1852
  [181:0:2.5] Jhansi (adopted son Damodar Rao not recognised) | 1854
  [181:0:2.6] Nagpur (Bhonsle, Raghuji III) | 1854
[181:0:3] - **Chronology:** **Satara (1848) → Sambalpur (1849) → Jhansi (1854)**.
[181:0:4] - **Not annexed under lapse:** **Jaipur**, **Bharatpur**, "Karnataka" – and **Awadh** (misgovernment) and **Punjab** (conquest).
[181:0:5] - **Kittur (1824):** an earlier refusal to recognise an adopted son – **Rani Chennamma** fought the British.
[181:0:6] - **Withdrawn** by **Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858)**, read by **Canning** at the **Allahabad Durbar**; adoption accepted; princes guaranteed in return for **paramountcy**.
[181:0:7] - Canning called the loyal princes **"breakwaters to the storm"**.
[181:0:8] > A-R (CDS 2009): the revolt broke out soon after Dalhousie left (1856), and his **annexationist policy** caused great discontent – R explains A.
[181:0:9] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.156-157, p.201; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.37; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.132, p.156; app notes 1:181; years of Jaitpur and Udaipur: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 1 | Annexation of Awadh (1856) – the "Misgovernment" Plea
[181:1:0] - **Awadh annexed Feb 1856** by Dalhousie on the ground of **"misgovernment" (maladministration)** – **not** lapse, war or subsidiary alliance.
[181:1:1] - Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was **dethroned and exiled to Calcutta**; the British accused him of **failing to control the rebellious chiefs and taluqdars** (after the 1801 Subsidiary Alliance he had no army of his own).
[181:1:2] - He was in fact widely loved; his couplet **"Dar-o-deewar pe hasrat se nazar karte hain, khush raho ahle-watan hum to safar karte hain"** was later sung by revolutionaries.
[181:1:3] - **Summary Revenue Settlement 1856** – made directly with **village proprietors**; **taluqdars** were **disarmed, forts destroyed**, estates confiscated (taluqdars' share of villages fell from 67% to 38%).
[181:1:4] - **Bengal Army** sepoys hurt – Awadh was their home; their **families bore the new revenue burden**.
[181:1:5] TABLE head: Annexation | Year | Ground
  [181:1:5.0] Satara | 1848 | Doctrine of Lapse
  [181:1:5.1] Punjab | 1849 | Conquest (Second Anglo-Sikh War; Duleep Singh)
  [181:1:5.2] Jhansi | 1854 | Doctrine of Lapse
  [181:1:5.3] Awadh | 1856 | Misgovernment
[181:1:6] > Pairs: Satara **1848** (not 1849), Punjab **1849** (not 1848), Jhansi **1854** (not 1855), Awadh **1856** – correct.
[181:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.132, p.135-136; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.37; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.157; app notes 1:181
## SUB 2 | Mughal Emperor, Nana Saheb and Other Princely Grievances
[181:2:0] TABLE head: Measure | Detail
  [181:2:0.0] Dalhousie (1849) | Bahadur Shah's successors to leave the Red Fort (move to the Qutub, Mehrauli)
  [181:2:0.1] Canning (1856) | Successors to lose the imperial title and be mere princes
  [181:2:0.2] Titles abolished (1855) | Carnatic Nawab, Tanjore Raja
  [181:2:0.3] Pension denied | Nana Saheb, adopted son of Baji Rao II (last Peshwa)
  [181:2:0.4] Jhansi | Rani Lakshmibai – adopted son refused the throne
  [181:2:0.5] Awadh | Begum Hazrat Mahal – annexation; proclaimed son Birjis Qadr ruler
[181:2:1] - The policy of annexation made **Nana Saheb, the Rani of Jhansi and Bahadur Shah** staunch enemies; fear of annexation **turned a sepoy mutiny into a wider revolt**.
[181:2:2] TABLE head: Centre | Leader | British opponent
  [181:2:2.0] Delhi | Bahadur Shah II | John Nicholson (recaptured Delhi)
  [181:2:2.1] Kanpur | Nana Saheb (Peshwa, 5 June 1857) | Colin Campbell
  [181:2:2.2] Lucknow | Begum Hazrat Mahal | Colin Campbell
  [181:2:2.3] Bareilly | Khan Bahadur Khan | –
  [181:2:2.4] Faizabad | Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah (from Chinapattan, Madras) | –
  [181:2:2.5] Auwa | Thakur Kushal Singh | –
  [181:2:2.6] Assam | Maniram Dutt | –
  [181:2:2.7] Jagdishpur (Bihar) | Kunwar Singh | –
[181:2:3] - The revolt **began at Meerut** (10 May 1857).
[181:2:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.131-132; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.201-202; Rocket Indian History Part 2 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-02.txt) p.90; app notes 1:181
## SUB 3 | Subsidiary Alliance – Background (Wellesley, 1798)
[181:3:0] - Ruler keeps a **British subsidiary force at his cost**, accepts a **Resident**, gives up an **independent foreign policy** (no other Europeans in service).
[181:3:1] TABLE head: State | Year
  [181:3:1.0] Nizam of Hyderabad (FIRST) | Sep 1798, again 1800
  [181:3:1.1] Mysore, Tanjore | 1799
  [181:3:1.2] Awadh | Nov 1801
  [181:3:1.3] Peshwa | Dec 1802 (Treaty of Bassein)
  [181:3:1.4] Bhonsle / Scindia | Dec 1803 / Feb 1804
  [181:3:1.5] Holkar (last Maratha) | 1818
[181:3:2] - **AP angle:** 1800 – the Nizam ceded **Rayalaseema** to pay for the force = **"Ceded Districts"**.
[181:3:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 1:181; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.201

=== NOTES 1:182 | Revolt of 1857 – Economic, Socio-religious, Administrative and Military Causes
## SUB 0 | Military Grievances – the Sepoys Start the Revolt
[182:0:0] - The revolt **began as a mutiny of the sepoys** (not zamindars, peasants or plantation workers); **discontent of soldiers** was the first trigger; civilians joined later.
[182:0:1] TABLE head: Grievance | Detail
  [182:0:1.0] General Service Enlistment Act 1856 (Canning) | New Bengal Army recruits to serve overseas – crossing the sea meant loss of caste
  [182:0:1.1] Bhatta | Foreign service allowance stopped for service in Sindh and Punjab
  [182:0:1.2] Promotion | An Indian could rise no higher than Subedar
  [182:0:1.3] Pay | Sepoy paid much less than his British counterpart of the same rank
  [182:0:1.4] Caste marks | Ban on caste and sectarian marks, beards, turbans
  [182:0:1.5] Post Office Act 1856 | Free postage of sepoys withdrawn
  [182:0:1.6] Troop ratio | About 2,32,000 sepoys : 45,000 Europeans (about 5:1); Indians about 86% of the army
  [182:0:1.7] Awadh | "Nursery of the Bengal Army"; the largest number of rebel sepoys came from Oudh (over 75,000)
[182:0:2] - Sepoys = **"peasants in uniform"** – they carried rural grievances into the army.
[182:0:3] - European troops had been drawn off for the **Crimean and Persian wars**.
[182:0:4] - **Not a cause:** the **inefficiency of the officers** (BPSC 2018).
[182:0:5] - **Earlier mutinies:** Bengal 1764; **Vellore 1806** (new dress code, ban on caste marks and earrings); **Barrackpore Nov 1824** (**47th NI** refused to go to **Burma by sea**); 38th NI 1852; 1844 battalions over batta. The **Santhal revolt 1855-56** was a **civil**, not a sepoy, revolt.
[182:0:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.203; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.133-134, p.138; PMF Modern History Part 4 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-04.txt) p.5; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.37-38; app notes 1:182
## SUB 1 | Immediate Cause – Enfield Rifle and Greased Cartridges
[182:1:0] - **Immediate cause:** the new **Enfield rifle**; its cartridge paper, reportedly greased with **cow and pig fat**, had to be **bitten off** – offended Hindus and Muslims alike → suspicion that the British were **interfering in religion** and converting them.
[182:1:1] - Enfield **replaced the Brown Bess** musket; introduced **December 1856** (app notes; some accounts say late 1856 or Jan 1857); training at **Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot**.
[182:1:2] - **Bone-dust rumour:** the Company's **flour (atta)** was said to be mixed with **bone dust**.
[182:1:3] - **Chapatis** passed from village to village across **North India**; symbols of the revolt = **lotus and chapati**.
[182:1:4] TABLE head: Event | Date
  [182:1:4.0] 19th NI, Berhampur – refused cartridges | Feb 1857
  [182:1:4.1] Mangal Pandey (34th BNI), Barrackpore | 29 March 1857; hanged 8 April 1857
  [182:1:4.2] 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry, Meerut – 10 years' prison | 9 May 1857
  [182:1:4.3] Meerut rising | 10 May 1857
  [182:1:4.4] Rebels at Delhi proclaim Bahadur Shah II Shahenshah-e-Hindustan | 11-12 May 1857
[182:1:5] - **First martyr:** **Mangal Pandey**.
[182:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.38; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.203-204; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.138, p.152; Rocket Indian History Part 2 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-02.txt) p.91; app notes 1:182
## SUB 2 | Socio-religious Causes
[182:2:0] TABLE head: Measure | Year | Note
  [182:2:0.0] Abolition of Sati | 1829 | William Bentinck (not Dalhousie) – resented by orthodox opinion
  [182:2:0.1] Religious (Caste) Disabilities Act / Lex Loci | 1850 | A convert to Christianity could inherit ancestral property (Spectrum misprints 1856)
  [182:2:0.2] Hindu Widow Remarriage Act | 1856 | Orthodoxy resented it
[182:2:1] - **Christian missionaries** preached under **police protection**; Western education, **railways and the telegraph** fed fears of mass conversion.
[182:2:2] - After 1858 the Crown promised **religious neutrality**.
[182:2:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.38; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.134-135; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.202; app notes 1:182
## SUB 3 | Economic, Political and Administrative Causes
[182:3:0] TABLE head: Class / cause | Grievance
  [182:3:0.0] Peasants | High, rigid land revenue → debt → land lost to moneylenders and traders
  [182:3:0.1] Taluqdars of Awadh | About 21,000 dispossessed (Summary Settlement 1856)
  [182:3:0.2] Estate owners | Inam Commission (1852, Bombay) – about 20,000 estates confiscated
  [182:3:0.3] Artisans | British machine goods duty-free, Indian goods heavily taxed; loss of princely patronage
  [182:3:0.4] Annexed courts | Officials, retainers and soldiers thrown out of work
  [182:3:0.5] Administration | Corruption in police and lower courts – courts favoured the rich; Indians excluded from high posts
[182:3:1] - **"Absentee sovereignty"** and **"drain of wealth"** – transfer of resources to Britain.
[182:3:2] - Lapse (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur), Awadh "misgovernance" (Wajid Ali Shah deposed), Mughal title.
[182:3:3] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.200-202; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.37; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.135; app notes 1:182
## SUB 4 | Books on 1857 and Other Books
[182:4:0] - **Sir Syed Ahmed Khan** – **Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** ("The Causes of the Indian Revolt", written 1858, published 1859) – the **first Indian-language work** on the causes; cause: **no Indian in the Legislative Council**.

  [182:4:1.0] The Indian War of Independence, 1857 (1909) | V.D. Savarkar
  [182:4:1.1] The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857 | R.C. Majumdar

  [182:4:1.3] Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies | S.B. Chaudhuri
  [182:4:1.4] 1857: The Great Rebellion | Ashok Mehta
  [182:4:1.5] The Great Mutiny | Christopher Hibbert
  [182:4:1.6] The Peasant and the Raj | Eric Stokes
  [182:4:1.7] The Indian Mutiny of 1857 | G.B. Malleson
[182:4:2] - **P.E. Roberts:** "just a **sepoy mutiny**" over greased cartridges.

  the movement of peasants from villages to princely courts | the transfer of religious authority from temples to courts | *the transfer of economic resources from India to Britain | the migration of British officials to Indian villages
  x: Company rule was seen as 'absentee sovereignty', rule from distant Britain, under which India's wealth was drained to Britain. Both terms describe resources being transferred from India to Britain.

[n12af53b3364] sub3

  x: Annexations displaced thousands of officials, retainers and soldiers who had depended on princely courts for employment and patronage.

=== NOTES 1:185 | Nature of 1857 – the Historiographical Debate
## SUB 0 | Savarkar, Majumdar, Sen – the Indian Historians
[185:0:0] TABLE head: Historian | Verdict
  [185:0:0.0] V.D. Savarkar | "First War of Indian Independence" – a planned national war; book The Indian War of Independence 1857 (1909) – not Tilak, Patel or Ganesh Savarkar
  [185:0:0.1] R.C. Majumdar | "The so-called First National War of Independence of 1857 is neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence"; did not accept it as a revolution
  [185:0:0.2] S.N. Sen | "What began as a fight for religion ended as a war of independence"; official historian – Eighteen Fifty-Seven (1957)
  [185:0:0.3] Majumdar and Sen | Indian nationalism in the mid-19th century was embryonic; "not an organised national revolt"
  [185:0:0.4] S.B. Chaudhuri | "First War of Independence it certainly was"
  [185:0:0.5] Tara Chand | Not inspired by nationalism
  [185:0:0.6] Nehru | Essentially a feudal rising (The Discovery of India)
  [185:0:0.7] Eric Stokes | Local, elitist – many peasant and elite risings
  [185:0:0.8] Rudrangshu Mukherjee | Peasant and taluqdar resistance in Awadh (Awadh in Revolt)
[185:0:1] - Majumdar was appointed to write the official history but parted with it and published **The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857** (1957) independently.
[185:0:2] > Majumdar is the **sceptic** – never put him with Savarkar.
[185:0:3] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.212-214, p.219; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.36; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.155; app notes 1:185
## SUB 1 | British and Contemporary Views
[185:1:0] TABLE head: Holder | View
  [185:1:0.0] Sir John Lawrence, J.R. Seeley | "Mere sepoy mutiny"
  [185:1:0.1] P.E. Roberts | "Just a sepoy mutiny" over greased cartridges
  [185:1:0.2] Sir James Outram and W. Taylor | A conspiracy – Muslims (Mohammedans) exploiting Hindu grievances
  [185:1:0.3] L.E.R. Rees | War of fanatic religionists against Christians
  [185:1:0.4] T.R. Holmes | Conflict of civilisation vs barbarism
  [185:1:0.5] Benjamin Disraeli (Commons, 1857) | "Is it a military mutiny, or is it a national revolt?"
  [185:1:0.6] Karl Marx (New-York Tribune) | "In truth a national revolt"
  [185:1:0.7] Sir Syed Ahmad Khan | Cause: no Indian in the Legislative Council
  [185:1:0.8] Aitchison | "In this instance we could not play off the Mohammedans against the Hindus" – Hindu-Muslim unity of 1857
  [185:1:0.9] R. Coupland | "Indian Nationalism was the child of British Rule"
[185:1:1] - **Mirza Ghalib** – the poet who **witnessed** the revolt in Delhi.
[185:1:2] - **Joseph Noel Paton** painted **"In Memoriam"** (1858) – British women and children awaiting death.
[185:1:3] - **William Dalrymple** – **The Last Mughal: The Fall of a Dynasty, Delhi 1857** (2006).
[185:1:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.211-214, p.219; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.153; app notes 1:185; Paton, Dalrymple: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 2 | Labels and Books
[185:2:0] TABLE head: School | Label / view
  [185:2:0.0] British / imperialist | "Sepoy Mutiny" / "Indian Mutiny"
  [185:2:0.1] Indian / nationalist | "First War of Independence"
  [185:2:0.2] Feudal reaction | Dispossessed princes and taluqdars regaining lost positions
  [185:2:0.3] Others | Great Rebellion, Revolt of 1857, Indian Insurrection
[185:2:1] # Books
[185:2:2] TABLE head: Book | Author
  [185:2:2.0] The Indian War of Independence 1857 | V.D. Savarkar
  [185:2:2.1] Eighteen Fifty-Seven | S.N. Sen (Government-commissioned centenary history)
  [185:2:2.2] The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857 | R.C. Majumdar
  [185:2:2.3] 1857: The Great Rebellion | Ashok Mehta
  [185:2:2.4] The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859 | Marx and Engels
  [185:2:2.5] Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (1859) | Syed Ahmad Khan
  [185:2:2.6] Awadh in Revolt | Rudrangshu Mukherjee
[185:2:3] > All true: a widespread but unsuccessful uprising; began at **Meerut** and spread to Delhi, Agra, Kanpur, Lucknow; Western historians call it the "Indian/Sepoy Mutiny", India the "First War of Independence".
[185:2:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.211-212; PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.140-141; app notes 1:185
## SUB 3 | Nature – Statement Judgements and Hindu-Muslim Unity
[185:3:0] - Began as a **military mutiny** → became a **popular rebellion**; a **traditional uprising** of classes against a common foreign enemy – **no idea of a nation-state**.
[185:3:1] - **Not carefully planned** by rajas, nawabs and taluqdars; **rumours and prophecies did play a role** (Plassey centenary, 23 June 1857); the British did **not** control it quickly or easily.
[185:3:2] - **Rebel proclamations repeatedly appealed to all sections irrespective of caste and creed** (Azamgarh Proclamation, 25 Aug 1857 – under "Muhammad and Mahavir"; urged allegiance to the **Badshahi**).
[185:3:3] - **Hindu-Muslim unity:** **Bahadur Shah II** accepted by both as **symbolic head**; cow slaughter banned; both well represented in leadership. British response: **divide and rule** (not handing power to the INC).
[185:3:4] - **Significance:** failed, but broke the myth of British invincibility; seeds of later nationalism. Same "mutiny or revolt?" debate on the **RIN revolt** (HMIS Talwar, **1946**).
[185:3:5] - Largely confined to **North India**; most of India neutral.
[185:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.139, p.152-154; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.211; app notes 1:185
## SUB 4 | Social Groups, the Educated Class and Failure
[185:4:0] TABLE head: Group | Role
  [185:4:0.0] Sepoys | Spearhead – Meerut, Delhi
  [185:4:0.1] Awadh taluqdars, peasants, artisans | Joined (Awadh, western UP)
  [185:4:0.2] Big zamindars of Bengal | Loyal
  [185:4:0.3] Educated middle class | Remained neutral / did not support – thought British rule was modernising; a reason for failure
[185:4:1] - **Main cause of failure:** **lack of common strategy and central organisation**; limited spread; Rajput and other major rulers backed the British.
[185:4:2] - **AP:** "Andhra was little affected for want of local leaders" is true; Korukonda Subba Reddy, Dandasena, the **Kadiri** (Rayalaseema) attempt were sporadic; **Annapurnayya** ("Andhra Netaji") – 18 months RI for the article **"Chicharapidugu"** on 1857.
[185:4:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.149-151; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.209-210; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 6 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-06.txt) p.41; app notes 1:185

=== NOTES 1:186 | Consequences of 1857 – Queen's Proclamation, Government of India Act 1858, Army Reorganisation
## SUB 0 | Queen's Proclamation, 1 November 1858 – Allahabad, Objects, Promises
[186:0:0] # Basics
[186:0:1] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [186:0:1.0] Date | 1 November 1858 (not 10 May 1857, the Meerut outbreak)
  [186:0:1.1] Place | Durbar at Allahabad (Prayagraj) – not Calcutta, Bombay or Madras
  [186:0:1.2] Read by | Lord Canning – not Bentinck, Burnham or Harcourt Butler
  [186:0:1.3] Addressed to | "the Princes, Chiefs and Peoples of India"
  [186:0:1.4] Called | "Magna Carta of the Indian people"
  [186:0:1.5] Effect | Announced the assumption of the Government of India by the Crown (transfer under the Act of 2 Aug 1858)
[186:0:2] - **Objects (UPSC 2014, asked in three banks):** (1) **disclaim any intention to annex Indian States** ✔ (2) **place the Indian administration under the British Crown** ✔ (3) regulate the Company's trade ✘ – the Company had no trade left (commercial functions ended 1833) → **1 and 2 only**.
[186:0:3] - Pardon for those who laid down arms by **2 January 1859**, except those directly involved in murdering British subjects.
[186:0:4] # Promises – Kept vs Broken
[186:0:5] TABLE head: Promise | Detail | Fate
  [186:0:5.0] Princes | No further annexation; rights, dignity and honour respected; Company treaties honoured; right to adopt an heir respected | Kept – the assurance actually fulfilled (UPPCS 1994)
  [186:0:5.1] Religion | No interference in religion and social customs; no forced conversions | Kept in policy (non-interference)
  [186:0:5.2] Public service | Office open to all by merit, irrespective of race or creed | Broken – ICS stayed European
  [186:0:5.3] Laws, property | Due regard to ancient rights, usages and customs | Partly
[186:0:6] - **Right to adopt re-established = Queen's announcement of 1858** (UPPCS 2004, twice) – not the GoI Act 1858 and not a "Charter of 1860"; Canning then issued adoption *sanads* to the princes.
[186:0:7] - Equal employment was the promise broken: SoS **Kimberley** – an adequate number of civil servants "**shall always be Europeans**"; **1858–1885 = "Era of Broken Promises"**.
[186:0:8] - **Madras Native Association (1852)**, founded by **Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty**, was the first to petition against the non-implementation of the Proclamation.
[186:0:9] > Allahabad 1858 = Proclamation read by Canning; Delhi 1877 = Empress of India proclaimed under Lytton.
[186:0:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.182-183 (file p.214-215), p.539 (file p.571); PMF Modern History Part 3 p.383-384 (file p.203-206, UPSC 2014 PYQ with answer a); Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.91; NextGen modern level 2 part 2 p.3; old app notes row 186
## SUB 1 | Lord Canning – Governor-General in 1857 and First Viceroy
[186:1:0] # Canning (1856-62)
[186:1:1] - **Governor-General during the Revolt of 1857 = Lord Canning** (asked 8 times: UPSC 2006, IAS 2006, UPRO 2013, UKPSC 2016, WBCS 2017, State PSCs) – not Dalhousie (left 1856), Hardinge, Lytton, Minto, Bentinck, Hastings, Amherst, Auckland.
[186:1:2] - **First Viceroy of India = Canning** (1858) – the GoI Act 1858 gave the Governor-General the added title "Viceroy"; Clive, Cornwallis and Ripon are wrong options. Canning was the last GG of the Company and the first Viceroy of the Crown.
[186:1:3] - Made **Allahabad** the **emergency headquarters** of the government in 1857-58 and read the Proclamation there.
[186:1:4] - **White Mutiny (1859-60) under Canning:** the Company's **European troops** resented transfer to the Crown without a new bounty; their **batta** was stopped; Canning's legalistic reading of the transfer angered them; most took a free discharge and passage home.
[186:1:5] - Other Canning measures: **portfolio system (1859)**, Indian Councils Act 1861, Indian High Courts Act 1861 (High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras), Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856, withdrawal of the Doctrine of Lapse; called loyal princes "**breakwaters to the storm**".
[186:1:6] TABLE head: Title | First holder | Created by
  [186:1:6.0] Governor-General of Bengal | Warren Hastings | Regulating Act 1773
  [186:1:6.1] Governor-General of India | William Bentinck | Charter Act 1833
  [186:1:6.2] Viceroy and Governor-General | Canning | GoI Act 1858
  [186:1:6.3] Secretary of State for India | Lord Stanley | GoI Act 1858
[186:1:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.182-184 (file p.214-216, White Mutiny box); PMF Modern History Part 3 p.384 (file p.205); Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.90, p.96; old app notes row 186
## SUB 2 | Government of India Act, 1858 – Transfer to the Crown
[186:2:0] # Core change
[186:2:1] - Passed **2 August 1858** – "**Act for the Better Government of India**" (also called Act for the Good Government of India); introduced by Lord Stanley.
[186:2:2] - **Transferred the government of India from the East India Company to the British Crown** (UPPCS 2007) – not the Charter Acts of 1833/1853 or the Indian Councils Act 1861; Queen Victoria declared sovereign of British India. **Year of transfer = 1858**, not 1857, 1859 or 1947.
[186:2:3] - The Revolt "**gave a death blow to the system of East India Company rule**" (UPPCS Mains 2010) – the true statement; British writers called it a "mutiny", not Indian historians.
[186:2:4] TABLE head: Aftermath | Date
  [186:2:4.0] British recaptured Delhi | 20-21 Sept 1857
  [186:2:4.1] Rani Lakshmibai died | 18 June 1858
  [186:2:4.2] GoI Act passed | 2 Aug 1858
  [186:2:4.3] Queen's Proclamation | 1 Nov 1858
  [186:2:4.4] Peel Commission | 1859
  [186:2:4.5] East India Company dissolved | 1874
[186:2:5] - Board of Control and Court of Directors abolished → **Secretary of State for India** (cabinet minister, responsible to Parliament) with **supreme control over the Government of India** (CDS 2008) + **Council of India of 15 members** (London; abolished by the 1935 Act).
[186:2:6] - After 1870 (Suez Canal 1869, Red Sea cable 1870) the SoS became the **de facto ruler**; the Viceroy was responsible to him.
[186:2:7] TABLE head: Act | Year | What it did
  [186:2:7.0] Pitt's India Act | 1784 | Dual control – Company stayed
  [186:2:7.1] Charter Act | 1833 | GG of India (Bentinck); Company purely administrative
  [186:2:7.2] Charter Act | 1853 | Company stayed, no fixed term
  [186:2:7.3] GoI Act | 1858 | Company rule ended; Crown rule via SoS and Viceroy
  [186:2:7.4] Indian Councils Act | 1861 | After the transfer
[186:2:8] # British India and the princely states
[186:2:9] - After 1858 India had **two kinds of territory: British India** (provinces, ruled directly through governors and the Viceroy) and **Princely States** (ruled by Indian princes under **British paramountcy**). The reverse statement ("provinces under local kings, states under British rule") is **incorrect** (AP FBO 2019).
[186:2:10] - Same office-holder: **Viceroy** for the princely states, **Governor-General** for British India.
[186:2:11] # Ends and Andhra angle
[186:2:12] - **Bahadur Shah II** – proclaimed **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** by rebels; exiled to **Rangoon**, died **1862**. East India Company (charter **31 Dec 1600**) lost rule 1858, **dissolved 1874**.
[186:2:13] - **Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema** stayed in the **Madras Presidency** under the Crown; **Telangana** stayed with the **Nizam** under British suzerainty.
[186:2:14] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India p.182 (file p.214); PMF Modern History Part 3 p.383-384 (file p.203-205); NextGen modern level 2 part 2 p.3; old app notes row 186
## SUB 3 | Empress of India (1876-77) and the Delhi Durbars
[186:3:0] - **Royal Titles Act, 1876** (Disraeli; Viceroy **Lytton**): Queen Victoria **assumed the title "Empress of India" (Kaiser-i-Hind) in 1876**.
[186:3:1] - It was **proclaimed in India at the Delhi Durbar (Imperial Assemblage), 1 January 1877** – so exam keys give **1877** for "appointed/proclaimed Empress", **1876** for "under the Royal Titles Act".
[186:3:2] - **Delhi Durbars** = coronation ceremonies held **to mark the succession of an Emperor/Empress** of India – **1877, 1903, 1911** (not to listen to petitions or declare laws).
[186:3:3] > 1876 Act / title → 1 Jan 1877 Delhi proclamation (Lytton) → Durbars 1903 (Edward VII, Curzon), 1911 (George V, Hardinge).
[186:3:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.63 (Delhi Durbar 1877), p.11; Spectrum Modern India p.539 (file p.571); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 (Lytton: Royal Title Act 1876, Delhi Durbar 1877); old app notes row 186
## SUB 4 | Army Reorganisation and Divide and Rule
[186:4:0] # Peel Commission (1859)
[186:4:1] TABLE head: Measure | Detail
  [186:4:1.0] European : Indian ratio | 1:2 in the Bengal Army; 2:5 in the Madras and Bombay armies
  [186:4:1.1] Artillery | Exclusively European; key posts and officers European
  [186:4:1.2] "Division and counterpoise" | Regiments mixed by caste, community and region to balance each other
  [186:4:1.3] Recruitment | From the "martial races" – Gurkhas, Sikhs, Punjabis, Pathans (Punjab, Nepal, NWFP) who had stayed loyal – not from Awadh, Bihar, Central India, Bengal or the South (BPSC 2008)
[186:4:2] - **Army Amalgamation Scheme 1861** moved the Company's European troops to the Crown. **Eden Commission (1879)** → single **Indian Army (1895)** with **four commands**.
[186:4:3] # Other policy shifts
[186:4:4] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [186:4:4.0] Divide and rule | Muslims first blamed and targeted; later cultivated against the educated Hindu middle class
  [186:4:4.1] Landed class | Awadh taluqdars restored to proprietary rights → conservative loyalists
  [186:4:4.2] Non-interference | Reforming zeal abandoned
  [186:4:4.3] Racial attitude | Racial arrogance grew; English-educated "Babus" distrusted
[186:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.5-6; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.156; Spectrum Modern India p.183-184 (file p.215-216); old app notes row 186
## SUB 5 | Indian Councils Act, 1861 – Portfolio System
[186:5:0] - **Portfolio system:** introduced by **Canning in 1859**; the **Indian Councils Act, 1861** gave it statutory recognition – it **strengthened the Viceroy's authority over his executive council by substituting the portfolio (departmental) system for corporate functioning** (IAS 2002) – not the Acts of 1858, 1892 or 1909.
[186:5:1] - Each of the five members was placed in charge of a department (home, revenue, military, finance, law).
[186:5:2] - Lesson of 1857: associate Indians with law-making – at least **half the additional members non-official**; Viceroy's **ordinances valid six months**.
[186:5:3] - **1862:** Canning nominated the first **three Indians** – **Raja of Benares, Maharaja of Patiala, Sir Dinkar Rao**.
[186:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.388 (file p.209); old app notes row 186

  x: The Peel Commission of 1859 raised the European share and kept the artillery European. The Eden Commission came later, in 1879.

  Which commission recommended abolishing the separate presidency armies, which led to a single Indian Army in 1895?
  Peel Commission | *Eden Commission | Hunter Commission | Aitchison Commission
  x: The Eden Commission (1879) recommended ending the three presidency armies; a single Indian Army with four commands followed in 1895.

=== NOTES 1:188 | Raja Rammohan Roy and the Brahmo Samaj; Abolition of Sati; Debendranath and Keshab Chandra Sen
## SUB 0 | Rammohan Roy – Titles, Life and Works
[188:0:0] # Titles – who is called what
[188:0:1] TABLE head: Title | Person
  [188:0:1.0] Father of Indian Renaissance; Maker / Father of Modern India; first 'Modern Man' of India | Rammohan Roy
  [188:0:1.1] First Indian political reformer; pioneer of political agitation | Rammohan Roy
  [188:0:1.2] Prophet of Indian nationalism (most books, among Roy/Gandhi/Tagore/Dayananda) | Rammohan Roy – ⚠ C.R. Das and NextGen Rocket give it to Aurobindo Ghosh
  [188:0:1.3] Father of Indian Nationalism | Rammohan Roy in most books; NextGen gives Dadabhai Naoroji – neither Gokhale, Tilak nor Surendranath
  [188:0:1.4] 'Raja' | conferred on Roy by Mughal emperor Akbar II (1830)
  [188:0:1.5] Maharishi | Debendranath Tagore – NOT Rammohan Roy
[188:0:2] - **Life:** 1772-1833, born Radhanagar (Hooghly); knew more than a dozen languages – **Sanskrit**, Persian, Arabic, English, Greek, Hebrew.
[188:0:3] - **Views (IAS 2025):** greatly respected the **traditional philosophic systems of the East**, yet wanted Indians to accept the **rational and scientific approach**, human dignity and social equality → **both statements correct**.
[188:0:4] - **England:** went in **1830** as envoy of **Akbar II**; **died at Bristol, 27 Sep 1833**; samadhi/grave at **Arnos Vale cemetery, Bristol** (reburied 1843).
[188:0:5] - Honoured by the **Société Asiatique of Paris** (founded 1822).
[188:0:6] - **Political demands:** Indianisation of superior services, separation of executive and judiciary, **trial by jury** and judicial equality – opposed the **Jury Act 1827**; fixed maximum rents for ryots; protested the **Press Ordinance 1823**.
[188:0:7] - Worked for women, ryots and the nation – not "exclusively the middle class" (CDS 2010); saw religions as embodiments of **universal theism**.
[188:0:8] # Works and journals
[188:0:9] TABLE head: Work | Year / language
  [188:0:9.0] Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin ('Gift to Monotheists') | 1803-09, Persian
  [188:0:9.1] Precepts of Jesus | 1820, English
  [188:0:9.2] Brahmunical Magazine ('Brahman Sevadhi') – defended Hinduism against missionaries | 1821, Roy (⚠ not Debendranath)
  [188:0:9.3] Sambad Kaumudi | 1821, Bengali weekly
  [188:0:9.4] Mirat-ul-Akhbar | 1822, Persian weekly
[188:0:10] # Institutions
[188:0:11] TABLE head: Body | Fact
  [188:0:11.0] Atmiya Sabha | 1815 (Spectrum 1814), Calcutta – his first society
  [188:0:11.1] Hindu College | 1817, Roy helped David Hare; later Presidency College
  [188:0:11.2] Calcutta Unitarian Committee | 1821, Roy (not Keshab)
  [188:0:11.3] Anglo-Hindu (English) School | 1822
  [188:0:11.4] Vedanta College | 1825 – Indian + Western learning
  [188:0:11.5] Brahmo Sabha | 20 Aug 1828
[188:0:12] - **Hindu College founder (UPSC 2009 key: Rammohan Roy):** David Hare founded it in 1817 with Roy's support; Alexander Duff only reached Calcutta in 1830. **David Hare** = Roy's collaborator in education (CDS 2008).
[188:0:13] - **Social campaigns:** against **sati, polygamy, child marriage**; for **widow remarriage**, women's education and property rights.
[188:0:14] > Roy titles: Renaissance, Modern India, Modern Man, political reformer; 'Raja' from Akbar II; died Bristol 1833.

## SUB 1 | Brahmo Samaj, 1828 – Founding and Beliefs
[188:1:0] - **Founded:** **Brahmo Sabha**, **20 August 1828**, Calcutta, by **Raja Rammohan Roy**; later called the **Brahmo Samaj**. First secretary Tarachand Chakravarti.
[188:1:1] - **Year traps:** 1829 = sati ban; **1843** = Debendranath joined; correct founding year = **1828** (option added where missing).
[188:1:2] - **Monotheism:** worship of **one formless, eternal God**; denounced **polytheism and idol worship**; no images in Samaj halls; no faith in **avatars**.
[188:1:3] - **Reason + Upanishads:** rested on reason and the Vedas/Upanishads but **rejected the infallibility of the Vedas** – no scripture above reason and conscience.
[188:1:4] - **No priestly class** needed to interpret texts; criticised **caste**; took in the best of Western/other religious thought.
[188:1:5] - **Correct statements:** opposed idolatry ✔; denied need for priests ✔; "Vedas infallible" ✘ (IAS 2012); "accepted need of priestly class" ✘ (SI 2023: a, b, c).
[188:1:6] - **Nature:** a **monotheistic reformist** movement within Hinduism (not polytheistic, not political); **reformist**, while the **Arya Samaj** is **revivalist**.
[188:1:7] - **Significance:** condemned sati, purdah, child marriage, polygamy; backed widow remarriage and women's education; influence hardly went beyond **Bengal**.
[188:1:8] - **Opponent:** **Radhakant Deb's Dharma Sabha (1830)** – orthodox, against the sati ban.
[188:1:9] - **Brahmo Dharma Gitanjali:** collection of devotional songs sung in Samaj prayers.
[188:1:10] > Brahmo = one God + reason; no idols, no avatars, no priests, no infallible scripture.
[188:1:11] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.239-240, p.243, p.256; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.162, p.166, p.169-170, p.172; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.72; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.125; old app notes row 188
[188:1:12] - **Renamed:** the Brahmo Sabha became the **Brahmo Samaj** under **Debendranath Tagore**.
## SUB 2 | Debendranath Tagore, Keshab Chandra Sen and the Splits
[188:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [188:2:0.0] 1839 | Debendranath Tagore founds the Tattvabodhini Sabha (organ Tattvabodhini Patrika, Bengali) to spread Roy's ideas
  [188:2:0.1] 1843 (Spectrum 1842) | Debendranath joins and revitalises the Brahmo Samaj
  [188:2:0.2] 1857-58 | Keshab Chandra Sen joins; Debendranath makes him acharya
  [188:2:0.3] 1865-66 | Keshab dismissed; forms the Brahmo Samaj of India (Bharatvarshiya) in 1866; Debendranath's body = Adi Brahmo Samaj
  [188:2:0.4] 1870 | Keshab founds the Indian Reform Association
  [188:2:0.5] 1872 | Native (Civil / Brahmo) Marriage Act – after Keshab's petition; legal Brahmo/inter-caste marriage; minimum age 14 (bride), 18 (groom)
  [188:2:0.6] 1878 | Keshab marries his minor daughter to the Maharaja of Cooch Behar → Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (Ananda Mohan Bose, Shibchandra Deb, Umesh Chandra Datta / Shivnath Shastri)
  [188:2:0.7] 1881 | Keshab's Naba Bidhan (New Dispensation)
[188:2:1] - **Debendranath Tagore** (1817-1905), 'Maharishi', father of Rabindranath; also first **secretary of the British Indian Association (1851)**; did NOT found the Atmiya Sabha or the Brahmo Samaj.
[188:2:2] - **Keshab** spread the Samaj to U.P., Punjab, **Bombay** and **Madras** – his visits inspired the **Prarthana Samaj** (1867) and the **Veda Samaj** (Madras, 1864); under him the Samaj campaigned for **women's education** (IAS 2001 III ✔).
[188:2:3] - **Dev Samaj:** **Shiv Narayan Agnihotri**, an ex-Brahmo, Lahore **1887**.
[188:2:4] > Atmiya 1815 → Brahmo 1828 → Tattvabodhini 1839 → split 1866 → Indian Reform Assn 1870 → Marriage Act 1872 → Sadharan 1878.
[188:2:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.242-243, p.256, p.276, p.864; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.170-172, p.187; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.21; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.72; old app notes row 188
[188:2:6] - Keshab, a non-Brahmin, became the first **non-Brahmin acharya** of the Brahmo Samaj.
[188:2:7] - **Tattvabodhini Sabha** merged into the Brahmo Samaj in **1859**.
## SUB 3 | Abolition of Sati, 1829
[188:3:0] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [188:3:0.0] Campaign | Rammohan Roy, from 1818 – scriptures do not sanction it; vigilance at cremation grounds, petitions
  [188:3:0.1] Law | Bengal Sati Regulation XVII, 4 Dec 1829 – sati a crime
  [188:3:0.2] Governor-General | Lord William Bentinck
  [188:3:0.3] Extended | Madras and Bombay, 1830
  [188:3:0.4] Opposition | Dharma Sabha (Radhakant Deb, 1830); Privy Council appeal rejected 1832
[188:3:1] - **Rammohan Roy opposed sati** – "Roy supported sati" is the wrong statement (MPPSC 1994).
[188:3:2] - **Widow remarriage:** Roy demanded it; **Vidyasagar** got it legalised – **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856**.
[188:3:3] > Sati banned = Bentinck, 1829, Regulation XVII; campaign = Rammohan Roy.
[188:3:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.240, p.245; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.165-166, p.174; old app notes row 188
## SUB 4 | Reform Bodies at a Glance – Founders, Years and Matches
[188:4:0] TABLE head: Body | Founder | Year / place
  [188:4:0.0] Atmiya Sabha | Rammohan Roy | 1815, Calcutta
  [188:4:0.1] Brahmo Samaj | Rammohan Roy | 1828, Calcutta
  [188:4:0.2] Tattvabodhini Sabha | Debendranath Tagore | 1839
  [188:4:0.3] Paramahansa Mandali | Dadoba Pandurang | 1849, Maharashtra
  [188:4:0.4] Radhaswami Satsang | Tulsi Ram (Shiv Dayal Saheb) | 1861, Agra
  [188:4:0.5] Veda Samaj | inspired by Keshab | 1864, Madras
  [188:4:0.6] Prarthana Samaj | Atmaram Pandurang (not Phule, Ranade or Ramabai Ranade) | 1867, Bombay
  [188:4:0.7] Satyashodhak Samaj | Jyotiba Phule | 1873
  [188:4:0.8] Arya Samaj | Dayananda Saraswati (not Ranade, Vivekananda, Roy) | 1875, Bombay
  [188:4:0.9] Theosophical Society | Blavatsky and Olcott (not Ranade) | 1875, New York; HQ Adyar, Madras
  [188:4:0.10] Dev Samaj | Shiv Narayan Agnihotri | 1887, Lahore
  [188:4:0.11] Ramakrishna Mission | Swami Vivekananda | 1897
  [188:4:0.12] SNDP Yogam | Sree Narayana Guru | 1903
  [188:4:0.13] Sharada Sadan | Pandita Ramabai | 1889 – home for widows
[188:4:1] - **Watchwords:** Brahmo – **monotheism**; Arya – **back to the Vedas**; Theosophical – **universal brotherhood**; Ramakrishna Mission – **service to mankind**; Prarthana – women and depressed classes; Satyashodhak – social justice for lower castes.
[188:4:2] - **Wrong pairs asked:** Dayanand – Brahmo Samaj ✘; Prarthana – Phule ✘; Prarthana – Ramabai Ranade ✘; Ranade – Theosophical ✘; Atmiya Sabha – Debendranath ✘.
[188:4:3] - **Where it began:** reform movements started in **Bengal** with Rammohan Roy.
[188:4:4] - **Chronology of reformers:** Rammohan Roy → Vidyasagar → Jyotiba Phule → Dayananda (C – A – D – B).
[188:4:5] - **Sanskrit scholars:** Dayananda, Vidyasagar **and** Rammohan Roy – all three.
[188:4:6] > Founding order: Brahmo 1828 → Prarthana 1867 → Satyashodhak 1873 → Arya 1875 → RK Mission 1897.
[188:4:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.72; Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.243-247, p.251-257; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.163, p.177, p.184, p.187-188; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.80; old app notes row 188

=== NOTES 1:189 | Prarthana Samaj, Young Bengal Movement (derozio), Paramahansa Mandali
## SUB 0 | Prarthana Samaj (1867), Ranade and the Social Conference
[189:0:0] - **Founded:** **1867, Bombay**, by **Dr. Atmaram Pandurang**, helped by **Keshab Chandra Sen** (visits 1864, 1867); grew out of the **Paramahansa Sabha**.
[189:0:1] - **Leaders:** **M.G. Ranade** (joined 1870, **chief mentor** – gave it an all-India character), **R.G. Bhandarkar**, **N.G. Chandavarkar**.
[189:0:2] - **Beliefs:** **monotheism**, attached to the Maharashtra **bhakti** tradition; aimed to **reform Hindu society from within**; relied on education and **persuasion**, not confrontation; did not outright forbid image worship.
[189:0:3] - **Four-point agenda:** (i) disapproval of **caste**, (ii) **women's education**, (iii) **widow remarriage**, (iv) **raising the age of marriage** for both sexes – **abolition of untouchability is not in the list** (CDS 2012; ⚠ PMF adds a later Depressed Class Mission).
[189:0:4] - **Statements (Astt. Comm. 2019):** reform of Hindu society ✔, Maharashtra-based ✔, monotheism ✔; "it greatly influenced the Brahmo Samaj" ✘ – the Brahmo Samaj influenced it.
[189:0:5] - **In Andhra:** spread by **Veeresalingam** (Rajahmundry, 1878 – see Andhra reform row).
[189:0:6] # Ranade and the Indian National Social Conference
[189:0:7] - **Indian (National) Social Conference:** founded by **M.G. Ranade** and **Raghunath Rao**; first session **Madras, 1887**; met **at the same time and venue as the INC** – its "social reform cell", because Congress (Dadabhai, 1886) kept to political questions only (UPSC 2012).
[189:0:8] - **Ranade** relied on **legislation**; worked against child marriage and purdah (UPSC 1996 passage); also Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870); **not** the Theosophical Society.
[189:0:9] - **Widow Remarriage Association:** Ranade, usually dated **1861** (⚠ PMF: 1865).
[189:0:10] > Prarthana Samaj = Atmaram Pandurang 1867; chief mentor Ranade; agenda = caste, women's education, widow remarriage, marriage age.
[189:0:11] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.243-244, p.259, p.864; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.161, p.177-178, p.182, p.195; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.72; old app notes row 189
[189:0:12] - **Induprakash** (Anglo-Marathi, 1862) is associated with **M.G. Ranade** (founded by Vishnu Shastri Pandit per PMF).
[189:0:13] - **R.G. Bhandarkar** – Sanskrit scholar and orientalist; first Indian V-C of Bombay University.
[189:0:14] - **Ranade:** social, religious, political and economic reforms are interdependent and must proceed together.
## SUB 1 | Western India Reformers – Lokahitawadi, Jambhekar, Widow Remarriage, Deccan Education Society
[189:1:0] TABLE head: Person | Known for
  [189:1:0.0] Gopal Hari Deshmukh | 'Lokahitawadi' – pen name in the weekly Prabhakar (Shatapatre, 1848-50); "if religion does not sanction social reform, change religion"
  [189:1:0.1] Balshastri Jambhekar | Darpan (1832), first Marathi paper; attacked Brahminical orthodoxy and tried to reform popular Hinduism in Bombay; father of Marathi journalism
  [189:1:0.2] Vishnu Shastri Pandit | Vidhva Vivaha Uttejak Mandal (Society for the Encouragement of Widow Remarriage) – 1866; Indu Prakash
  [189:1:0.3] Karsondas Mulji | Satya Prakash (Gujarati, 1852) for widow remarriage
  [189:1:0.4] Gopal Ganesh Agarkar | co-founder of DES and Fergusson College; first editor of Kesari; Sudharak
[189:1:1] - **'Lokahitawadi' = Gopal Hari Deshmukh** – not Ranade, Gokhale, Chiplunkar, Vidyasagar or Lajpat Rai.
[189:1:2] - **Deccan Education Society (1884):** founded by **Tilak, Agarkar, Vishnushastri Chiplunkar**, Namjoshi, Apte; **Ranade was only a patron**; not founded by Ambedkar.
[189:1:3] > Lokahitawadi – Prabhakar; Jambhekar – Darpan; Karsondas – Satya Prakash; Vishnu Shastri – 1866 widow society.
[189:1:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.229, p.246-248; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.50, p.179, p.181, p.195; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.171; old app notes row 189
[189:1:5] - **Dnyanodaya** was the Marathi journal of the **American Marathi Mission**.
## SUB 2 | Paramahansa Mandali (1849)
[189:2:0] - **Founded:** **1849, Maharashtra (Bombay)**, by **Dadoba Pandurang**, **Durgaram Mehtaji** (of the Manav Dharma Sabha, Surat) and others; Bipan Chandra dates religious reform in Bombay from **1840** by the Mandali.
[189:2:1] - **First socio-religious organisation in Maharashtra** – religious reform in Bombay began with it, not with the Prarthana Samaj (1867).
[189:2:2] - **A secret society**; believed in **one God**; aim: **against idolatry and the caste system** – members **ate food cooked by lower castes**; backed **widow remarriage and women's education**.
[189:2:3] - **Branches:** **Poona**, Satara; exposure in 1860 ended it; reorganised as the Prarthana Samaj (1867).
[189:2:4] > Paramahansa Mandali = secret, 1849, Dadoba Pandurang, anti-caste and anti-idolatry.
[189:2:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.244, p.246; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.176-177; old app notes row 189
## SUB 3 | Young Bengal Movement – Derozio
[189:3:0] - **Leader:** **Henry Louis Vivian Derozio** (1809-31), Anglo-Indian teacher at **Hindu College** (1826-31); inspired by the **French Revolution**; first nationalist poet of modern India.
[189:3:1] - **Derozians:** radical rationalism – question all authority; women's rights; demanded press freedom, trial by jury, Indians in higher services.
[189:3:2] - **Academic Association (1828):** debating forum of Derozio and his students.
[189:3:3] - **Dismissed** from Hindu College in **1831**; died of cholera the same year. Failed: radicalism bookish, no link with the masses.
[189:3:4] > Young Bengal = Derozio, Hindu College, Academic Association 1828, removed 1831.
[189:3:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.244-245; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.172-173; old app notes row 189

=== NOTES 1:190 | Arya Samaj and Dayananda Saraswati – Satyarth Prakash, Shuddhi, Dayanand Anglo-vedic Schools
## SUB 0 | Arya Samaj, 1875 – Founder and Founding
[190:0:0] - **Founder:** **Swami Dayananda Saraswati** (Mool Shankar, 1824-1883), born in a **Brahmin** family in **Morvi state (Tankara), Gujarat**; guru **Swami Virajananda** of Mathura; died at Ajmer, 1883.
[190:0:1] - **First Arya Samaj:** **Bombay, 1875** (10 April); headquarters later at **Lahore** (1877); strongest base Punjab.
[190:0:2] - Founder = **Dayananda** – not Vivekananda, Gokhale, Ramakrishna, Ranade, V.R. Shinde, Chandavarkar or Keshab.
[190:0:3] - **Wrong date trap:** "Arya Samaj founded in 1835" ✘ (IAS 2001).
[190:0:4] - **Current linkage:** **International Arya Mahasammelan 2025**, New Delhi, **30 Oct-2 Nov 2025** – 150 years of the Arya Samaj and Dayananda's **200th birth anniversary**.
[190:0:5] > Arya Samaj = Dayananda, Bombay 1875, HQ Lahore.
[190:0:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.252; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.185-186; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.72; Rocket CA 2026-02 p.39, p.41; old app notes row 190
[190:0:7] - **IAS 2001 statements:** Keshab's Brahmo Samaj campaigned for women's education ✔; Vinoba Bhave's **Sarvodaya Samaj** worked among refugees ✔; Lajpat Rai did not oppose the Arya Samaj ✘ → **III and IV**.
## SUB 1 | Doctrines, Satyarth Prakash and Titles
[190:1:0] - **'Back to the Vedas':** Vedas = **infallible**, "India's Rock of Ages"; a revival of Vedic learning and purity, not of Vedic times; rejected the **Puranas**.
[190:1:1] - **Attacked:** idolatry, polytheism, caste rigidity and untouchability, child marriage, priestly ritual; caste by **merit/occupation, not birth** (CDS 2009: all three statements ✔).
[190:1:2] - **Supported:** widow remarriage, inter-caste marriage, women's education; minimum marriage age 25 (boys) and 16 (girls); **ten principles**.
[190:1:3] - **Satyarth Prakash** ('The Light of Truth', 1875, **Hindi**, revised 1882) – Dayananda's main work and the **Arya Samaj's** sacred text.
[190:1:4] - **Revivalist** in form (cf. reformist Brahmo/Prarthana Samaj).
[190:1:5] # Titles and slogans
[190:1:6] TABLE head: Said / title | Person
  [190:1:6.0] 'India for the Indians' | Dayananda Saraswati (political message)
  [190:1:6.1] Martin Luther of India | Dayananda Saraswati
  [190:1:6.2] First to use the term 'Swaraj' | Dayananda (as usually given)
  [190:1:6.3] Prophet of Indian Nationalism | not Dayananda – Aurobindo
[190:1:7] > Dayananda: Back to the Vedas, Satyarth Prakash, India for the Indians, Martin Luther of India.
[190:1:8] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.252-254, p.291; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.162, p.186-187; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.49; old app notes row 190
[190:1:9] - Dayananda is also called the **'Grandfather of the Indian Nation'** (as usually given in quiz books).
## SUB 2 | Shuddhi, DAV Schools, the 1893 Split and Social Base
[190:2:0] - **Shuddhi** (purification): started by the **Arya Samaj** (Dayananda) to **reconvert** to Hinduism those who had become Muslims or Christians; also tried to raise untouchables; aggressive campaign of the 1920s (Shraddhanand) sharpened communalism.
[190:2:1] - **DAV:** **Dayananda Anglo-Vedic School/College, Lahore, 1886** (after Dayananda's death) – **Lala Hansraj** first headmaster/founder; Western-style education.
[190:2:2] - **1893 split:** **College Party** – Lala Hansraj, Lala Lal Chand, **Lala Lajpat Rai** (kept DAV); **Mahatma / Gurukul Party** – Guru Datta Vidyarthi and **Munshi Ram (Swami Shraddhanand)**, who set up the **Gurukul** (Gujranwala 1900, **Kangri, Haridwar 1902**).
[190:2:3] - **Swami Shraddhanand** spoke on Hindu-Muslim unity from the pulpit of the **Jama Masjid, Delhi, 4 April 1919** (Rowlatt satyagraha).
[190:2:4] - **Impact (A-R):** gave Hindus **self-respect and self-confidence**, which **undermined the myth of white superiority** – R explains A.
[190:2:5] - **Social base:** **Punjab and western U.P.**, mainly the **trading castes**; wider than the Brahmo Samaj, whose influence hardly went beyond Bengal; famous for social service in calamities.
[190:2:6] - **Lala Lajpat Rai:** Arya Samaj leader, ran the paper **The People** (not "unconnected"); **Al Hilal** (1912) = **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad**.
[190:2:7] - **Hyderabad, 1938-39:** Arya Samaj satyagraha against the **Nizam's curbs on religious and civil rights**, alongside the State Congress satyagraha.
[190:2:8] > Shuddhi = Arya Samaj; DAV Lahore 1886 = Hansraj; Gurukul Kangri 1902 = Shraddhanand; split 1893.
[190:2:9] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.243, p.254-255; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.187; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.173; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.73; old app notes row 190
[190:2:10] - **Bharatiya Hindu Shuddhi Sabha** – 1923, led by Swami Shraddhanand.
[190:2:11] - The Arya Samaj was called a **'nursery of militant nationalists'** – it shaped Lajpat Rai and Shraddhanand.
