=== NOTES 1:191 | Ramakrishna Paramahansa and Swami Vivekananda; Ramakrishna Mission; Theosophical Society
## SUB 0 | Swami Vivekananda – Life, Chicago 1893, Ideas, Books and Sayings
[191:0:0] # Life
[191:0:1] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [191:0:1.0] Birth name | Narendranath Datta
  [191:0:1.1] Born | Calcutta, 12 January 1863 (Spectrum prints 1862); died 1902
  [191:0:1.2] Guru | Ramakrishna Paramahamsa (= Gadadhar Chattopadhyay) of Dakshineswar
  [191:0:1.3] National Youth Day | His birthday, 12 January – declared by the Government of India in 1984, first observed 1985 (12 August is the UN's *International* Youth Day)
  [191:0:1.4] Western disciple | Sister Nivedita = Margaret Elizabeth Noble (Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu = Mother Teresa; Madeleine Slade = Mirabehn)
  [191:0:1.5] Vedanta Societies | USA and Britain – Vedanta Society of New York (1894)
  [191:0:1.6] Titles | Best representative / preacher of Neo-Hinduism (later 19th century) – not Ramakrishna, Bankim or Rammohan; "Cyclonic Hindu"; called "Prophet of Indian Nationalism" in many MCQ banks; Bose: "spiritual father of the modern nationalist movement" (Bengal)
[191:0:2] # Chicago and after – order of events
[191:0:3] TABLE head: Date | Event
  [191:0:3.0] Dec 1892 | Meditated on the Kanyakumari rock
  [191:0:3.1] Feb 1893 | Spoke at Mahboob College, Secunderabad
  [191:0:3.2] 11 Sep 1893 | World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago – opened with "Sisters and Brothers of America"; represented Hinduism (not 1863, 1872, 1881, 1890, 1892, 1894, 1895, 1897, 1899, 1901)
  [191:0:3.3] 10 Nov 1896 | First lecture on Practical Vedanta, London
  [191:0:3.4] 1897 | Returned via Colombo, Ramnad, Madras → *Lectures from Colombo to Almora*; toured Andhra (organised by Nyapathi Subba Rao)
  [191:0:3.5] 1 May 1897 | Ramakrishna Mission
  [191:0:3.6] 1898 | Belur Math
[191:0:4] - **Others at Chicago 1893:** Brahmo Samaj – **P.C. Mozoomdar**; Jainism – **Virchand Gandhi**; Buddhism (Ceylon) – **Anagarika Dharmapala**. Of Dayananda, Gandhi and Rammohan Roy, none attended (Roy d. 1833, Dayananda d. 1883).
[191:0:5] - Keynote at Chicago: a balance of the **spiritualism of the East and the materialism of the West**; Hinduism "the mother of religions".
[191:0:6] # Ideas
[191:0:7] - **Practical Vedanta:** Vedanta to be lived in daily life; serving the poor is serving God – **"Daridra Narayana"** (God manifest in the poor); "service of jiva is worship of Shiva". Not Dayananda, Rammohan or Gandhi.
[191:0:8] - Followed **Vedanta, "a fully rational system"**; criticised Indians for **losing touch with the outside world** ("stagnant and mummified"); **condemned the caste system**, ritual and superstition – but did **not** call the Veda infallible (that is Dayananda) → CDS 2011: **I, II and III**.
[191:0:9] - **Vedanta the religion of all**; revived the best Hindu traditions; admired the **status of women in the West** → CDS 2009: **I, II and III**.
[191:0:10] - **"Our religion is in the kitchen"** – his attack on touch-me-not orthodoxy ("Our God is the cooking-pot").
[191:0:11] - Humanitarian relief = a **monastic duty**; knowledge without action is useless.
[191:0:12] # Books, journals, sayings
[191:0:13] TABLE head: Work / saying | Note
  [191:0:13.0] Karma Yoga, Raja Yoga, Jnana Yoga, Bhakti Yoga | Vivekananda's books (not Ranade, Rammohan or Ramakrishna)
  [191:0:13.1] My Master | Vivekananda's book on Ramakrishna (Ramakrishna wrote no books)
  [191:0:13.2] Prabuddha Bharata / Udbodhan | Journals – English / Bengali
  [191:0:13.3] "If education were identical with information, the libraries would be the greatest sages and encyclopaedias the rishis" | Vivekananda
  [191:0:13.4] A teacher's success | His renunciation of personal gain and service to others (Vivekananda)
  [191:0:13.5] "So long as millions live in hunger and ignorance, I hold every man a traitor" | Vivekananda
[191:0:14] - Not Vivekananda: "**Good government is no substitute for self-government**" – credited to **Dayananda Saraswati**.
[191:0:15] > Chicago = 1893; RK Mission = 1897; Belur = 1898; Youth Day = 12 Jan (declared 1984).
[191:0:16] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.249-252; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.175-176; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.125; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.48; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.71; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.25 (1897 Andhra tour); Rocket Indian Society p.8 (first Youth Day 1985); old app notes row 191
## SUB 1 | Ramakrishna Mission, 1897 – Founder, Year, Work
[191:1:0] - **Founded 1 May 1897 by Swami Vivekananda**, at Balaram Bose's house, **Baghbazar, Calcutta**, in his guru's name – not by Ramakrishna (died 1886), Vidyasagar, Dayananda, Rammohan Roy, Gokhale, Shyamji Krishna Varma, M.N. Das Gupta or Ranganathananda.
[191:1:1] - **Year = 1897** – not 1861, 1879, 1886, 1891, 1892, 1893, 1898 or 1899. "Founded the Mission in **1879**" = the INCORRECT statement.
[191:1:2] - **HQ: Belur Math** on the Hooghly, Howrah (land bought **1898**); Math and Mission are twin bodies, legally and financially separate.
[191:1:3] - Motto: **"Atmano Mokshartham Jagad Hitaya Cha"** – for one's own liberation and the welfare of the world.
[191:1:4] - **Two wings:** (1) a **monastic order** of renunciation and practical spirituality; (2) **lay disciples** – preaching, philanthropy, humanitarian work.
[191:1:5] - **Work:** schools, hospitals, orphanages, **famine and disaster relief**; social and spiritual – **non-political, non-sectarian, not proselytising**; unlike the Arya Samaj it accepts image worship.
[191:1:6] - **Current linkage (1 Feb 2026):** RKM's **Vivekananda Human Excellence Centre, Vijayawada**, inaugurated by RKM President Swami Gautamananda.
[191:1:7] > RK Mission = Vivekananda, 1 May 1897, Calcutta; HQ Belur Math.
[191:1:8] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.249, p.251-252; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.175, p.200; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.44, p.99, p.104; old app notes row 191 (Vijayawada centre, 2026)
## SUB 2 | Annie Besant – Career, Central Hindu College, BHU and Writings
[191:2:0] # Milestones
[191:2:1] TABLE head: Year | Milestone
  [191:2:1.0] 1885 | Joined the Fabian Society (British gradualist socialism) – the Fabian among Hume, M.M. Dutt and R. Palme Dutt
  [191:2:1.1] 1889 | Joined the Theosophical Society
  [191:2:1.2] 1893 | Came to India
  [191:2:1.3] 1898 | Central Hindu College (School), Benaras – 7 July 1898
  [191:2:1.4] 1907 | President of the Theosophical Society after Olcott's death
  [191:2:1.5] 1914 | *Commonweal* (weekly, Jan) and *New India* (Madras Standard renamed, Aug)
  [191:2:1.6] 1916 | Home Rule League (1 Sep 1916); National (BT) College, Madanapalle
  [191:2:1.7] 1917 | First woman President of the INC – Calcutta session
[191:2:2] - Besant flashcard statements (TS President 1907 ✔, first woman INC President 1917 ✔, Central Hindu College 1898 ✔) → **all three correct**.
[191:2:3] - Besant did **not found** the Theosophical Society (Blavatsky and Olcott did, 1875); she **was** one of the founders of BHU (her Central Hindu College was its nucleus) and **believed in the transmigration of the soul** (karma and reincarnation).
[191:2:4] - Pairs: **Annie Besant – New India** ✔ (also Commonweal); Hind Swaraj – Gandhi; India Wins Freedom – Azad; Tilak – Kesari/Mahratta.
[191:2:5] - **At the Feet of the Master** (1910) – **Jiddu Krishnamurti** ("Alcyone"), Besant's adopted ward, written at about 14 – not Besant, Radhakrishnan or C.R. Reddy.
[191:2:6] - *Isis Unveiled*, *The Secret Doctrine* – **H.P. Blavatsky**; *My Master* – Vivekananda (not Besant, not Olcott).
[191:2:7] # Central Hindu College and BHU
[191:2:8] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [191:2:8.0] Central Hindu College/School, Benaras | Founded by Annie Besant, 1898 – nucleus of BHU (not Malaviya, Dayananda, Tilak, Madam Cama, Sarojini Naidu, Sucheta Kripalani)
  [191:2:8.1] Banaras Hindu University | Founded 1916 by Madan Mohan Malaviya with Besant
  [191:2:8.2] Foundation stone | Viceroy Lord Hardinge II, 4 February 1916 (Basant Panchami) – not Malaviya, Besant or the Maharaja of Benaras
  [191:2:8.3] First Central University | BHU – BHU Act 1915 (AMU 1920; Calcutta, Madras, Bombay 1857 were affiliating universities; Allahabad central only in 2005)
  [191:2:8.4] Religious education in universities | Vigorously advocated by Malaviya
[191:2:9] - **DACE current linkage:** Dr. Ambedkar Centres of Excellence (free civil-services coaching for SC students, 31 central universities) launched **22 April 2022 at BHU, Varanasi** by Dr. Virendra Kumar.
[191:2:10] > 1898 = Central Hindu College (Besant); 1916 = BHU (Malaviya; stone by Hardinge).
[191:2:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.188-190 (Besant career; UPSC 2013 PYQ); Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.266; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.61 (Central Hindu School 7 July 1898); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.70-71; NextGen AP History Part 18 p.5; news.careers360.com and indiaeducationdiary.in (DACE launch at BHU, 22 Apr 2022); old app notes row 191
## SUB 3 | Theosophical Society, 1875 – Founders, Adyar, Beliefs
[191:3:0] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [191:3:0.0] Founded | New York, November 1875 – not London, Paris or Adyar (same year as the Arya Samaj)
  [191:3:0.1] Founders | Madame H.P. Blavatsky (Russian) and Col. H.S. Olcott (American), with William Q. Judge – not Annie Besant, Hume, Rammohan, Gandhi, Vivekananda
  [191:3:0.2] Came to India | 1879
  [191:3:0.3] HQ | Adyar, near Madras, from 1882 – not Madanapalle, Pondicherry, Kanchipuram
  [191:3:0.4] Success in India | Mainly due to Annie Besant (President 1907-33)
  [191:3:0.5] Telugu name | Divya Gnana Samajam
[191:3:1] - **Beliefs:** **universal brotherhood** of humanity without distinction of race, creed, sex, caste or colour; study of ancient religions; **karma, reincarnation, transmigration of the soul**; drew on Upanishads, Samkhya, Yoga, Vedanta; opposed child marriage and caste discrimination.
[191:3:2] - A Western-led **revivalist** movement allied with the Hindu renaissance; gave Indians self-respect – and led straight into the **Home Rule** movement.
[191:3:3] - **A-R trap:** HQ at Adyar ✔, but it was **not** founded at Madras ✘ → A true, R false.
[191:3:4] - Wrong statement (MPPSC 1995): "**Gandhi was born in Gandhinagar**" ✘ – Porbandar, 2 Oct 1869; Besant a Theosophist, Adyar HQ, Dayananda–Arya Samaj are all correct.
[191:3:5] > TS = Blavatsky + Olcott, New York 1875 → Adyar 1882; Besant President 1907.
[191:3:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.265-266; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.188, p.190; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.98-99, p.104; NextGen AP History Part 18 p.5; old app notes row 191 (Telugu name)
## SUB 4 | Madanapalle and Theosophy in Andhra
[191:4:0] - **Besant (National) Theosophical College, Madanapalle** – founded by **Annie Besant**, May **1916** (NextGen; PMF gives 19 July 1915) as part of her **National Education** scheme; first principal **James H. Cousins** – not Jiddu Krishnamurti (born at Madanapalle), Konda Venkatappayya or Mutnuri Krishna Rao.
[191:4:1] - **Jana Gana Mana:** written 1911; **Tagore translated it into English as "Morning Song of India" at Madanapalle, 28 Feb 1919** (stayed 25 Feb–2 Mar 1919); **Margaret Cousins** set the tune; Tagore called the college "the Shantiniketan of South India" → UPSC 2021: option on Tagore ✔.
[191:4:2] - UPSC 2021 wrong options: Pingali Venkayya did not design the flag there; Pattabhi did not lead Quit India from there; Blavatsky and Olcott set up the HQ at **Adyar**, not Madanapalle.
[191:4:3] TABLE head: Andhra link | Fact
  [191:4:3.0] Guntur, 1882 | Krishna Divyajnana Lodge library – first public library in Guntur district
  [191:4:3.1] Kandukuri Veeresalingam | First Theosophical High School in Andhra
  [191:4:3.2] Home Rule workers | Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao (Secretary), Konda Venkatappayya, Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao
[191:4:4] > Madanapalle = Besant's National/BT College (1916) + Tagore's English Jana Gana Mana (1919).
[191:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.189-190; NextGen modern India level 3 part 1 p.97 (National College, Madanapalle, May 1916, Cousins); NextGen AP History Part 18 p.5; old app notes row 191 (Guntur lodge, Veeresalingam, Home Rule workers)
## SUB 5 | Ramakrishna Paramahamsa (1836-1886)
[191:5:0] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [191:5:0.0] Original name | Gadadhar Chattopadhyay
  [191:5:0.1] Role | Mystic and priest of the Kali temple, Dakshineswar, near Calcutta
  [191:5:0.2] Guru | Totapuri (Vedanta)
  [191:5:0.3] Wife | Sarada Devi (Saradamani / Shardamani), married 1859 – the "Holy Mother" – not Rammohan Roy's wife, Vivekananda's mother or Keshab's daughter
  [191:5:0.4] Chief disciple | Swami Vivekananda
[191:5:1] - **Teachings:** "**As many faiths, so many paths**"; **Krishna, Hari, Ram, Christ, Allah** = different names of one God; salvation through **renunciation, meditation and bhakti**; "service of man is service of God". Wrote no books.
[191:5:2] - Laid the foundation of the **Ramakrishna Math** with his young monks; did **not** found the Mission.
[191:5:3] > Gadadhar = Ramakrishna; Narendranath = Vivekananda; Saradamani = Ramakrishna's wife.
[191:5:4] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.249-250; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.174-175 (PMF prints 1834); old app notes row 191

=== NOTES 1:192 | Muslim, Sikh and Parsi Reform – Aligarh, Deoband, Ahmadiya, Wahabi, Faraizi, Singh Sabha
## SUB 0 | Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement
[192:0:0] # Sir Syed (1817-1898)
[192:0:1] - In the Company's **judicial service** in 1857; **loyalist**; knighted 1888; **never connected with the Congress** – asked Muslims to keep away from it (Ferozshah Mehta, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Ghaffar Khan were all Congressmen).
[192:0:2] - Aim: modernise Muslims through **English / Western scientific education** and a **rational reading of the Quran**; promoted **Urdu**; opposed purdah and polygamy.
[192:0:3] - Early view: India a bride, Hindus and Muslims "**her two eyes**"; turned after the **Hindi-Urdu controversy (1867)**.
[192:0:4] TABLE head: Body / work | Year | Note
  [192:0:4.0] Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind | 1859 | Sir Syed, "Causes of the Indian Revolt"
  [192:0:4.1] Scientific Society | 1864, Ghazipur (PMF: 1863) → Aligarh | Sir Syed – translated Western science, history into Urdu; not Cornwallis or a company
  [192:0:4.2] MAO school (Madarsatul Uloom Musalmanan-i-Hind) | 1875 | Sir Syed Ahmad Khan – not Jinnah, Muhammad Ali or Shaukat Ali
  [192:0:4.3] Renamed Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College | 1877 | Modelled on Oxford and Cambridge – the centre of the Aligarh Movement
  [192:0:4.4] Muhammadan Educational Conference | 1886 | Sir Syed
  [192:0:4.5] United Indian Patriotic Association | 1888 | Sir Syed + Raja Shiva Prasad of Benaras – to counter the Congress
  [192:0:4.6] MAO Defence Association | 1893 | Sir Syed with Theodore Beck; loyalist, anti-Congress
  [192:0:4.7] Aligarh Muslim University | 1920 | MAO College raised to AMU
  [192:0:4.8] Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq | – | Sir Syed's journal
  [192:0:4.9] The Indian Musalmans | 1871 | W.W. Hunter – not Sir Syed
[192:0:5] - **Years-match (APPSC AEE):** Arya Samaj **1875**, Prarthana Samaj **1867**, MAO College **1877**, SNDP Yogam **1903** → A-1, B-4, C-2, D-3.
[192:0:6] # Aligarh Movement and MAO principals
[192:0:7] - **Initial objective:** promote **modern Western scientific education** among Indian Muslims (not a Muslim state, not traditional madrasa reform, not Hindu-Muslim unity against the British); social reform; built a **modern educated Muslim middle class**.
[192:0:8] - **Principals:** first **H.G.I. Siddons**; then **Theodore Beck (1883-99)** – encouraged Muslim separatism / communalism and **turned Sir Syed against the Congress**; then Theodore Morison.
[192:0:9] - **Pairs (IAS 1998):** Beck – MAO College ✔; Ilbert Bill – Ripon ✔; Pherozeshah Mehta – INC ✔; **Badruddin Tyabji – Muslim League ✘** (he was INC President 1887) → **1, 2 and 3**.
[192:0:10] - Later Aligarh leaders: Chiragh Ali, Altaf Husain Hali, Nazir Ahmad, Mohsin-ul-Mulk (not Mahmud-ul-Hasan – Deoband).
[192:0:11] - **Mohammedan Literary Society: Calcutta, 1863, Nawab Abdul Latif** – "Father of Muslim Renaissance in Bengal" (not Sir Syed, Ameer Ali, Salimullah); not Aligarh.
[192:0:12] > Aligarh = Sir Syed, MAO 1875/1877, Beck; Literary Society = Abdul Latif, Calcutta 1863.
[192:0:13] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.261-264; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.191-193, p.201; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.61 (MAO 1875, renamed 1877, AMU 1920); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.71; old app notes row 192
## SUB 1 | Deoband School (Darul Uloom) and Nadwatul Ulama
[192:1:0] - **Darul Uloom, Deoband, 1866** (PMF: 1867), **Saharanpur district, United Provinces = Uttar Pradesh**, by **Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi** – not 1885, 1888 or 1900.
[192:1:1] - **Aims:** propagate pure teachings of the **Quran and Hadis**, **keep alive jihad against foreign rulers**, **train religious leaders** – not Western education.
[192:1:2] - Politics: **welcomed the Congress**; **fatwa (1888)** against Sir Syed's United Patriotic Association and MAO Association; **Mahmud-ul-Hasan** gave it political content → **Jamiat-ul-Ulema** (1919).
[192:1:3] TABLE head: Feature | Aligarh | Deoband
  [192:1:3.0] Learning | Western, scientific | Quran and Hadis
  [192:1:3.1] British | Loyal | Anti-British
  [192:1:3.2] Congress | Opposed | Welcomed
[192:1:4] - **Nadwatul Ulama:** decided at **Kanpur** 1893, first session 1894; prime founder and first manager **Muhammad Ali Mungeri**; office moved to **Lucknow 1898**.
[192:1:5] - **Shibli Numani** – supporter of Deoband who wanted English and European science taught; "**founded the Nadwatal Ulama and Darul Uloom in Lucknow in 1894-96**" (Spectrum) → so "Dar-ul-Ulum was established by" (UPPCS 2014, options Shibli / Hussain Ahmad / Chakralavi / Ahmad Raza Khan) = **Shibli Numani**. (Deoband's own Darul Uloom = Nanautavi and Gangohi.)
[192:1:6] > Deoband 1866 (Nanautavi, Gangohi), UP; Nadwa Lucknow (Shibli, Mungeri).
[192:1:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.263-264; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.193; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.71; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.44; old app notes row 192 (Nadwa founding detail)
## SUB 2 | Wahabi Movement – Barelvi, Patna, Anti-British; Hyderabad Angle
[192:2:0] - Inspired by **Abdul Wahab of Arabia** and **Shah Waliullah** (1702-63); popularised by Shah Abdul Aziz; Indian founder **Syed Ahmad Barelvi** (of Rae Bareli).
[192:2:1] - Aim: return to pure Islam; convert **Dar-ul-Harb into Dar-ul-Islam**; fought the **Sikhs** in Punjab, then after 1849 the **British** → character: **anti-British** (APPSC G2 2011, three versions) – not pro-British, anti-Muslim or merely pro-Muslim.
[192:2:2] - **Chief centre: Patna** (base at Sithana in the NW tribal belt) – not Lahore, Amritsar or Pune.
[192:2:3] - Main followers: **Muslim peasants and weavers / artisans**; trials at **Ambala (1864)** and **Patna (1865)**; crushed in the 1870s.
[192:2:4] - **Titu Mir** (Narkelberia, 1831), a disciple of Barelvi, led Muslim peasants of Bengal against zamindars and indigo planters.
[192:2:5] - **Hyderabad:** Wahabi conspiracy **1839** led by **Mubariz-ud-Daula**, the Nizam's brother, who resisted British influence in the Deccan; arrested 1839, died in prison.
[192:2:6] - **Nasaraiah** (Sayyid Muslim, d. 1825): popular among the **Madigas**; preached **one God**, opposed idol worship; **Vinukonda–Narasaraopet** (Guntur).
[192:2:7] - **Osmania University** (Hyderabad, 1918) taught through **Urdu**.
[192:2:8] > Wahabi = Barelvi, Patna, anti-British; Hyderabad 1839 = Mubariz-ud-Daula.
[192:2:9] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.183, p.259-260; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.36, p.71; NextGen AP History Part 7 p.10 ("The wahabi movement was - Anti British"); NextGen AP History Part 21 p.10 (1839, Mubaraz-ud-Doulah); NextGen AP History Part 16 p.7 (Nasaraiah); Rocket AP History p.36; old app notes row 192
## SUB 3 | Faraizi, Taiyuni and Ahmadiyya Movements
[192:3:0] - **Faraizi (Fara'idi) Movement:** founded **1818** by **Haji Shariatullah** in **East Bengal (Faridpur)** – the Faraizis = **followers of Haji Shariatullah** (not Dadu Dayal, Arya Samaj or Muslim League); aim: enforce Islamic duties (*faraiz*), purge un-Islamic practices.
[192:3:1] - **Dudu (Dadu) Miyan**, his son, made it revolutionary from **1840** – peasants against **zamindars and indigo planters**; told followers not to pay rent; arrested 1847, died 1862 → **leader of the Farazi rebellion** (not Wazir Ali, Shamsher Gazi, Aga Muhammad Raza).
[192:3:2] - Founder vs leader trap: *founder* = Haji Shariatullah; *leader / rebellion* = Dudu Miyan.
[192:3:3] - **Taiyuni movement:** **Karamat Ali Jaunpuri** (Bengal) – opposed Faraizi radicalism; pairing it with Rashid Ahmad Gangohi (Deoband) is the **wrong pair**.
[192:3:4] - **Ahmadiyya:** **Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, Qadian (Gurdaspur, Punjab), 1889** (not 1866); claimed to be the Messiah; liberal, spread Western education, **opposed jihad**; rejected by orthodox Muslims.
[192:3:5] - Pairs (APPSC G2): Aligarh – Sir Syed ✔; Faraizi – Haji Shariatullah ✔; Ahmadiyya – Mirza Ghulam Ahmad ✔; Taiyuni – Gangohi ✘.
[192:3:6] > Faraizi = Haji Shariatullah 1818 (Dudu Miyan led); Ahmadiyya = Qadian 1889.
[192:3:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.184, p.260-261; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.126 ("Followers of Haji Shariatullah – Faraizi sect"); Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.44, p.51; old app notes row 192 (Taiyuni, Qadian district)
[192:3:8] - **Faraizis and Wahabis:** the Faraizis later joined the Wahabi movement.

=== NOTES 1:193 | Sikh, Parsi and Other Reform Movements – Singh Sabha, Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha
## SUB 0 | Kuka (Namdhari) Movement – Punjab, Ram Singh, First Boycott
[193:0:0] - **Region: Punjab** (not U.P., Malabar, Bihar, Bengal or Maharashtra); founded **1840** by **Bhagat Jawahar Mal (Sian Sahib)** in western Punjab (Spectrum) – he **started** the Kuka revolt.
[193:0:1] - **Baba (Satguru) Ram Singh** – disciple of Balak Singh; **organised** it and founded the **Namdhari** sect (**1857**, **Bhaini, Ludhiana**) – not Guru Ram Das, Nanak or Gobind Singh, not Nankana Sahib.
[193:0:2] - Practices: **white clothes**, no meat, alcohol or drugs, a **lathi**; against idol, tomb, tree and snake worship and **Brahmin-led rituals**; widow remarriage, intermarriage.
[193:0:3] - **Boycott** of British **goods, English education, law courts and the postal system** → **Ram Singh = first to use non-cooperation and boycott (Swadeshi) as a political weapon** (APPSC 2025) – before Tilak, Pal or Gandhi.
[193:0:4] - Suppression: **Malerkotla clash, 1872** – Kukas blown from cannons; Ram Singh **deported to Rangoon (Burma)**; Kuka movement under Viceroy Northbrook.
[193:0:5] - Kuka and Wahabi both began as religious revolts and became anti-British political movements.
[193:0:6] > Kuka = Punjab; begun by Jawahar Mal (1840); Ram Singh, Bhaini, boycott; Malerkotla 1872.
[193:0:7] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.183; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams 06 p.3, p.71; gktoday.in and studyiq.com Kuka pages (1840, Jawahar Mal; Namdhari 1857 – web search results); old app notes row 193
[193:0:8] - **Namdhari (Kuka) movement** – among the earliest movements to resist British rule in Punjab.
## SUB 1 | Singh Sabha, Nirankari and the Akali Movement
[193:1:0] - **Singh Sabha:** **Amritsar, 1873**; more radical **Lahore Singh Sabha, 1879**; aims – modern Western education for Sikhs through **Khalsa schools**, **Gurmukhi/Punjabi** literature, remove un-Sikh practices, counter missionaries.
[193:1:1] - **Khalsa College, Amritsar – 1892** (foundation stone) by Singh Sabha leaders – not 1894, 1896 or 1898.
[193:1:2] - **Nirankari:** **Baba Dayal Das** (1855); God as **Nirankar** (formless); issued **hukamnamas**; own priests; **cooperated with the British** and became a separate group in Sikhism.
[193:1:3] TABLE head: Akali step | Year
  [193:1:3.0] SGPC formed; Akali (Gurdwara Reform) Movement begins | 1920
  [193:1:3.1] Nankana Sahib massacre | 1921
  [193:1:3.2] Guru-ka-Bagh morcha | 1922
  [193:1:3.3] Sikh Gurdwaras Act – gurdwaras under the SGPC | 1922, amended 1925
[193:1:4] - **Akali movement** = offshoot of the Singh Sabha; freed gurdwaras from corrupt **Udasi mahants**; leader **Kartar Singh Jhabbar**; later the **Akali Dal**. It is a **Sikh** movement – "Akali Movement – Tamilians" is the **wrong pair** (Rahnumai – Parsis, Aligarh – Muslims, Arya Samaj – Hindus are right).
[193:1:5] > Singh Sabha 1873 Amritsar → Khalsa College 1892 → Akali / SGPC 1920 → Act 1925.
[193:1:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.264-265; old app notes row 193 (Lahore 1879, Khalsa College 1892, Nirankari, Akali dates)
## SUB 2 | Parsi Reform – Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha, 1851
[193:2:0] - **Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha** (Religious Reform Association), **Bombay, 1851** – to reform the **Parsis** (not Sikhs, Muslims or Anglo-Indians).
[193:2:1] - Founders: **Naoroji Furdonji** (first president), **Dadabhai Naoroji**, **K.R. Cama**, **S.S. Bengalee**.
[193:2:2] - Organ: **Rast Goftar** ("Truth-Teller"), edited by **Dadabhai Naoroji** – not Malabari.
[193:2:3] - Work: restore Zoroastrian purity; **women's education**, removal of purdah, higher marriage age, legal status and uniform inheritance laws for Parsi women.
[193:2:4] - **Behramji M. Malabari** – child-marriage campaign → **Age of Consent Act, 1891**; Seva Sadan (1908).
[193:2:5] > Rahnumai = Parsis, Bombay 1851, Furdonji, Rast Goftar.
[193:2:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.256, p.264; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.190, p.200; old app notes row 193
## SUB 3 | Other Hindu Bodies – Radhasoami, Dev Samaj, Dharma Sabha, Bharat Dharma Mahamandal
[193:3:0] TABLE head: Body | Founder | Place, year
  [193:3:0.0] Radhasoami Satsang | Shiv Dayal Singh (Khatri) – "Soamiji Maharaj", also called Shiv Dayal Sahab | Agra, 1861 (not Haridas Swami, Agnihotri, Shraddhanand)
  [193:3:0.1] Dev Samaj | Shiv Narayan Agnihotri (ex-Brahmo) | Lahore, 1887; text Deva Shastra
  [193:3:0.2] Dharma Sabha | Radhakant Deb | Calcutta, 1830 – orthodox; opposed the abolition of sati
  [193:3:0.3] Bharat Dharma Mahamandal | Pandit Din Dayalu Sharma | Haridwar, 1887; combined 1902, HQ Varanasi – orthodox Hindus
  [193:3:0.4] Sanatan Dharma Rakshini Sabha | orthodox | Calcutta – the correctly matched pair (UPPCS 2022)
[193:3:1] - **Radhasoami:** one God, the **guru** and satsang; inner spiritual life.
[193:3:2] - **Dev Samaj:** eternity of the soul, supremacy of the guru, good action; no bribes, alcohol or meat; against child marriage.
[193:3:3] - **Bengali leader who opposed reform and supported orthodoxy = Radhakant Deb** (yet he favoured Western education, even for girls).
[193:3:4] > Radhasoami = Agra 1861; Dev Samaj = Lahore 1887; Dharma Sabha = Calcutta 1830.
[193:3:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (Ahir 2019) file p.256; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.47, p.88, p.98; old app notes row 193 (Radhasoami Agra 1861, Bharat Dharma Mahamandal)

=== NOTES 1:194 | Anti-caste and Non-brahmin Movements – Phule, Narayana Guru, Periyar, Ambedkar, Justice Party, Adi-andhra
## SUB 0 | Justice Party (South Indian Liberal Federation)
[194:0:0] # Background, aim and social base
[194:0:1] - **Why:** Brahmins were about **3%** of the Madras Presidency population but held **over 90%** of government jobs.
[194:0:2] - **Aim:** to further the interests of **non-Brahmins** (APPSC 2008, AP History PYQ ×2) – end Brahmin dominance in jobs, education, politics and religion; basically an **anti-Brahmin party** – "the first political party in India founded against Brahmins".
[194:0:3] - **Agenda of SILF:** social justice, a rightful place in services, political representation (information technology is an anachronism).
[194:0:4] - **Demand:** separate **communal representation** for non-Brahmins, on the lines given to Muslims by the Morley-Minto Reforms; opposed the Brahmin-dominated Congress.
[194:0:5] - **Social base:** non-Brahmin landed gentry, **intermediate landed castes** (Andhra: **Reddys, Kammas, Kapus**). Dalits built a parallel "Adi" movement.
[194:0:6] - **British view:** backed it to weaken **Home Rule**; used against Home Rule and Gandhi's movements; it **supported the British in the Second World War** (Congress, Forward Bloc, Yugantar did not).
[194:0:7] - **Andhra Mahasabha (Vijayawada, 1917)** sought reserved seats for non-Brahmins – **Ponaka Pattabhirama Reddy** and **Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary**.
[194:0:8] # Founding (1916-17)
[194:0:9] TABLE head: Event | Date | Detail
  [194:0:9.0] South Indian People's Association | 20 Nov 1916, Victoria Memorial Hall, Madras | ~30 non-Brahmin leaders
  [194:0:9.1] South Indian Liberal Federation (SILF) – official name | Dec 1916 | soon called the Justice Party
  [194:0:9.2] Non-Brahmin Manifesto | Dec 1916 | signed by P. Thyagaraya Chetty
  [194:0:9.3] Daily Justice (English) | 26 Feb 1917 | gave the party its name
  [194:0:9.4] First general meeting | Coimbatore, Jul 1917 | first Andhra meeting: Bikkavolu
[194:0:10] - **Founders:** **Dr T.M. Nair, P. Theagaraya Chetty, Dr C. Natesa Mudaliar** – not K. Kamaraj, not A.P. Patro; symbol **Scales**.
[194:0:11] - **Year traps:** formed **1916** (not 1910); name "Justice Party" from 1917.
[194:0:12] - **Papers:** **Justice** (English daily, edited by **T.M. Nair**); **Dravidan** (Tamil, 1917); took over the Telugu **Andhra Prakasika**.
[194:0:13] # Elections and Chief Ministers under dyarchy
[194:0:14] TABLE head: Election / CM | Fact
  [194:0:14.0] 1920 (Congress boycotted) | won 63 of 98 seats – formed the first ministry
  [194:0:14.1] A. Subbarayalu Reddiar | first CM, 17 Dec 1920 – Jul 1921 (resigned, ill health)
  [194:0:14.2] Panagal Raja (Panaganti Ramarayaningar) | CM 1921-26, two ministries; died 16 Dec 1928
  [194:0:14.3] 1923 | only 44 seats; ministry with nominated members' support
  [194:0:14.4] 1926 | Justice 22; Swaraj 41 → independent P. Subbarayan ministry (1926-30)
  [194:0:14.5] B. Munuswamy Naidu | 1930-32
  [194:0:14.6] Bobbili Raja | 1932-37 (P.T. Rajan acted 1936)
  [194:0:14.7] K.V. Reddy Naidu | Apr-Jul 1937 (interim)
  [194:0:14.8] 1937 | routed by Congress (Rajaji ministry)
[194:0:15] - **1920:** party president **P. Theagaraya Chetty declined** office, so **Subbarayalu Reddiar** became first CM. ⚠ "Leader of the Justice Party in 1920" – keys give Subbarayalu Reddiar (head of the ministry); strictly the party president was Theagaraya Chetty.
[194:0:16] - Formed government **four times** from 1920.
[194:0:17] # Andhra leaders and the separate-Andhra question
[194:0:18] TABLE head: Leader | Note
  [194:0:18.0] Panagal Raja | party president; CM 1921-26; said the Cooum river should be the boundary – north to the Andhras, south to the Tamils
  [194:0:18.1] Bobbili Raja | CM 1932-37; opposed a separate Andhra state once CM (1932); 2nd Round Table Conference delegate
  [194:0:18.2] K.V. Reddy Naidu (Eluru) | Minister 1920; CM 1937; backed an Andhra province only with a non-Brahmin majority
  [194:0:18.3] A.P. Patro | Education Minister; Andhra University Act
  [194:0:18.4] Munukuru Rama Rao | Krishna organiser
[194:0:19] - The party did **not** support the separate Andhra movement: **M. Suryanarayana's** 1922 resolution was withdrawn at **Patro's** urging.
[194:0:20] - **No-confidence motion** against Panagal: **C.R. Reddy**, Nov 1923. 1926: Swaraj leader **C.V.S. Narasimha Raju** declined to form a ministry.
[194:0:21] # Legislation and reforms
[194:0:22] TABLE head: Measure | Year | Detail
  [194:0:22.0] Communal G.O. | 1921 (not 1937) | proportional share for non-Brahmins in jobs and education; forerunner of reservation
  [194:0:22.1] Women's franchise resolution | 1921 | Madras first province to let women vote
  [194:0:22.2] Andhra University Act | 1926 | inaugurated 26 Apr 1926; Education Minister A.P. Patro
  [194:0:22.3] Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act | 1926 | –
  [194:0:22.4] Annamalai University | 1929 | –
  [194:0:22.5] Estate Land Act (1908) amended | Bobbili Raja | for zamindari tenants
[194:0:23] - Caste-based roster (50% educational seats); schools and scholarships.
[194:0:24] - **Andhra University:** first Chancellor **Lord Goschen**; first HQ **Bezawada**, later **Waltair**.
[194:0:25] # Decline
[194:0:26] - No mass base; opposed the freedom struggle; Telugu-Tamil rivalry; deaths of Thyagaraya Chetty (1925) and Panagal (1928); **Natesa Mudaliar** criticised neglect of the poor and Harijans.
[194:0:27] - **1937** defeat → Periyar dominant → **Dravidar Kazhagam (1944)**.
[194:0:28] > Justice Party = SILF, 1916, non-Brahmins; first CM Subbarayalu Reddiar (1920); Panagal 1921-26; Bobbili 1932 opposed Andhra state; Andhra University 1926.

## SUB 1 | Jyotiba Phule and the Satyashodhak Samaj
[194:1:0] # Jyotiba Phule (1827-1890)
[194:1:1] - Born **1827**, Satara; a gardener's son – **Mali community**, Maharashtra.
[194:1:2] - Title **"Mahatma"** given by **Vithalrao Krishnaji Vandekar (1888)**; called **"Father of Indian Social Revolution"**.
[194:1:3] - **Creed:** all men have the same features and intellect – **nobody is sacred by birth**; aimed at complete abolition of caste; against Sanskritic Hinduism.
[194:1:4] - **1848**: girls' school, **Pune**; taught by **Savitribai Phule** (Maharashtra) – **India's first woman teacher**; home for widows 1854; pioneer of widow remarriage → the Indian women's movement is credited largely to Phule's inspiration.
[194:1:5] - **Savitribai** headed the Samaj's women's section; worked for lower-caste girls.
[194:1:6] # Satyashodhak Samaj ("Society of Truth Seekers")
[194:1:7] - Founded **24 September 1873, Pune**, by **Jyotiba Phule** – its **first president**; an **anti-caste movement in Maharashtra** (UPSC 2016 ×3) – not a tribal, temple-entry or peasant movement.
[194:1:8] - Aim: **upliftment of the backward classes** – **Shudras and Ati-Shudras** against **Arya-Brahmin** exploitation (not for Arya-Brahmins); end of **priestly monopoly**; education of women and lower castes; social service.
[194:1:9] - Leaders from malis, telis, kunbis, saris, dhangars.
[194:1:10] - **Satyashodhak marriages**: **without priests**; allowed **inter-caste** marriage.
[194:1:11] - Symbol: **King Bali** (the oppressed) against the Brahmanical symbol of **Rama**.
[194:1:12] - **Ideas (CDS 2015 – all three true):** set up **1873** ✔; Brahmins = progeny of **'alien' Aryans** ✔; his 1880s-90s focus on the **Kunbi** peasantry privileged **Maratha identity** ✔.
[194:1:13] - **Din Bandhu** (Marathi weekly, **Pune, 1877**) – the Samaj's organ, started by **Krishnarao Bhalekar**, credited to **Phule's** movement; spread it to remote Maharashtra; later edited by **N.M. Lokhande**. Phule also ran Dinmitra.
[194:1:14] # Works of Phule
[194:1:15] TABLE head: Work | Note
  [194:1:15.0] Gulamgiri (1873) | "Slavery"; compared caste oppression with slavery
  [194:1:15.1] Shetkaryacha Asud | "The Cultivator's Whipcord"
  [194:1:15.2] Sarvajanik Satyadharma Pustak | published posthumously, 1891
  [194:1:15.3] Tritiya Ratna, Brahmananche Kasab | also Phule
[194:1:16] - Phule's symbol = **King Bali**; Justice Party symbol = **Scales**.

## SUB 3 | Adi-Andhra and Adi-Hindu Movements
[194:3:0] # Terms
[194:3:1] - **"Adi"** = original inhabitants; rejected "Panchama". **Adi-Andhra** = Dalits of the Andhra (Madras) region; **Adi-Hindu** = Dalits of Hyderabad State.
[194:3:2] - Early root: **Adi-Andhra Sabha (1890)**, first called the Pariya Mahasabha.
[194:3:3] # Madiri Bhagya Reddy Varma (born 1888, Hyderabad)
[194:3:4] - Original name **Madari Bhagaiah**; **"Father of the Dalit movement"** in Hyderabad/Andhra; used the terms **Adi-Andhra and Adi-Hindu** for Panchamas.
[194:3:5] - **Jagan Mitra Mandali (1906)** (not 1960) → **Manya Sangham (1911)** → **Adi-Hindu Social Service League**; journal **Adi Hindu**.
[194:3:6] - **Sahapankti bhojanams** (community dinners) and **Buddhism** (Buddha Jayanti from 1913) for Dalit consciousness; against child marriage, liquor, Devadasi system.
[194:3:7] - Presided over the **All India Adi Hindu Conference, Lucknow, 1930** – chose **Ambedkar** for the Round Table Conferences.
[194:3:8] # Sessions and conferences
[194:3:9] TABLE head: Event | Place | Year / person
  [194:3:9.0] Jagan Mitra Mandali | Hyderabad | 1906
  [194:3:9.1] First Adi-Andhra session (first Provincial Panchama Mahajana Sabha) | Vijayawada (Krishna district) | 1917 (4-6 Nov); organiser Guduru Ramachandra Rao
  [194:3:9.2] Second conference | Machilipatnam | 1919; President Chilukuri Venkataswamy
  [194:3:9.3] First Adi-Andhra Sadassu | Amalapuram | 1921; Undru Tatayya
  [194:3:9.4] Adi Andhrapathi Sangham | – | 1922; Undru Tatayya
  [194:3:9.5] All India Adi Hindu Conference | Lucknow | 1930; Bhagya Reddy Varma
  [194:3:9.6] Adi Andhra Mahasabha | Vizianagaram | 1936; Kusuma Dharmanna urged socialism
[194:3:10] - **⚠ Who chaired the 1917 Vijayawada sabha:** the key and South First give **Sundru Venkaiah** (Eluru); Samvit Kendra and the old notes give **Bhagya Reddy Varma** (Venkaiah in the reception). Key the option offered – Sundru Venkaiah when both appear.
[194:3:11] - 1917 resolution: replace "Panchama" by **Adi Hindu** (Hyderabad) and **Adi Andhra** (Madras); seats in local bodies; special schools; wells in Dalit wadas.
[194:3:12] - First Adi-Andhra session district = **Krishna** (Vijayawada), not Amalapuram (APPSC-GS 2025).
[194:3:13] - **Temple entry:** in the Adi-Andhra phase a Harijan **temple entry** took place at **Siddhantam** (Krishna district), **1933** (17 Dec), during **Gandhi's** Andhra tour; Gandhi collected **Harijana Bhiksha** (1932-33); Communists organised a **Coolie Sangham**.
[194:3:14] # Other Andhra Dalit leaders
[194:3:15] TABLE head: Leader | Role
  [194:3:15.0] Jala Rangaswamy | "Adi Andhra Mahatma", Seva Dhurandhara; papers Jai Bheem, Veera Bharati; book Nimna Jatula Charitra
  [194:3:15.1] Arige Ramaswamy | Madiga leader; Arundhatiya bodies for Madigas (Arundhatiya Mahasabha 1931); land rights, local-body seats
  [194:3:15.2] Undru Tatayya | Burma businessman; Dalit school at Ponnamanda (1922)
  [194:3:15.3] Kusuma Dharmanna | Adi-Andhra poet
  [194:3:15.4] Gurram Jashuva (1895-1971) | first modern Telugu Dalit poet; Gabbilam (1941); title Kavi Kokila; Padma Bhushan 1970
  [194:3:15.5] Boyi Bhimanna | Paleru, Gudiselu Kalipotunnai, Pilli Shatakam, Paleru Nundi Padmasri Daka
[194:3:16] - **Madigas** = "Arundhatiya" → **Arundhatiya Yuvajana Sangham** for marginalised Madigas (not the Adi-Hindu Social Service League).
[194:3:17] > Bhagya Reddy Varma: Jagan Mitra Mandali 1906 → Adi-Hindu League; Vijayawada 1917; Lucknow 1930. Jai Bheem = Jala Rangaswamy. Siddhantam 1933.

[194:4:6] - Place: **Vaikom (Travancore, Kerala)**; against **untouchability** – right of lower castes to use the **roads around the Vaikom temple** → part of the **Temple Entry Movement** (APPSC G2 2024; TSPSC 2015).
[194:4:7] - Leaders: **T.K. Madhavan, K.P. Kesava Menon, K. Kelappan**; backed by Narayana Guru.
[194:4:8] - **Periyar** jailed → title **"Vaikom Veerar"**.
[194:4:9] - **Gandhi** visited in 1925 and negotiated a compromise; **not a direct participant**.
[194:4:10] - Outcome → **Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation, 12 Nov 1936**.

## SUB 5 | Periyar and the Self-Respect Movement
[194:5:0] - **E.V. Ramasamy Naicker = "Periyar"**; joined the **Congress in 1920**, took part in **Non-Cooperation** (cut 1000 coconut trees in the 1921 anti-liquor drive); President and secretary of the provincial Congress.
[194:5:1] - **1925**: left Congress over **communal representation** and caste segregation at the **Cheranmadevi Gurukulam**.
[194:5:2] - **Self-Respect Movement (1925)** – the populist phase of the non-Brahmin movement, founded by **Periyar** (UPSC 2025 – not Ambedkar, Jadhav or Javalkar): rationalism; against caste hierarchy and Brahmin priests; **self-respect marriages without priests** (from 1928); women's equality.
[194:5:3] - **Aims:** equality for backward classes, acting by reason, end of superior/inferior caste notions – a lack of belonging to the state was never an aim.
[194:5:4] - **Journals:** **Kudi Arasu** (Tamil weekly, May 1925 – the movement's organ), Viduthalai, Puratchi / Revolt.
[194:5:5] - **Caste movements (APPSC G1 2018):** Satyashodhak (Maharashtra) + Self-Respect (Tamil Nadu) ✔; Ghadar (Punjab) and Bijolia (Rajasthan) ✘.
[194:5:6] - In Andhra: inspired Bhagya Reddy Varma and Jala Rangaswamy to adopt the "Adi" identity and demand temple entry.
[194:5:7] TABLE head: Event | Year
  [194:5:7.0] Anti-Hindi agitation | 1937
  [194:5:7.1] Dravidistan demand | Erode 1940
  [194:5:7.2] Dravidar Kazhagam | 1944
  [194:5:7.3] DMK – C.N. Annadurai | 17 Sept 1949; in power 1967
[194:5:8] > Self-Respect = Periyar, 1925; Kudi Arasu; left Congress 1925; Vaikom Veerar.
[194:5:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.125-126; Spectrum Modern India (Ahir) file p.258, p.870; NextGen AP History - APPSC Exams 18 p.22; old app notes row 194
## SUB 6 | Andhra Rationalists and Caste Associations
[194:6:0] # Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary (Kavi Raju)
[194:6:1] - Rationalist/atheist attack on **Puranic** caste stories, yagas and caste; Chairman of **Tenali** Municipality.
[194:6:2] - Works: **Suta Puranam**, **Shambuka Vadha**, Kurukshetra Sangramam, Khooni.
[194:6:3] - Song **"Veeragandham techinamu veerulevaro telupudi"** → **Civil Disobedience Movement**.
[194:6:4] - Popular title: **Kavi Raju**.
[194:6:5] # Gora (Goparaju Ramachandra Rao)
[194:6:6] - **Atheist Centre**: **Mudunuru, 1940** (Krishna district) → **Vijayawada, 1947**; books **Positive Atheism**, We Become Atheists.
[194:6:7] - Ran **night schools** in Dalit habitations of **Krishna district**; worked against caste and untouchability (stayed in Harijan localities).

=== NOTES 1:195 | Social and Religious Reform in Andhra – Veeresalingam, Gurajada, Venkataratnam Naidu, Gidugu
## SUB 0 | Reform-Era Journals – Vivekavardhini, Satihita Bodhini and Their Rivals
[195:0:0] # Veeresalingam's journals
[195:0:1] TABLE head: Journal | Year | Fact
  [195:0:1.0] Vivekavardhini | 1874 | Rajahmundry; first Telugu social-reform journal – social and literary reform, women's education; exposed official corruption and nautch/Bhogam melas
  [195:0:1.1] Hasya Sanjeevani | 1876 | humour journal – his satirical reply to Kokkonda's Hasyavardhini
  [195:0:1.2] Satihita Bodhini | 1883 (not 1886) | monthly for women; merged into Telugu Zenana in 1904
  [195:0:1.3] Satya Samvardhini | 1891 | journal started by Veeresalingam (NextGen, Rocket) – ⚠ old app notes credited Rayasam Venkata Siva
  [195:0:1.4] Chintamani | 1891 | political journal – Veeresalingam with Nyapati Subbarao
  [195:0:1.5] Satyavadini | 1905 | reply to Kasibhatta's Arya Mata Bodhini
[195:0:2] - **The Vivekavardhini quarrel:** **Kokkonda Venkataratnam** (orthodox, opposed women's education) ran **Andhra Bhasha Sanjeevini**; Veeresalingam first answered him in **Umaranga Nayakulu's Purushartha Pradayini** (Machilipatnam), then founded **Vivekavardhini**; Kokkonda replied with **Hasyavardhini**, Veeresalingam with **Hasya Sanjeevani**.
[195:0:3] - **Hasyavardhini = Kokkonda Venkataratnam** – NOT Veeresalingam.
[195:0:4] - **Odd one out:** Satihita Bodhini, Hasya Sanjeevani, Vivekavardhini (Veeresalingam) vs **Brahma Prakasika** (Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu).
[195:0:5] # Other journals of the reform era
[195:0:6] TABLE head: Journal | Founder / editor | Fact
  [195:0:6.0] Telugu Zenana / Janana | Rayasam Venkata Sivudu | 1893-1907, women's education; Satihita Bodhini merged into it 1904 – so NOT founded by Veeresalingam
  [195:0:6.1] Hindu Reformer | Mannava Butchaiah Pantulu | pioneer Andhra Brahmo
  [195:0:6.2] Brahma Prakasika | Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu | 1886, Brahmo ideals
  [195:0:6.3] Andhra Prakasika | A.P. (A.C.) Parthasarathi Naidu | 1885, first Telugu political weekly – not P. Anandacharyulu
  [195:0:6.4] Prakasika | Gurajada Appa Rao | tried to start it, 1896
  [195:0:6.5] Satya Doota | Christian Association of Bellary | 1835, first Telugu journal
  [195:0:6.6] Andhra Sahitya Parishat Patrika | Jayanti Ramayya Pantulu | –
  [195:0:6.7] Andhra Patrika, Bharati | Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao | –
  [195:0:6.8] Udayini | Kompella Janardhana Rao | –
  [195:0:6.9] Krishna Patrika (1902) | Konda Venkatappayya (founder, first editor), later Mutnuri Krishna Rao | Machilipatnam
  [195:0:6.10] Andhra Geeta Svarajya | Tanguturi Prakasam | 1921, Madras
  [195:0:6.11] Desabhimani | – | urged a separate government for Telugu culture
  [195:0:6.12] Desha Matha | Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham | strongly backed the Home Rule movement
  [195:0:6.13] Nilagiri Patrika | Shabnavis Venkata Ramanarasimha Rao | 1922, Nalgonda – first Telugu paper in Telangana
  [195:0:6.14] Rayyat | M. Narasinga Rao | 1927, Urdu daily, Hyderabad
  [195:0:6.15] Chandamama | B. Nagireddy and Chakrapani | July 1947, Telugu children's magazine
[195:0:7] - **APPSC G2 2019 wrong pair:** key = "Telugu Janana – Veeresalingam" (founder was Rayasam Venkata Sivudu); ⚠ "Andhra Prakasika – P. Anandacharya" is also wrong (Parthasarathi Naidu).
[195:0:8] - **Firsts:** first Telugu journal **Satya Doota (1835)**; first social-reform journal **Vivekavardhini (1874)**; first political journal **Andhra Prakasika (1885)**.
[195:0:9] - By **1905** about **20** Telugu journals.
[195:0:10] > Vivekavardhini 1874, Hasya Sanjeevani 1876, Satihita Bodhini 1883, Satya Samvardhini 1891 = Veeresalingam; Hasyavardhini = Kokkonda; Zenana = Rayasam Venkata Sivudu.

## SUB 1 | Widow Remarriage, Girls' Schools and Reform Bodies
[195:1:0] # Milestones
[195:1:1] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [195:1:1.0] 1874 | first girls' school in Andhra – Dowlaiswaram (Dhavaleswaram), near Rajahmundry; first principal Malladi Achchanna Sastri
  [195:1:1.1] 1878 | Rajahmundry Social Reform Association – first organised reform body in Andhra; for widow remarriage, against nautch girls
  [195:1:1.2] 3 Aug 1879 | lecture at Rajahmundry: widow remarriage valid by Hindu scripture
  [195:1:1.3] 1880 | Widow Remarriage Association (Stree Punarvivaha Sangham), with Challapalli Bapayya and Basavaraju Gavarraju
  [195:1:1.4] 11 Dec 1881 | first widow remarriage in Andhra, Rajahmundry
  [195:1:1.5] 15 Dec 1881 | second remarriage – Ratnamma and Racharla Ramachandraiah
  [195:1:1.6] 1881 | second girls' school, Innispeta, Rajahmundry
  [195:1:1.7] 1897 / 16 Jan 1905 | widow homes at Madras / Rajahmundry (Vitantu Saranalayam)
  [195:1:1.8] 1906 | Hitakarini Samajam, Rajahmundry – he gave it all his property; Veeresalingam its founder president
[195:1:2] - **First widow remarriage:** **11 December 1881**, at the **Ananda Udyana Mandapam** behind his house; groom **Gogulapati Sriramulu**, bride **Seethamma (Gauramma)**; money from **Paidah (Pyda) Ramakrishnayya**, Kakinada.
[195:1:3] - By 1892 he had held about **20** widow remarriages.
[195:1:4] - Bengal comparison: **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856** (Act XV, **Lord Canning**); first Bengal remarriage **7 Dec 1856** (Vidyasagar).
[195:1:5] - **Hitakarini date:** **1906**, registered **2 May 1908** (Hans India); ⚠ NextGen gives 1905.
[195:1:6] - **Rajahmundry Social Reform Association:** founded **1878** (RAS 2021 stem says 1871 – still Veeresalingam); main aim = **widow remarriages**.
[195:1:7] - **Kakinada:** Paidah Ramakrishnayya, as municipal president, funded remarriages and built houses for the grooms.
[195:1:8] - **Opponents:** **Kokkonda Venkataratnam** (Andhra Bhasha Sanjeevini); **Vedam Venkataraya Sastri** – **Stree Punarvivaha Durvada Nirvaranam (1883)**, first major anti-remarriage book; **Kasibhatta Brahmayya Sastri** – **Aryananda Brundavani Sabha**, Kakinada; A.P. Parthasarathi Naidu also opposed him – **Uma Ranganayakulu** was his ally (general knowledge, not checked for Parthasarathi Naidu).
[195:1:9] - **Mrs Manning** (UK) willed **£50** to his widow home.
[195:1:10] - Also first in Andhra: a **night school**, a **Theosophical High School**, **co-education**.
[195:1:11] - **Evils fought:** ban on widow remarriage, child marriage, **dowry, bride-price**, caste, superstition, **nautch/Bhogam**, **official corruption**; scientific education was an aim, not an evil.
[195:1:12] - **Methods:** journals and satire, lectures, schools, remarriages at his own cost, widow homes, prayer without idols – the **press, not direct politics**.
[195:1:13] > 1874 girls' school (Dowlaiswaram) → 1878 Social Reform Association → 1880 Widow Remarriage Association → 11 Dec 1881 first remarriage → 1906 Hitakarini.
[195:1:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 21 p.26-27; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.6-7; Rocket AP History p.44; thehansindia.com (Hitakarini Samajam, 1906, regd 2 May 1908); old app notes row 195
[195:1:15] - **Social laws:** Sati Regulation 1829 (Bentinck); Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856 (Canning); Native Marriage Act 1872; Age of Consent Act 1891 (Lansdowne).
## SUB 2 | Kandukuri Veeresalingam – Life and Titles
[195:2:0] # Titles
[195:2:1] TABLE head: Title | Note
  [195:2:1.0] Father of the Andhra (Telugu) Renaissance; Father of the Social Reform Movement in Andhra | most asked
  [195:2:1.1] Vidyasagar of South India (Iswarachandra Vidyasagar of the South) | given by M.G. Ranade, 1898, when Veeresalingam presided over the Indian Social Reform Congress, Madras
  [195:2:1.2] Rao Bahadur | British government, 1893
  [195:2:1.3] Gadya Tikkana ('Tikkana of prose'), Gadya Vajmaya Brahma, Yuga Karta, Andhra Vaitalikudu | –
  [195:2:1.4] Raja Rammohan Roy of Andhra (Andhra Rammohan Roy) | –
[195:2:2] - **Ranade**, not Tilak, Naoroji, Tagore, Keshab, Debendranath, D.K. Karve, N.G. Chandavarkar, Vedam Venkataraya Sastri or Mrs Manning, gave the Vidyasagar title.
[195:2:3] - **Not his titles:** Andhra Ratna (Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya), Andhra Kesari (Prakasam), Andhra Bhishma (Nyapathi Subba Rao).
[195:2:4] # Life
[195:2:5] - **Born 16 April 1848, Rajahmundry** (Subbarayudu and Purnamma); father died when he was four; first guru Atmuri Lakshmi Narasimham.
[195:2:6] - Wife **Rajyalakshmamma (Bapamma)**, married 1860.
[195:2:7] - Matriculation **1869** → first teacher's job at **Korangi** (headmaster, 1872) → Telugu pandit, Rajahmundry → **Telugu Pandit, Presidency College, Madras (1899-1904)**.
[195:2:8] - **Died 27 May 1919, Madras** (Vedanivas).
[195:2:9] - **Thought (NDA 2017):** believed in **universal education** (girls' schools, night school, co-education), science and morality, cultural nationalism.
[195:2:10] - Fought superstition – joined Korangi school on a New Moon day; gave up the sacred thread (1906); held an inter-caste marriage.
[195:2:11] > Born 1848, died 27 May 1919 Madras; Rao Bahadur 1893; Ranade's "Vidyasagar of South India" 1898.
[195:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.5-7; NextGen AP History Part 21 p.25-27; NextGen AP History Part 19 p.25; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kandukuri_Veeresalingam; old app notes row 195
## SUB 3 | Veeresalingam's Literary Works – the First Telugu Novel
[195:3:0] TABLE head: Work | Fact
  [195:3:0.0] Rajasekhara Charitra (1878) | first Telugu novel; based on Goldsmith's The Vicar of Wakefield
  [195:3:0.1] Satyaraju Purvadesayatralu | based on Swift's Gulliver's Travels
  [195:3:0.2] Brahma Vivaham | satire on the opponents of reform
  [195:3:0.3] Satyavati Charitra, Victoria Maharani Charitra, Esuchristu Charitra | prose works
  [195:3:0.4] Autobiography | first Telugu autobiography
  [195:3:0.5] Abhijnana Sakuntalam, Malavikagnimitram, Ratnavali, Panchatantra | first to render Sanskrit drama into Telugu
[195:3:1] - **First Telugu novel = Rajasekhara Charitra** – NOT Malapalli (Unnava Lakshminarayana), Hemalatha or Ramachandra Vijayam (Chilakamarthi), Ekavira, Chivaraku Migiledi.
[195:3:2] - **Odd one out:** Rajasekhara Charitra is a **novel**; Gayopakhyanam (Chilakamarthi) and Kichaka Vadha are **plays**.
[195:3:3] - He was the **first to render drama in Telugu** – the **modern Telugu stage** began with him.
[195:3:4] - **Kasibhatta Brahmayya Sastri** called Rajasekhara Charitra a mere translation.
[195:3:5] - **Kasiyatra Charitra** (travelogue) = **Enugula Veeraswamayya**, not C.P. Brown.
[195:3:6] - **C.P. Brown** (Collector of Cuddapah): Telugu-English dictionaries, Vemana's verses; praised Telugu's word-for-word explanation.
[195:3:7] - **Life or Death: A Plea for Vernaculars** = P.T. Srinivasa Ayyangar.
[195:3:8] > Rajasekhara Charitra 1878 ← Vicar of Wakefield; Satyaraju ← Gulliver's Travels; first autobiography.
[195:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.6-7, p.10-11; NextGen AP History Part 21 p.26; NextGen AP History Part 6 p.7; Rocket AP History p.9, p.20; old app notes row 195
## SUB 4 | Brahmo and Prarthana Samaj in Andhra
[195:4:0] - **First Prarthana (Brahmo) Samaj in Andhra:** **Rajahmundry, 1878**, by **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** – not Sivanatha Sastri, Venkataratnam Naidu or Mokkapati Subbarayudu.
[195:4:1] - Founded **under the influence of Mannava Butchaiah Pantulu** – the **first Andhra Brahmo**, editor of the **Hindu Reformer**.
[195:4:2] - **Founder of the Brahmo Samaj in (united) Andhra = Veeresalingam**; **R. Venkataratnam Naidu spread it**.
[195:4:3] - **Brahmo Trinity (Brahmatraya):** **Veeresalingam, Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu, Desiraju Peda Bapayya** – not Chilakamarthi or Mannava.
[195:4:4] - **Desiraju Peda Bapayya (Bapatla):** first practising (**Anushthana**) Brahmo; helped Veeresalingam become an Anushthana Brahmo (giving up the sacred thread); paper **Voice of Truth**; **Young Men's Prayer Union**, **Temperance and Social Purity Association**, Rajahmundry.
[195:4:5] - **Chembeti Sridharalu Naidu** (Madras): renamed the Veda Samaj the **Dakshina Bharata Brahmo Samaj**; **translated Brahmo books into Tamil and Telugu**.
[195:4:6] - **Centres:** Rajahmundry (Veeresalingam), **Kakinada** (Venkataratnam's Brahma Mandir), **Pithapuram** (Raja Surya Rao, patron) – "all are correct".
[195:4:7] TABLE head: Year | Samaj | Founder
  [195:4:7.0] 1878 | Prarthana Samaj, Rajahmundry | Veeresalingam
  [195:4:7.1] 1882 | Brahmo Samaj, Machilipatnam | R. Venkataratnam Naidu
  [195:4:7.2] 1887 | Brahmo Samaj (Brahmo Mandir), Rajahmundry | –
  [195:4:7.3] 1888 | Kakinada Samaj | Tayi Surya Prakasarao Naidu
  [195:4:7.4] 1898 | Guntur Samaj | Pillarisetty Sitaramayya
[195:4:8] - **K. Seethamma** organised its women's wing.
[195:4:9] - Prarthana Samaj did **not** reject idol worship or caste outright; the Brahmo Samaj did.
[195:4:10] - **Pithapuram Raja** gave **Rs 1 lakh** to the Brahma Dharma Prachara Nidhi – to train preachers and translate Bengali Brahmo books.
[195:4:11] - Decline: splits after Venkataratnam Naidu joined the **Justice Party**.
[195:4:12] > 1878 Rajahmundry Prarthana Samaj = Veeresalingam (influence: Mannava Butchaiah); Trinity = Veeresalingam, Venkataratnam Naidu, Peda Bapayya.
[195:4:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.2, p.6, p.8; NextGen AP History Part 6 p.8; Rocket AP History p.22, p.33; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.188; old app notes row 195
## SUB 5 | Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu – Social Purity and Anti-Nautch
[195:5:0] - **Titles:** **Brahmarshi** (1932), Kulapati, Abhinava Socrates, **Knighthood (1924)** – first non-official educator knighted; the Telugu "Uttama Purusha".
[195:5:1] - **Papers:** **Brahma Prakasika**, Fellow Worker, People's Friend.
[195:5:2] - **Social Purity Association (Samajika Shuddhi Samajam):** **1891**, Bandar (Machilipatnam) – against **Bhogam melas** (nautch).
[195:5:3] - **Bhogam (devadasi) caste** disappeared from Andhra society mainly through **his** efforts – not Veeresalingam, Gurajada or Unnava.
[195:5:4] - **Career:** Noble College lecturer; principal, **Mahbub College, Secunderabad** (Hyderabad) and **Pithapuram Raja's College, Kakinada (1905-18)**; **Vice-Chancellor, Madras University (1919-22)** – first Telugu VC.
[195:5:5] - **Brahmo work:** inspired by **Pandit Sivanath Sastri**; Brahmo Samaj Machilipatnam (1882); **Brahma Mandir at Kakinada**; condemned idol worship.
[195:5:6] - Kept away from the **national movement**; did not join the Theosophical (Divyajnana) Society.
[195:5:7] > Venkataratnam Naidu = Brahmarshi; Social Purity Association 1891; anti-Bhogam; VC Madras.
[195:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.8; Rocket AP History p.20, p.43, p.56; old app notes row 195
## SUB 6 | Gurajada, Gidugu, Tripuraneni and the Language Movement
[195:6:0] # Gurajada Appa Rao (1861-1915)
[195:6:1] - **Kanyasulkam** – social play on **bride-price** and child marriage, in spoken (vyavaharika) Telugu, **Srikakulam dialect**; written 1890, **first staged 13 Aug 1892** (Jagannatha Vilasa Nataka Sangham, Vizianagaram; NextGen: 1893), **published 1897** (Vavilla), 2nd edition 1909 dedicated to **Ananda Gajapati**.
[195:6:2] - Characters: **Madhuravani** – reformed courtesan; **Girisham** – educated fraud; Ramappa Pantulu – hypocrite; Buchamma – widow; **Soujanya Rao** – reformer.
[195:6:3] - Kanyasulkam is NOT by Kommaraju Lakshmana Rao, Veeresalingam or Panuganti.
[195:6:4] - Other works: **Mutyala Saralu** (1910, new metre), **Diddubatu** (first modern Telugu short story), **Purnamma** (girl married off for money), Kanyaka; Saranga Dhara (1883) – English poem with brother Shyamala Rao.
[195:6:5] - Song **Desamunu Preminchumanna** – "Desamante matti kadoyi, desamante manushuloyi" (a country is its people, not its soil).
[195:6:6] - Patron court: **Vizianagaram** (Ananda Gajapati); titles Navayuga Vaitalikudu.
[195:6:7] # Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (1863-1940)
[195:6:8] - Born **29 Aug 1863, Ponduru (Srikakulam)**; Telugu teacher at **Parlakimidi**; **Telugu Language Day = 29 August** (his birthday).
[195:6:9] - **Father of the Vyavaharika (spoken Telugu) movement**, against the Sanskritised **granthika** style; title Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Pitamaha; **Kaisar-e-Hind (1934)**.
[195:6:10] - **Savara:** script, Savara-Telugu dictionaries, **Savara grammar/manual in English (1931)**, Savara-English dictionary (1936).
[195:6:11] - Works: **A Memorandum on Modern Telugu**, Bala Kavi Saranyam; monthly **Telugu (1919)**.
[195:6:12] - **Vartamana Vyavaharikandhra Bhasha Parivartaka Samajam:** **founded by Veeresalingam** (president), **Gidugu secretary** – not founded by Gidugu.
[195:6:13] - Grammars: Andhra Bhashanusasanam – Malladi Suryanarayana Sastri; Vyavaharika Bhasha Vyakaranam – Vadlamudi Gopalakrishnayya; Aadhunikapramanikandhra Vyakaranam – Vajjala Venkateswarlu.
[195:6:14] - Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Samstha (1910, after a Visakhapatnam meeting); inspired by **J.A. Yates**.
[195:6:15] TABLE head: Side | Leaders
  [195:6:15.0] Granthika (classical) | Kokkonda Venkataratnam, Jayanti Ramayya Pantulu (Andhra Sahitya Parishad; A Defence of Literary Telugu, 1913), Vedam Venkataraya Sastri
  [195:6:15.1] Vyavaharika (spoken) | Gidugu, Gurajada (Minute of Dissent, 1914), Tapi Dharma Rao (Janavani)
[195:6:16] - **Madras University (April 1913):** Telugu Composition Committee for the **Intermediate** course; the majority kept the **literary dialect**.
[195:6:17] - Telugu got **classical language** status in **2008**.
[195:6:18] # Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary – 'Kaviraju'
[195:6:19] - Rationalist; attacked caste and Brahmin priestly dominance through literature – **Sutapuranam**, **Sambuka Vadha**, Khooni.
[195:6:20] - Song **"Veeragandhamu techinaramu"** – Civil Disobedience.
[195:6:21] - **Statements (NTRUHS JA):** Veeragandhamu – Tripuraneni ✔; Gadya Tikkana – Veeresalingam ✔; Kanyasulkam in vernacular – Gurajada ✔ → **A, B and C**.
[195:6:22] > Kanyasulkam = Gurajada (1892/1897); Gidugu = vyavaharika, 29 Aug; Samajam = Veeresalingam president, Gidugu secretary.
[195:6:23] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.9, p.12-13; NextGen AP History Part 6 p.13; Rocket AP History p.9, p.22; thehansindia.com (Gidugu, 2018-08-29); old app notes row 195
[195:6:24] - Gurajada worked alongside **Veeresalingam** in the literary and cultural renaissance.
## SUB 7 | Background – Centres, Women's Bodies and Missions
[195:7:0] - **Rajahmundry** = Andhra's first renaissance centre and centre of reform, prose, journalism and the novel; peak **1870-1935**; led by the **English-educated middle class**; other centres Kakinada, Machilipatnam, Bapatla (Peda Bapayya), Guntur; **Kavi Club, Kumudavalli (1897)**.
[195:7:1] - Cradle of the language movement: **North Coastal Andhra** (Vizianagaram, Srikakulam, Parlakimidi).
[195:7:2] - **Atmuri Lakshmi Narasimham** – first guru of the early reform movement.
[195:7:3] - **Ram Mohan Roy School (1909)** – Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham.
[195:7:4] # Women's bodies
[195:7:5] TABLE head: Body | Leader / year
  [195:7:5.0] First women's association | Kotikalapudi Seethamma, Rajahmundry, 1902
  [195:7:5.1] Stree Samajam, Brundavanapuram (Machilipatnam) | Bhandaru Acchamamba, 1902
  [195:7:5.2] Hindu Sundari, Kakinada | Mosalikanti Ramabai, Vempati Shantabai
  [195:7:5.3] Devadasi Bill | Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, Chodagam Ammannaraja – passed 1947
[195:7:6] - **First Andhra Social Reform Conference, 1908:** **Masulipatnam** (printed key; not verified).
[195:7:7] - **Karunalayam (1909)** – Pithapuram Raja; the only orphanage in Andhra.
[195:7:8] # Missions and other bodies

  [195:7:9.0] London Missionary Society | 1805, Jammalamadugu (Cuddapah)

  [195:7:9.2] Church Mission Society | Krishna-Godavari from 1841; Machilipatnam school 1843 (Rev. Noble)
  [195:7:9.3] Lutheran (Pennsylvania Synod) | Guntur, Prattipadu, Nallapadu
  [195:7:9.4] North German Mission | Godavari

  [195:7:9.6] Madras Mahajana Sabha | 1884
  [195:7:9.7] Andhra Desa Library Association | Iyyanki Venkata Ramanaiah, 1914
  [195:7:9.8] Sri Krishnadevaraya Andhra Bhasha Nilayam | Komarraju Lakshmana Rao, Ravichettu Ranga Rao, Nayani Venkata Ranga Rao; Hyderabad, 1901
  [195:7:9.9] MIM | Mahmood Nawaz Khan Qiledar, 1927
[195:7:10] - **American Baptist Mission date:** **1866** (NextGen, Rocket; Ongole church "began functioning from 1866" – Hans India) – ⚠ some keys give 1867.
[195:7:11] - Mission schools admitted **Sudras and Panchamas**.
[195:7:12] - **Theosophical Society:** New York **1875** (Blavatsky, Olcott); Adyar **1882**; **Jiddu Krishnamurti** – born **Madanapalle** 1895, identified by **Leadbeater** (1909), left **1929**.
[195:7:13] - Titles: **Andhra Ratna** – Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya; **Kavi Raju** – Tripuraneni; **Father of Andhra Drama** – Dharmavaram Krishnamacharyulu.
[195:7:14] > Kotikalapudi Seethamma – Rajahmundry 1902; American Baptist Mission 1866 (Ongole, Lone Star).

=== NOTES 1:196 | Cultural Institutions and the Telugu Renaissance in the Early 20TH Century
## SUB 0 | C.P. Brown and the Colonial Scholars of Telugu
[196:0:0] # Charles Philip Brown (1798-1884)
[196:0:1] - **Post:** British revenue officer; **Collector of Cuddapah (Kadapa)**; learnt Telugu from **Kodandarama Pantulu**.
[196:0:2] - **Vemana:** **C.P. Brown collected the poems of Vemana** (about 2,000) and published **Verses of Vemana (1829)**; named Vemana's metre **Ataveladi**.
[196:0:3] - **Dictionaries:** **C.P. Brown** compiled the **first Telugu-English and English-Telugu dictionaries (1852-53)** – not Munro, Campbell or Cotton; his Telugu Grammar came in **1840**.
[196:0:4] - **Classics:** edited **Nannaya, Tikkana and Pothana**; preserved Mackenzie's **Kaifiyats** in the Madras Library.
[196:0:5] - **"Italian of the East":** **C.P. Brown called Telugu the "Italian of the East"** (exam answer); the phrase is first traced to the 15th-century traveller **Nicolo de Conti**.
[196:0:6] - **C.P. Brown Memorial Trust Library = Kadapa (Cuddapah)**, built on the site of Brown's old bungalow ("Brown's College") – not Rajahmundry, Kakinada or Anantapur (APPSC G2 2001, 2005 and AP History ×2).
[196:0:7] # Other scholars
[196:0:8] TABLE head: Scholar | Contribution
  [196:0:8.0] Benjamin Schultze | German Lutheran, Danish-Halle Mission; came 1719; began the first Telugu Bible translation (1727); Telugu Bible and books printed at Halle, Germany (1746-47)
  [196:0:8.1] Colin Mackenzie (1754-1821) | Reached the Amaravati Stupa in 1797; first Surveyor General (1815); collected the Kaifiyats with the Kavali brothers (Borraiah, Venkataramaiah, Lakshmaiah)
  [196:0:8.2] William Carey | Serampore Mission; first printed Telugu Bible (NT 1812, full 1818-19); Telugu typefaces
  [196:0:8.3] A.D. Campbell | First systematic Telugu grammar (1816)
  [196:0:8.4] Thomas Munro | Kept Telugu as an administrative language
[196:0:9] # Gentoo
[196:0:10] - **Gentoo:** European name for the **Telugu** people and language (Madras Presidency), most likely from Portuguese **gentio** ("gentile, heathen") – so "a term of the Portuguese" (APPSC G2 2019 key). William Brown's **Grammar of the Gentoo Language (1817)** used the same word for Telugu.
[196:0:11] > Recall angle: library → Kadapa; Vemana and the dictionary → C.P. Brown; first systematic grammar → Campbell; Kaifiyats → Mackenzie.
[196:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.19-20; NextGen previous papers p.21, p.34, p.42; Rocket AP History p.3, p.10; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._P._Brown; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentoo_(term); app notes 1:196 (sub 1, 2)
## SUB 1 | Telugu Literary Works and Their Authors
[196:1:0] TABLE head: Work | Author | Note
  [196:1:0.0] Rajasekhara Charitramu (1878) | Kandukuri Veeresalingam | First Telugu novel (Rushi, Mohita are not his)
  [196:1:0.1] Hitasuchini (1862) | Swamineni Muddu Narasimham (Naidu) | First collection of essays in modern Telugu prose; condemned caste discrimination – not Mamidi Venkayya or Atmuri Lakshminarasimham
  [196:1:0.2] Kasiyatra Charitra | Enugula Veeraswamy (Veeraswamayya) | Translator in the Madras court; Hindu Literary Society; women's education
  [196:1:0.3] Ramachandra Vijayam | Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham | "Andhra Milton", blind bard; also Ganapati, play Gayopakhyanam
  [196:1:0.4] Asamardhuni Jeevayatra | Tripuraneni Gopichand | First psychological novel in Telugu; middle-class life – not Sri Sri, N.G. Ranga or Rachakonda
  [196:1:0.5] Musalamma Maranamu (printed 1900) | Kattamanchi Ramalinga (C.R.) Reddy | A woman gives her life to save the village from a reservoir breach
  [196:1:0.6] Kavitva Vicharamu (1914) | C.R. Reddy | Start of modern Telugu literary criticism
  [196:1:0.7] Kanyasulkam | Gurajada Apparao | Bride-price; first staged 1893
  [196:1:0.8] Gabbilam (1941) | Gurram Jashuva | A bat carries a Dalit's prayer to God
  [196:1:0.9] Veyi Padagalu | Viswanatha Satyanarayana | "A Thousand Hoods"
  [196:1:0.10] Ramayana Kalpavrukshamu | Viswanatha Satyanarayana | First Telugu Jnanpith
  [196:1:0.11] Sakshi essays (from 1913) | Panuganti Lakshminarasimha Rao | Prose humour and social criticism
[196:1:1] - **C.R. Reddy** was the **first Vice-Chancellor of Andhra University (1926)** (first at Vijayawada, later Visakhapatnam) – not Radhakrishnan or Venkataratnam Naidu; Lord Goschen was its first Chancellor.
[196:1:2] - **Veeresalingam** first rendered Kalidasa's **Abhijnana Shakuntalam** and **Malavikagnimitram** into Telugu.
[196:1:3] > Trap: Asamardhuni Jeevayatra (×3) = Gopichand; Musalamma Maranamu = C.R. Reddy, not Gopichand or Gurajada.
[196:1:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.4-6, p.10; NextGen AP History Part 18 p.12; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.18; NextGen AP History Part 6 p.12; Rocket AP History p.9, p.21; app notes 1:196 (sub 4)
## SUB 2 | Telugu Firsts – Printing, the Bible and Early Journals
[196:2:0] TABLE head: First | Work / person | Year
  [196:2:0.0] Kavya in pure Telugu | Yayati Charitra – Ponnekanti Telaganaryudu | 1572
  [196:2:0.1] First book printed in Telugu | The Bible – Benjamin Schultze's translation, printed at Halle | 1746-47
  [196:2:0.2] First printed Telugu Bible in India | William Carey, Serampore | NT 1812
  [196:2:0.3] First systematic grammar | A.D. Campbell | 1816
  [196:2:0.4] First Telugu journal | Satyaduta (Satyadoota) – Christian Mission (Christian Society) of Bellary | 1835
  [196:2:0.5] Second Telugu journal | Vartamana Tarangini – Sayyad Rahamtulla | 8 June 1842
  [196:2:0.6] Shakespeare in Telugu | Seesari Charitra (Julius Caesar) – Vavilala Vasudeva Sastri | 1875
  [196:2:0.7] First social drama | Nandaka Rajyam – Vavilala Vasudeva Sastri | –
  [196:2:0.8] First translation from Arabic | Char Darvesh → Nagu Pakirula Charitra – Erramalli Mallikarjunudu | –
  [196:2:0.9] First Andhra Mahamahopadhyaya | Kokkonda Venkataratnam – "Andhra Bhasha Johnson" | 1907
[196:2:1] - **First Telugu journal published from Bellary = Satyaduta** (NextGen PYQ book); the old key "Tatvabodhini" was wrong.
[196:2:2] - **Tatvabodhini (1864-70):** a Telugu journal of the 1858-85 period, praised for its impact – not the first, and not the Bellary mission paper. (Do not confuse with Debendranath Tagore's Bengali **Tattvabodhini Patrika**, 1839.)
[196:2:3] # Other early journals
[196:2:4] TABLE head: Journal | Place | Fact
  [196:2:4.0] Vrittanti (Chennapuri Vrittanti) | Madras | 1837-38
  [196:2:4.1] Hitavadi | Masulipatnam | 1848, J. Edmund Sharky, Christian propaganda
  [196:2:4.2] Ginnekasu | Madras | 1849, weekly
  [196:2:4.3] Dinavartamani | Madras | 1855-72, weekly
  [196:2:4.4] Vivekavardhini | Rajahmundry | 1874, Veeresalingam – answered Kokkonda's Andhra Bhasha Sanjivani
[196:2:5] - **Place pairs:** **Bellary – Satyaduta**; Halle – Schultze's books; Serampore – Carey's Bible; Masulipatnam – Hitavadi.
[196:2:6] - **Press curbs:** Warren Hastings (1798), **Adams Regulation (1823)**, **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, Press Acts (**1908, 1910**) – controls on the press, not self-government.
[196:2:7] - In the early missionary period **education in Andhra was mostly by Christian missionaries**.
[196:2:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 11 p.1-2; NextGen previous papers p.23, p.31, p.45; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.17, p.20; Rocket AP History p.3, p.20; app notes 1:196 (sub 0, 3)
## SUB 3 | Literary Associations and Cultural Bodies
[196:3:0] - **Andhra Sahitya Parishat:** founded **1911 at Madras**, later at **Kakinada**; sessions at **Rajahmundry** (1912, 1913) presided over by **Kokkonda Venkataratnam**; since **1973** the **Andhra Sahitya Parishat Government Museum and Research Institute, Kakinada**.
[196:3:1] - **Sri Krishnadevaraya Andhra Bhasha Nilayam** (Hyderabad, **1901**): Komarraju Lakshmana Rao, Ravichettu Ranga Rao, Nayani Venkata Ranga Rao.
[196:3:2] - **Vijnana Chandrika Mandali:** publishing body; first editor **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao**, later Komarraju Lakshmana Rao. **Komarraju Lakshmana Rao** also published the Telugu encyclopaedia **Andhra Vijnana Sarvasvam**.
[196:3:3] - **Young Men's Association, Rajahmundry:** active in **Bipin Chandra Pal's Rajahmundry visit** (1907). **Young Men's Literary Association** (Guntur): **Jonnavittula Gurunatham**.
[196:3:4] - **Rajahmundry** – Veeresalingam's base, a cultural capital since **Eastern Chalukya** times.
[196:3:5] - **Kokkonda Venkataratnam** – orthodox scholar, "Andhra Bhasha Johnson"; **Veeresalingam** – Gadya Tikkana, father of the Telugu renaissance.
[196:3:6] - **Telugu Language Day – 29 August**, birth anniversary of **Gidugu Ramamurthy**; Telugu a **classical language** since **2008**.
[196:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.9-12; app notes 1:196 (sub 5, 6, 7)

=== NOTES 1:197 | Women's Question in the 19TH Century – Widow Remarriage, Age of Consent, Education, Women's Organisations
## SUB 0 | Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar and Widow Remarriage
[197:0:0] # Vidyasagar (1820-1891)
[197:0:1] - **Widow remarriage:** the reformer who worked successfully to **legalise widow remarriage**; he **cited the ancient (Vedic) texts** (Parashara) to show widows could remarry → **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856)**, drafted under **Dalhousie**, **passed under Lord Canning** (July 1856).
[197:0:2] - **First lawful Hindu widow remarriage:** **Calcutta, 7 December 1856**, under his supervision.
[197:0:3] - **Women's education:** in 1850 Bethune made him **Secretary of the Hindu Female School**, later the **Bethune School** (founded **1849** by **J.E.D. Bethune**, with Dakshinaranjan Mukherjee); he ran about **35 girls' schools**.
[197:0:4] - **Principal of the Sanskrit College, Calcutta** (1851) – opened it to non-Brahmins; title "**Vidyasagar**" (Ocean of Learning) for his Sanskrit learning.
[197:0:5] - **Books:** **Bahubivah (Bahu Bibaho)** against polygamy; Bidhobabivah (widow remarriage); **Barnaparichay** (Bengali primer); his prose shaped modern **Bengali**.
[197:0:6] - **Somprakash (Som / Shome Prakash), 1858:** Bengali weekly **started on Vidyasagar's plan**, edited by Dwarkanath Vidyabhushan – keys answer **Vidyasagar**.
[197:0:7] - **Quote:** "I have no time to think about God; a lot of work has to be done on this earth" – **Vidyasagar**.
[197:0:8] - **Not his:** **Sambad Kaumudi** (1821) and **Mirat-ul-Akhbar** (1822) were **Rammohan Roy**'s; the 1829 sati ban was Roy's campaign under **Bentinck** (not Keshab Chandra Sen).
[197:0:9] - Andhra link: he sent support for **Veeresalingam's** third widow remarriage.
[197:0:10] # Widow remarriage elsewhere
[197:0:11] TABLE head: Reformer | Body / work
  [197:0:11.0] Vishnu Parashuram Shastri Pandit | Widow Remarriage Association (Society), Bombay, 1850s (PMF: Vidhva Vivaha Uttejak Mandal, 1866); led the campaign in Maharashtra; journal Indu Prakash
  [197:0:11.1] M.G. Ranade | Widow Remarriage Association, 1865
  [197:0:11.2] D.K. Karve | Married a widow (1893); Widow Marriage Association (1893)
  [197:0:11.3] Karsondas Mulji | Satya Prakash (Gujarati, 1852)
[197:0:12] > Trap: the Widow Remarriage **Society/Association** was founded by **Vishnu Shastri Pandit**, not Vidyasagar (who led the law campaign). Bankim Chandra was one of the **first two graduates of Calcutta University (1858)**.
[197:0:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.35, p.45, p.173-174, p.181, p.195; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.171; Spectrum p.228-229; app notes 1:197 (sub 2)
## SUB 1 | Social-Reform Acts – Year, Governor-General, Provision
[197:1:0] TABLE head: Year | Act | Governor-General | Provision
  [197:1:0.0] 1795, 1804 | Bengal Regulations XXI and III | – | Infanticide declared murder
  [197:1:0.1] 1802 | Anti-infanticide regulation | Wellesley | Child sacrifice at Sagar Island banned
  [197:1:0.2] 1829 | Sati Regulation (XVII) | William Bentinck | Sati illegal; abetment = culpable homicide
  [197:1:0.3] 1843 | Act V of 1843 | Ellenborough | Slavery illegal (Charter Act 1833 had directed abolition; IPC 1860 made slave trade an offence)
  [197:1:0.4] 1850 | Caste Disabilities Removal Act (Lex Loci, Act XXI) | Dalhousie | A convert to Christianity could still inherit ancestral property
  [197:1:0.5] 1856 | Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (Act XV) | Drafted Dalhousie, passed Canning | Widow remarriage legal; children legitimate
  [197:1:0.6] 1870 | Female Infanticide Prevention Act | Mayo | Compulsory registration of births; watch on female infants
  [197:1:0.7] 1872 | Native (Civil / Brahmo) Marriage Act – Act III of 1872 | – | A social-reform Act: girls 14, boys 18; inter-caste allowed; polygamy barred; urged by Keshab Chandra Sen
  [197:1:0.8] 1891 | Age of Consent Act | Lansdowne | Consent (consummation) for girls raised from 10 to 12
  [197:1:0.9] 1929 | Child Marriage Restraint Act (Sarda Act) | Irwin | Prevention of child marriage: girls 14, boys 18; moved by Har Bilas Sarda; in force 1 April 1930
[197:1:1] - **Order:** Caste Disabilities (1850) → Widows' Remarriage (1856) → Age of Consent (1891) → Child Marriage Restraint (1929).
[197:1:2] - **Ages ladder:** consent 10 (IPC 1860) → **12 (1891)** → 14 (1925) → 16 (1949) → 18 (POCSO 2012 / BNS); marriage 14/18 (1872, 1929) → **18/21** (1978 amendment; **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006**). The 2021 proposal to raise women's age to 21 is not law (as of 2026).
[197:1:3] - **Thuggee:** suppressed by **Colonel William Sleeman** (1830s).
[197:1:4] - Keshab's 1878 marriage of his minor daughter to the **Cooch Behar** prince broke the 1872 Act and split the Brahmo Samaj.
[197:1:5] > Trap: Female Infanticide Act = **1870 (Mayo)**, not 1856; 1872 and 1929 = **14/18**, 1891 = **12**.
[197:1:6] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.228-229; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.25, p.171, p.174, p.196; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.18; Rocket Indian Society p.39; app notes 1:197 (sub 0, 1, 4)
## SUB 2 | Age of Consent Act 1891 – Malabari, Tilak, Rakhmabai
[197:2:0] - **Behramji M. Malabari** (1853-1912): **Parsi** from Western India (born Baroda), "**greatest Parsi social reformer of the 19th century**"; editor of **Indian Spectator** and **Voice of India**; **Notes on Infant Marriage and Enforced Widowhood (1884)**; **chief crusader for the Age of Consent Act**.
[197:2:1] - **Tilak opposed** the Bill (Kesari) as foreign interference in Hindu custom – so "Tilak supported the Bill" is the wrong statement; the Moderates (Ranade, Telang, Bhandarkar) supported it.
[197:2:2] - **Rakhmabai case (1884-88):** married as a child, she refused to live with husband Dadaji; he sued for **restitution of conjugal rights** – the case raised **age of consent** and conjugal rights, **not women's education**; she became one of India's first women doctors.
[197:2:3] - **Phulmoni Dasi** (1889-90): a child bride's death that pushed the 1891 Act.
[197:2:4] - The 1891 Act made intercourse with a girl **below 12** an offence, married or not.
[197:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.185, p.196, p.198; Spectrum p.229, p.255; app notes 1:197 (sub 3)
## SUB 3 | Western India Women Reformers – Phule, Ramabai, Karve

  [197:3:0.1] Pandita Ramabai (1858-1922) | Titles "Pandita" and "Saraswati" (Calcutta, 1878); Arya Mahila Samaj, Pune, 30 Nov 1882 (against child marriage); Sharada Sadan (Bombay 1889, moved to Poona) – home for widows; Mukti Mission, Kedgaon (1898); *The High-Caste Hindu Woman*
  [197:3:0.2] D.K. Karve (1858-1962) | Known for widow remarriage (married a widow, Widow Marriage Association 1893); Hindu Widows' Home, Hingne, Poona (1896); first Women's University (1916), now SNDT (Indian Women's University); Bharat Ratna 1958
  [197:3:0.3] Tarabai Shinde | *Stri Purush Tulana* (1882)
  [197:3:0.4] Anandibai Joshi (1865-87) | First Indian woman with a degree in Western medicine

## SUB 5 | Andhra – Veeresalingam and Women's Reform
[197:5:0] - **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** performed the **first widow remarriage in Andhra – 11 December 1881**, Rajahmundry (bride **Sitamma/Gauramma**, groom **Gogulapati Sriramulu**; aid from Pyda Ramakrishnaiah); second on 15 Dec 1881.
[197:5:1] - **Girls' schools:** **Dowlaiswaram, 1874** (first in Andhra); **Innispeta, Rajahmundry, 1881**; co-education.
[197:5:2] - **Widow Remarriage Association, Rajahmundry (1880)**; Madras widow home (**1897**); Hitakarini Samajam (**1905**).
[197:5:3] - Journal for women **Satihita Bodhini (1883)**.
[197:5:4] - Title **"Vidyasagar of South India"** from **M.G. Ranade**.
[197:5:5] TABLE head: Person | Contribution
  [197:5:5.0] Kandukuri Rajyalakshmamma | Veeresalingam's wife; hosted widow and inter-caste marriages; sheltered widows
  [197:5:5.1] Bandaru Achamamba | Abala Sachcharitra Ratnamala (lives of famous women); early Telugu woman historian and short-story writer
  [197:5:5.2] Unnava Lakshmibayamma | Widow asylum, Guntur (1902) → Sarada Niketan; monthly Sri Sarada Niketanam
  [197:5:5.3] Kotikalapudi Seethamma | Ahalya Bai; Sadhu Rakshana Shatakam
[197:5:6] > Dates: Bengal **7 Dec 1856** (Vidyasagar) vs Andhra **11 Dec 1881** (Veeresalingam).
