=== NOTES 1:198 | Growth of Nationalism – Factors; Pre-congress Political Associations
## SUB 0 | Pre-Congress Political Associations – Bengal, Bombay and London
[198:0:0] TABLE head: Association | Year | Founder / leader | Place
  [198:0:0.0] Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha | 1836 | Associates of Rammohan Roy | Calcutta (NextGen: the first organised political association)
  [198:0:0.1] Landholders' Society (Zamindari Association) | 1838 (PMF 1837) | Dwarkanath Tagore, Prasanna Kumar Tagore, Radhakant Deb | Calcutta – the first political organisation in the keys; landlords' interests
  [198:0:0.2] British India Society | 1839 | William Adam | London
  [198:0:0.3] Bengal British India Society | 1843 | George Thompson, Dwarkanath Tagore | Calcutta
  [198:0:0.4] British Indian Association | 1851 | Merger of the two above; first president Radhakant Deb, secretary Debendranath Tagore | Calcutta – the major landlord body of 1851
  [198:0:0.5] Bombay Association | 1852 | Jagannath Shankar Sheth | Bombay
  [198:0:0.6] Madras Native Association | 1852 | Gazula Lakshminarasu Chetty | Madras
  [198:0:0.7] East India Association | 1866 | Dadabhai Naoroji | London
  [198:0:0.8] Poona Sarvajanik Sabha | 1870 (began 1867) | M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi ("Sarvajanik Kaka"), S.H. Chiplunkar | Poona – not V.B. Phadke
  [198:0:0.9] Indian League | 1875 | Sisir Kumar Ghosh | Calcutta
  [198:0:0.10] Indian Association (Indian National Association) | 26 July 1876 | Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose | Calcutta – the most important pre-Congress body
  [198:0:0.11] Madras Mahajana Sabha | 1884 | M. Viraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer, P. Anandacharlu | Madras
  [198:0:0.12] Bombay Presidency Association | 1885 | Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang, Badruddin Tyabji | Bombay
[198:0:1] - **All the above were pre-Congress bodies** (INC 1885) – the Indian Association (1876) included.
[198:0:2] - **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha** sent the **1875 petition to the House of Commons** demanding India's **direct representation in the British Parliament**.
[198:0:3] - **Debendranath Tagore** was a founder (secretary) of the **British Indian Association**; he reorganised, but did not found, the Brahmo Samaj (Rammohan Roy, 1828).
[198:0:4] - **G.V. Joshi at the Delhi Durbar (1877):** asked the Queen to give Indians the **same political and social status as British subjects**.
[198:0:5] - **Indian Association:** fought the ICS age cut (21 → 19), the Arms and Vernacular Press Acts; held the all-India conference of **Dec 1883**.
[198:0:6] - **Chronology codes:** Bangabhasha 1836 → Landholders 1838 → BBIS 1843 → Indian League 1875; Bombay Assn 1852 → Indian League 1875 → Indian Assn 1876 → Madras Mahajana Sabha 1884; East India Assn 1866 → PSS 1870 → MMS 1884 → Bombay Presidency Assn 1885.
[198:0:7] - **Nature:** early bodies were **regional**, led by **landlords or the urban elite**, worked by **petitions and memorials**; after 1858 the **educated middle class** led them, and they grew into all-India coordination → **INC 1885**.
[198:0:8] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.275-278; NextGen Indian History (APPSC) Part 6 p.44-45; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.20-22, p.28; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.180; app notes 1:198 (sub 3, 8)
## SUB 1 | Nationalist Literature – Anandamath, Vande Mataram, Nil Darpan
[198:1:0] TABLE head: Work | Author | Fact
  [198:1:0.0] Nil Darpan (Neeldarpan) | Dinabandhu Mitra | Written 1858-59, published 1860; cruelty of indigo planters – earliest of Neeldarpan / Satyendranath Tagore's ICS (1863-64) / Arya Samaj (1875) / Anandamath (1882)
  [198:1:0.1] Anandamath | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | 1882; set in the Sannyasi Rebellion (1763-1800); contains Vande Mataram
  [198:1:0.2] Durgeshnandini | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | His first novel (1865)
  [198:1:0.3] Rajasimha, Rajani, Indira | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | Other novels
[198:1:1] - **Anandamath = "Bible of Bengali Patriotism"** – the book associated with the rise of the national movement (not Gitanjali, Gora, Satyarth Prakash, Gita Rahasya).
[198:1:2] - **Bankim made the Sannyasi Rebellion famous** – not the Bhil, Rangpur or Kuka revolts.
[198:1:3] - **Vande Mataram:** composed by **Bankim Chandra Chatterjee** – India's **National Song** (adopted 24 Jan 1950); **first sung at the INC by Rabindranath Tagore at the Calcutta session, 1896** (Tagore sang it, he did not compose it).
[198:1:4] - **Telugu translation** of Vande Mataram: **Y. Doraiswamayya and M. Ramarao**; "**The Cry of Mother India**" (Krishna Patrika, **15 Dec 1905**) – first nationalist song of Andhra.
[198:1:5] - **Nationalist poets of Bengal:** **Rangalal Banerjee, Hem Chandra Banerjee, Nabin Chandra Sen** – **Shiv Kumar Batalvi** is a post-independence Punjabi poet, not one of them.
[198:1:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 3 p.7, p.102, p.123; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.18; Spectrum p.547; app notes 1:198 (sub 6)
## SUB 2 | Madras and Andhra Associations
[198:2:0] # Madras Native Association (26 February 1852)
[198:2:1] - **Founder and first president:** **Gazula (Gajula) Lakshminarasu Chetty** – first person from Andhra in the national movement; also ran **The Crescent** (1844); secretary **Somasundaram Chettiyar**.
[198:2:2] - **First political body of South India**; began as a branch of the British Indian Association, then independent.
[198:2:3] - **Petitions:** 1852 (before the **Charter renewal of 1853**), **1859** and **1861** – against ryotwari over-assessment, torture by revenue men, the salt monopoly and **moturpha**, a **tax on trades and occupations** (looms).
[198:2:4] - Its agitation helped bring the **Torture Commission (1854)**.
[198:2:5] # Madras Mahajana Sabha (16 May 1884)
[198:2:6] - **President: P. Rangaiah Naidu**; **secretary: P. Anandacharlu** (NextGen); founders with M. Viraraghavachariar and G. Subramania Iyer.
[198:2:7] - Demanded larger councils and more Indian representation.
[198:2:8] # District associations
[198:2:9] - **Krishna District Association (1892):** organised by **Ramaswamy Gupta**; **first district association in the Madras Presidency**; conferences at **Guntur (July 1892)** and Machilipatnam (1893).
[198:2:10] - **Inspiration:** the **formation of the INC (1885)** led to the district associations.
[198:2:11] - **Angalur conference (1900)** of the Association demanded **agricultural banks**; its 1899 resolution led to **Krishna Patrika (1902)**.
[198:2:12] - **Kakinada (Coconada) Literary Association:** memorandums (1884-85) for a **higher ICS age limit** and **simultaneous examinations**.
[198:2:13] > Pairs: Madras Native Association **1852** ✓, Madras Mahajana Sabha **1884** ✓, Krishna District Association **1892** (1900 = Angalur conference ✗).
[198:2:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 p.17-18; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 3 p.4-5; NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.45, p.47, p.73; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 6 p.1; NextGen previous papers p.1; Rocket AP History p.14, p.44; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.20-21; app notes 1:198 (sub 4)
## SUB 3 | Factors of Nationalism; Lytton and the Ilbert Bill
[198:3:0] # Factors
[198:3:1] - **Political and administrative unification** – railways, telegraph, post, uniform laws; **K.M. Panikkar**: "the most notable achievement of British rule was the **unification of India**".
[198:3:2] - **Western education** – liberal ideas; **English as a link language**; rise of the **educated middle class**.
[198:3:3] - **Press and literature**; **rediscovery of India's past**; socio-religious reform.
[198:3:4] - **Contemporary world movements** – South American, Greek, **Italian** and Irish struggles; **German unification** – **Bismarck**'s "**blood and iron**" speech (1862).
[198:3:5] - **Economic critique** – drain of wealth, ruin of artisans.
[198:3:6] - Early associations trained the educated class in **petitions, memorials and all-India coordination** → INC 1885.
[198:3:7] # Lytton's resented measures (1876-80)
[198:3:8] TABLE head: Measure | Year | Why resented
  [198:3:8.0] ICS maximum age cut | 1876 | 21 → 19 (Lytton's period; ordered by Secretary of State Salisbury)
  [198:3:8.1] Delhi Durbar | 1877 | Proclaimed Queen Victoria Empress of India during famine
  [198:3:8.2] Vernacular Press Act | 1878 | Gagged the Indian-language press; Amrita Bazar Patrika (1868) turned English overnight in 1878
  [198:3:8.3] Arms Act | 1878 | Disarmed Indians but spared Europeans
  [198:3:8.4] Second Afghan War | 1878-80 | Burden on Indian revenues
[198:3:9] # Ilbert Bill (1883)
[198:3:10] - **Ripon**'s government, drafted by **Sir Courtenay Ilbert (Law Member)**: Indian magistrates and judges could **try European British subjects**; European agitation forced a compromise – a European accused could claim a jury of **at least half Europeans**; passed **25 January 1884**. **Not a measure of Lytton.**
[198:3:11] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.272, p.274-275, p.547; NextGen Indian History (APPSC) Part 6 p.43; general knowledge (Panikkar, Bismarck); app notes 1:198 (sub 0, 1, 2)
## SUB 4 | Surendranath Banerjee
[198:4:0] - **ICS:** passed **1869**, **dismissed in 1874** on a minor irregularity – the leader the British dismissed from the ICS.
[198:4:1] - Founded the **Indian Association (1876)** with A.M. Bose; toured India against the ICS age cut (**21 → 19**).
[198:4:2] - Convened the **Indian National Conference (1883, 1885)**, which **merged with the INC in 1886**.
[198:4:3] - Title **"Rashtraguru"**; paper **The Bengalee** (from 1879); autobiography **A Nation in Making**.
[198:4:4] - INC president at **Poona 1895** and **Ahmedabad 1902** – not Surat 1907.
[198:4:5] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.277, p.279; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.43; app notes 1:198 (sub 5)

  [198:5:0.2] The Hindu | Triplicane Six – G. Subramania Iyer, M. Veeraraghavachariar and others | 1878 weekly, Madras; daily from 1889
  [198:5:0.3] The Bengalee | Surendranath Banerjee | 1879
  [198:5:0.4] Swadesamitran (Tamil) | G. Subramania Iyer | 1882
  [198:5:0.5] Andhra Patrika | Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao | 1908 weekly, Bombay; later Madras
  [198:5:0.6] Swarajya (English daily) | Tanguturi Prakasam | 1921, Madras
[198:5:1] - Telugu **Swarajya** (Vijayawada, 1907-08) = **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao**.
[198:5:2] - **First Telugu journal = Satyadoota**; **first political journal = Andhra Prakasika**.

=== NOTES 1:199 | Foundation of the Indian National Congress 1885 – A.o. Hume, the Safety-valve Theory
## SUB 0 | Founding of the INC, 1885 – Who, When, Where
[199:0:0] # The core facts
[199:0:1] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [199:0:1.0] Year | 1885 (not 1883, 1886 or 1888)
  [199:0:1.1] Founder | A.O. Hume, a retired ICS officer (civil servant) – "Father/founder of the INC"
  [199:0:1.2] First President | W.C. (Womesh Chandra) Bonnerjee – not Hume, not S.N. Banerjea
  [199:0:1.3] General Secretary | A.O. Hume (1885-1906)
  [199:0:1.4] Dates | 28-31 December 1885
  [199:0:1.5] Venue | Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay
  [199:0:1.6] Delegates | 72 (only 2 Muslims); mainly lawyers, journalists and teachers
  [199:0:1.7] Viceroy | Lord Dufferin (1884-88) – not Ripon (left 1884), Lytton or Mayo
[199:0:2] - **Earlier name:** Hume's **Indian National Union** (1884) became the INC; the name **"Indian National Congress"** was suggested by **Dadabhai Naoroji** (not W.C. Bonnerjee).
[199:0:3] - **Prelude:** after the **Theosophical Convention at Madras (Dec 1884)** a private meeting of **17** people planned an all-India body.
[199:0:4] - **Venue shift:** planned for **Poona**, moved to Bombay at the last minute because of **cholera** in Poona (not plague).
[199:0:5] - **Absent:** **Surendranath Banerjea** and other Bengal leaders – busy with the **2nd Indian National Conference** at Calcutta (Dec 1885).
[199:0:6] - **Government officials** (e.g. some Indian officials) attended the first session as observers – NDA statement "some officials were present" ✓.
[199:0:7] - **Merger:** the **Indian National Conference** of the **Indian Association** (S.N. Banerjea, A.M. Bose; conferences 1883, 1885) **merged with the INC in 1886**.
[199:0:8] - **Dufferin's attitude:** Hume convinced him **not to obstruct** the Congress; he may have suggested an annual forum but did not found it; soon hostile – "**microscopic minority**" (1888), "factory of sedition".
[199:0:9] > Statement angle (NDA 2006): Dufferin's tenure ✓, Bonnerjee first president ✓, first session in Calcutta ✗ (Bombay), officials present ✓ → "I, II and IV".
[199:0:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) Ch11 p.247-248 and Appendix 3 p.824; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.368-370; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.416-418; Rocket Indian History 02 #102 p.58; inc.in plenary-sessions synopsis (cholera); scroll.in (Naoroji named the Congress)

  [199:1:0.0] First President | W.C. Bonnerjee (Bombay 1885); again Allahabad 1892
  [199:1:0.1] First Parsi President; thrice President | Dadabhai Naoroji – Calcutta 1886, Lahore 1893, Calcutta 1906

  [199:1:0.6] Other British Presidents | Alfred Webb (Madras 1894), Henry Cotton (Bombay 1904), Annie Besant (1917)
  [199:1:0.7] First woman President | Annie Besant (Calcutta 1917)

[199:1:1] - **Titles:** Dadabhai Naoroji = **"Grand Old Man of India"**; Pherozeshah Mehta = **"Lion of Bombay"**; Surendranath Banerjea = "Rashtraguru".
[199:1:2] - **Grandfather of the Congress / thrice Chairman** = **Dadabhai Naoroji** (APPSC Endowment).
[199:1:3] - **Naoroji and self-rule:** from **1904** he kept demanding self-government; at **Calcutta 1906** the word **"Swaraj"** was first used as the goal.
[199:1:4] - **Gandhi and the Congress:** left its primary membership on **30 Oct 1934** – at Independence he was **not a member**.

## SUB 5 | A.O. Hume and the Safety-valve Debate
[199:5:0] # A.O. Hume
[199:5:1] - **Retired ICS officer** (retired **1882**); demoted in **1879** after a clash with **Lytton**; settled at **Shimla**.
[199:5:2] - Drew the idea of local self-government from **Ripon**; closer to the **Bombay-Poona** leaders than to Calcutta.
[199:5:3] - Founded the **Indian National Union**; **first General Secretary** of the INC.
[199:5:4] - Title: **"Father of Indian Ornithology"**.
[199:5:5] # Theories of the INC's origin
[199:5:6] TABLE head: Theory / view | Person
  [199:5:6.0] Safety-valve – first mentioned | William Wedderburn, biography of Hume (1913)
  [199:5:6.1] Safety-valve – used against the Moderates | Lala Lajpat Rai (*Young India*, 1916)
  [199:5:6.2] Conspiracy theory (Marxist) – to abort a popular uprising | R.P. Dutt (*India Today*)
  [199:5:6.3] "Colonial myth"; Hume a lightning conductor | Bipan Chandra (*India's Struggle for Independence*)
  [199:5:6.4] "No Indian could have started the Congress…" | G.K. Gokhale
[199:5:7] - **Basis claimed:** seven volumes of **secret reports** Hume read at **Simla in 1878**.
[199:5:8] - **Lightning conductor:** Indian leaders used Hume to shield the young body from official hostility.
[199:5:9] ~~ Sources: Spectrum (Ahir) Ch11 p.248 and p.256 summary; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.370; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.417-418
## SUB 6 | Aims, Demands and Early Character
[199:6:0] - **Aims stated by W.C. Bonnerjee (1885):** (a) personal intimacy and **friendship among workers** in the national cause; (b) removing **race, creed and provincial prejudices** – **national unity**; (c) recording the opinions of the educated classes on **pressing (social) questions**; (d) laying down the **lines of political work** for the next 12 months.
[199:6:1] - **Exam answer:** the Congress kept **social issues off its platform** (Naoroji's rule at the 1886 session: only national questions) – so "to express views on social issues" is the option books treat as NOT an objective.
[199:6:2] - **First-session demands:** **simultaneous ICS examinations** in England and India; **elected** (not nominated) councils; **opposition to the annexation of Upper Burma**; **cut in military expenditure** – NOT complete provincial autonomy.
[199:6:3] - **Early demand:** **separation of the Executive and the Judiciary**.
[199:6:4] - **Character:** the **first all-India political platform**; urban, English-educated middle class – not a mass peasant body.
[199:6:5] ~~ Sources: oldspeeches.blogspot.com (Bonnerjee's 1885 address); NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.369-370; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.417-418; Rocket Indian History 02 #102 p.58

=== NOTES 1:200 | Moderate Phase (1885-1905) – Leaders, Methods, Demands and Achievements; Economic Critique of Colonialism
## SUB 0 | Dadabhai Naoroji – the Grand Old Man of India
[200:0:0] # Life and firsts
[200:0:1] - **Title:** **Grand Old Man of India**; Parsi educator, trader and India's **first economic thinker**.
[200:0:2] - **Professor:** In **1854** the **first Indian to become a full professor** (mathematics and natural philosophy, **Elphinstone College**, Bombay); later Professor of **Gujarati at University College, London**.
[200:0:3] - **Women's education:** Through the **Students' Literary and Scientific Society (1848)** he **pioneered women's education** in Bombay; its vernacular branch, the **Gyan (Dnyan) Prasarak Mandali**, spread knowledge among adults (UPSC 2009).
[200:0:4] - **Diwan of Baroda:** 1874.
[200:0:5] # Bodies, journals and books
[200:0:6] TABLE head: Item | Year | Fact
  [200:0:6.0] Rast Goftar | 1851 | Gujarati fortnightly ("Truth Teller")
  [200:0:6.1] Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha | 1851 | Parsi religious reform
  [200:0:6.2] London Indian Society | 1865 | With W.C. Bonnerjee
  [200:0:6.3] East India Association | 1866, London | To put India's case before the British public; first lecture 2 May 1867
  [200:0:6.4] Voice of India | 1883, Bombay | Edited by Naoroji
  [200:0:6.5] British Committee of the INC | 1889 | Helped found it (chairman: Wedderburn)
  [200:0:6.6] *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* | 1901 | Drain theory; called British rule "Un-British"
[200:0:7] - **Quote:** Britain was "**bleeding India white**". The line "**Kings are made for the public, the public is not made for the King**" is credited to Naoroji in exam keys (UPPCS 2015).
[200:0:8] # British Parliament
[200:0:9] TABLE head: Person | First | Year
  [200:0:9.0] Lal Mohan Ghose | First Indian to contest a House of Commons election (Deptford, Liberal) | 1885 (and 1886, lost)
  [200:0:9.1] Dadabhai Naoroji | First Indian elected to the House of Commons – Central Finsbury, Liberal Party | 1892 (MP 1892-95)
[200:0:10] - **⚠ Trap:** "First to contest" is **Lal Mohan Ghose**, not Naoroji (Naoroji is the first to **win**). Lal Mohan Ghose later presided over the **Madras Congress, 1903**.
[200:0:11] - In **1893** he moved a bill in the Commons for **simultaneous ICS examinations**; he served on the **Welby Commission (1895)**.
[200:0:12] # Congress President three times – and Swaraj
[200:0:13] TABLE head: Session | Year
  [200:0:13.0] Calcutta (2nd session) | 1886
  [200:0:13.1] Lahore | 1893
  [200:0:13.2] Calcutta | 1906 – Swaraj declared the goal for the first time
[200:0:14] - **Three times, not four** (UPPCS 2014 "four times" = the wrong statement).
[200:0:15] - **Self-rule:** He pressed for self-government in **1904, 1905 and 1906** (UPSC 2018); at **Calcutta 1906** he was the **first to use "Swaraj"** as the national demand.
[200:0:16] > Naoroji: first full Indian professor, first Indian MP (1892, Liberal), thrice INC president, Swaraj 1906, drain theory.
[200:0:17] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.39-40; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.67; Spectrum p.41, 591; Wikipedia "Lalmohan Ghosh"
## SUB 1 | G.K. Gokhale and the Servants of India Society
[200:1:0] # Gokhale (1866-1915)
[200:1:1] - **Born** 1866 near **Ratnagiri**; graduate of Elphinstone College (**1884**, at 18); taught at **Fergusson College**, Poona.
[200:1:2] - **Career (UPSC 1997 biography):** associate editor of **Sudharak** (Agarkar's paper), **Secretary of the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha**, Secretary of the Congress, witness before the **Welby Commission**, provincial and imperial legislator, **INC President at 39**.
[200:1:3] - **Guru chain:** **M.G. Ranade → Gokhale → Gandhi**; Gandhi called Gokhale his **political guru** ("Gokhale – My Political Guru").
[200:1:4] - **Deccan Sabha (1896):** founded by **Gokhale** under Ranade when Tilak's group captured the Sarvajanik Sabha.
[200:1:5] - **President, Banaras Congress, 1905** (21st session) – condemned the **partition of Bengal** and Curzon's rule, backed **Swadeshi**.
[200:1:6] - **Compared Curzon's rule to that of Aurangzeb.**
[200:1:7] - **Refused a knighthood** (recommended by Hardinge) and **a seat in the Council of the Secretary of State for India** (UPSC 2008).
[200:1:8] - Told Gandhi to spend his first year in India "**with his ears open but his mouth shut**"; Gandhi returned in **1915** on his advice.
[200:1:9] # Servants of India Society
[200:1:10] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [200:1:10.0] Founded | 12 June 1905
  [200:1:10.1] Place | Poona (Pune)
  [200:1:10.2] Founder | Gopal Krishna Gokhale – not Ranade (Prarthana Samaj), not Tilak
  [200:1:10.3] Co-founders | N.A. Dravid, G.K. Deodhar, A.V. Patwardhan
  [200:1:10.4] Aim | Train national workers (missionaries) for India's service by constitutional means
  [200:1:10.5] Later members | V.S. Srinivasa Sastri; exam keys add M.C. Setalvad, B.N. Rau, Alladi Krishnaswamy Iyer (UPSC 1997)
[200:1:11] - **Chronology:** Hicky's Bengal Gazette (**1780**) → Asiatic Society, William Jones (**1784**) → **Servants of India Society (1905)** → Ghadar Party, Lala Har Dayal (**1913**).
[200:1:12] > Gokhale's year is 1905 twice: Servants of India Society (June) and Banaras presidency (December).
[200:1:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.41-45; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.68, 71; Spectrum p.248, 857; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 2 p.82
## SUB 2 | Economic Critique of Colonialism – Drain of Wealth
[200:2:0] # The critique
[200:2:1] - **Greatest contribution of the Moderates** – "the most important contribution to the development of the national movement"; it **broke the myth of British benevolence**.
[200:2:2] - **Drain theory:** **Dadabhai Naoroji** (*Poverty and Un-British Rule in India*) – he laid the **economic foundation of Indian nationalism**; the INC adopted the drain theory at **Calcutta, 1896**.
[200:2:3] - **Channels of the drain:** **Home Charges**, **salaries and pensions** of British officials, interest on public debt, profits and dividends, unequal trade → India's wealth transferred to **Britain**.
[200:2:4] # Home Charges (UPSC 2011)
[200:2:5] - Spent in England for India: **India Office in London**, **salaries, pensions and furlough pay of British civil and military personnel**, interest on India's debt.
[200:2:6] - **Wars outside India** were charged to Indian revenues but as military/"extraordinary" charges, **not Home Charges** → answer **I and II only**.
[200:2:7] # Economic critics and their books
[200:2:8] TABLE head: Book | Author
  [200:2:8.0] Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) | Dadabhai Naoroji
  [200:2:8.1] The Economic History of India | R.C. Dutt (not R.P. Dutt)
  [200:2:8.2] Some Economic Aspects of British Rule in India | G. Subramania Iyer
  [200:2:8.3] Essays on Indian Economics | M.G. Ranade
  [200:2:8.4] Prosperous British India | William Digby
  [200:2:8.5] The Rise and Growth of Economic Nationalism in India (1966) | Bipan Chandra (historian)
[200:2:9] - **Economic critics of colonialism:** Naoroji, **G. Subramania Iyer**, **R.C. Dutt** – **all three** (UPSC 2015); also Ranade, Wacha, G.V. Joshi, Gokhale.
[200:2:10] - **R.C. Dutt:** colonial policies caused India's economic exploitation; INC president **Lucknow 1899**.
[200:2:11] - **Sir Syed Ahmed Khan did not accept** the drain theory – he saw British rule as modernising (UPSC 1996).
[200:2:12] # Ideas and theories – match
[200:2:13] TABLE head: Idea | Associated with
  [200:2:13.0] Drain Theory | Naoroji (also R.C. Dutt)
  [200:2:13.1] Doctrine of Lapse | Lord Dalhousie
  [200:2:13.2] Safety Valve Theory | Congress seen as a means of channelling political discontent (Hume)
  [200:2:13.3] Two-Nation Theory | Jinnah / Muslim League
  [200:2:13.4] Hindutva | V.D. Savarkar
  [200:2:13.5] Swaraj | Political self-government
  [200:2:13.6] Satyagraha; Trusteeship | Gandhi – trusteeship drawn from the Gita's non-possession (also credited to Ruskin's *Unto This Last*)
[200:2:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.30, 48; PMF Modern History Part 3 p.73-75; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.36-40; Spectrum p.580
## SUB 3 | Moderate Phase – Leaders, Methods and Demands
[200:3:0] # Phase and leaders
[200:3:1] - **Moderate (liberal) phase = 1885-1905**; leaders were staunch believers in **liberalism**; base **urban**, English-educated.
[200:3:2] TABLE head: Leader | Known as / for
  [200:3:2.0] W.C. Bonnerjee | First INC President (Bombay 1885); London Indian Society with Naoroji (1865)
  [200:3:2.1] Surendranath Banerjee | Rashtraguru; Indian Association; edited The Bengalee; wrote *A Nation in Making*; presided 1895 and 1902
  [200:3:2.2] Pherozeshah Mehta | Lion of Bombay; Bombay Presidency Association (1885); INC president 1890
  [200:3:2.3] M.G. Ranade | Judge, economist, reformer; Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, Prarthana Samaj; *Rise of the Maratha Power*; Gokhale's guru
  [200:3:2.4] G. Subramania Iyer | Founded The Hindu and Swadesamitran; Madras Mahajana Sabha
  [200:3:2.5] R.C. Dutt | Economic historian; INC president Lucknow 1899
  [200:3:2.6] Dinshaw Wacha | INC president Calcutta 1901
  [200:3:2.7] Madan Mohan Malaviya | "No taxation without representation"
[200:3:3] - **Bombay Trimurti:** **Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang, Badruddin Tyabji** – founders of the Bombay Presidency Association (1885).
[200:3:4] - **Founders of the INC:** A.O. Hume is regarded as the founder; **Naoroji and Dinshaw Wacha** are counted among its founders too.
[200:3:5] # Newspapers and editors (match)
[200:3:6] TABLE head: Newspaper | Editor
  [200:3:6.0] Voice of India | Dadabhai Naoroji
  [200:3:6.1] The Bengalee | Surendranath Banerjee
  [200:3:6.2] Indian Opinion | Mahatma Gandhi (South Africa)
  [200:3:6.3] Free Hindustan | Taraknath Das
[200:3:7] # Methods
[200:3:8] - **Constitutional agitation** within the law – **3 Ps: Prayers, Petitions, Protests**; resolutions, meetings, pamphlets.
[200:3:9] - Faith in **British justice and fair play**; British rule seen as "**providential**".
[200:3:10] - Two-pronged: build opinion in India and **persuade the British public**.
[200:3:11] - **Distrusted mass action** – no non-cooperation, passive resistance or civil disobedience.
[200:3:12] # Demands
[200:3:13] TABLE head: Area | Demands
  [200:3:13.0] Constitutional | Larger councils with elected members and control over the budget; self-government within the Empire
  [200:3:13.1] Administrative | Indianisation of the services; simultaneous ICS exams in India and England; higher ICS age limit; separation of the judiciary from the executive
  [200:3:13.2] Economic | Lower land revenue; abolition of the salt tax; cut in military expenditure; tariff protection for industry
  [200:3:13.3] Civil rights | Free speech, press, association; repeal of the Arms Act; protested Tilak's arrest and the deportation of the Natu brothers without trial
[200:3:14] - **NOT a Moderate demand:** **Purna Swaraj / complete independence** (NDA 2010).
[200:3:15] # Limitations
[200:3:16] - Annual session lasted **only about three days**; **no machinery between sessions**.
[200:3:17] - **Narrow social base** – urban, educated; most leaders came from **urban areas**.
[200:3:18] - **Partition of Bengal (1905)** exposed their "**naive faith**" in British justice.
[200:3:19] - Social reform: Moderates backed the **Age of Consent Bill**; **Tilak opposed** it.
[200:3:20] - Critics: Aurobindo – "begging institution"; Tilak – "Rights are not begged, they are claimed".
[200:3:21] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.46-49; Spectrum p.280-282, 288, 856-857; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.24, 38; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 2 p.87
## SUB 4 | Achievements and the Official Attitude
[200:4:0] # Achievements
[200:4:1] - **Pan-Indian national identity**; **economic critique** of colonial rule; training in **democratic politics** and civil liberties – but **not complete independence**.
[200:4:2] - Supported the **democratic and scientific culture of modern Europe** and **strongly criticised the economic side** of imperialism – both true (RPSC 2024).
[200:4:3] # Indian Councils Act, 1892
[200:4:4] - Passed under Viceroy **Lansdowne**.
[200:4:5] - **More non-official members**, chosen on **recommendation** of municipal and district boards, universities, chambers of commerce – **indirect election** introduced.
[200:4:6] - Members could **discuss the budget but not vote on or amend it**; could **ask questions**.
[200:4:7] - INC found it **inadequate**: **no direct vote**, **official majority** kept.
[200:4:8] # Welby Commission (1895)
[200:4:9] - **Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure** (1895) – the commonly known name; **Naoroji** was its first Indian member, **Wedderburn** also sat on it and **Gokhale** gave evidence.
[200:4:10] # What the Viceroys said
[200:4:11] TABLE head: Official | Remark
  [200:4:11.0] Dufferin (1887-88) | Congress represents only a "microscopic minority" of the people
  [200:4:11.1] Curzon (letter, 1900) | "The Congress is tottering to its fall, and one of my great ambitions while in India is to assist it to a peaceful demise"
[200:4:12] - **Curzon:** **youngest Viceroy** (1899, aged 39).
[200:4:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.46; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.30, 33, 46; PMF Modern History Part 5 p.181; Spectrum p.288
## SUB 5 | Bodies in Britain – British Committee and Parliamentary Committee

  [200:5:0.0] British Committee of the INC | July 1889, London | Sir William Wedderburn (chairman from July 1889), with Naoroji | Win support for the Congress in Britain; journal "India" (1890)
  [200:5:0.1] Indian Parliamentary Committee | 1893 | Wedderburn and W.S. Caine | Agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons (UPSC 2011)
[200:5:1] - **Wedderburn:** INC president **Bombay 1889**; Liberal MP from **1893**; wrote Hume's biography (1913).
[200:5:2] > 1889 = British Committee; 1890 = journal "India"; 1893 = Indian Parliamentary Committee.
[200:5:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.32, 46-47; Spectrum p.282; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.48

=== NOTES 1:201 | Growth of the Nationalist Movement in Andhra, 1885-1905
## SUB 0 | P. Anandacharlu and Andhra at the Early Congress
[201:0:0] # P. Anandacharlu (Panapakkam Anandacharyulu, 1843-1907)
[201:0:1] - **First Telugu (Andhra) President of the INC** – **7th session, Nagpur, 1891** (not Kakinada, Meerut or Lucknow; not 1889, 1890 or 1892).
[201:0:2] - **Secretary of the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884)**; attended the **first INC session (1885)**.
[201:0:3] - **⚠ Trap:** Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Konda Venkatappayya, Nyapathi Subbarao and Kaleswara Rao never were the first Telugu INC president.
[201:0:4] # Andhra at the first sessions
[201:0:5] - **Bombay 1885 (72 delegates):** Andhra delegates **P. Anandacharlu**, **P. Rangaiah Naidu**, **Nyapathi Subbarao (Rajahmundry)**, **Gutti Kesava Pillai (Gooty)**, **Venkata Subbarayudu (Machilipatnam)**.
[201:0:6] - **Demands of the first session:** **simultaneous ICS exams** in England and India; **elected legislative councils**; **cut in military expenditure**; **opposition to the annexation of Upper Burma**.
[201:0:7] - **Calcutta 1886:** presided by **Naoroji**; **21 Andhra members** out of 436.
[201:0:8] - Madras session **1914**: **256 Andhra delegates**.
[201:0:9] > NextGen's "Modern India Part 1" p.11 wrongly puts Anandacharlu at the 1886 session; the session list settles **Nagpur 1891**.
[201:0:10] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.856 (session list); NextGen Modern India L2 Part 6 p.1; NextGen Rocket Sheets AP History p.50; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.46-47
## SUB 1 | Associations – Madras Sabhas and the Krishna District Association
[201:1:0] # Madras associations
[201:1:1] TABLE head: Association | Year | Founder / office-bearers
  [201:1:1.0] Madras Native Association | 26 Feb 1852 | Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty (founder, first president)
  [201:1:1.1] Madras Mahajana Sabha | 16 May 1884 | P. Rangaiah Naidu (president), P. Anandacharlu (secretary); with G. Subramania Iyer, M. Veeraraghavachari
[201:1:2] # Krishna District Association (1892)
[201:1:3] - **Formed in 1892** – the **first district association in the Madras Presidency** (APPSC 2021), set up **on the lines suggested at the first INC session**, to fight British rule on social and public issues.
[201:1:4] - **Organiser: Ramaswamy Gupta** (not Gajula Lakshmi Narasu, Mutnuri Krishna Rao or Kokkonda Venkataratnam).
[201:1:5] - **First meeting (conference): Guntur, July 1892**; **second: Machilipatnam, 1893**.
[201:1:6] - **⚠ Key fixed:** one APPSC Group 2 (2012) key gives **Machilipatnam** for the first meeting – wrong; every NextGen source and Rocket give **Guntur**.
[201:1:7] - **1894:** Krishna ryots met at **Eluru** against higher water rates; the 1894 session was presided by **Nyapathi Subbarao**.
[201:1:8] - Its **1899 resolution** led to **Krishna Patrika (1902)**.

  [201:1:10.0] Krishna | 1892

  [201:1:10.4] Nellore | 1908
  [201:1:10.5] Kurnool | 1914

## SUB 2 | Early Telugu Press, 1835-1905
[201:2:0] TABLE head: Paper | Fact
  [201:2:0.0] Satyadoota (1835) | First Telugu journal – published by the Christian Association of Bellary
  [201:2:0.1] Andhra Prakasika (1885) | First political journal/weekly in Andhra; Telugu news weekly from Madras; editor A.C. (A.P.) Parthasarathi Naidu; supported the Congress
  [201:2:0.2] Krishna Patrika (2 Feb 1902) | Machilipatnam; started by Konda Venkatappayya with Dasu Narayana Rao; later edited by Mutnuri Krishna Rao
  [201:2:0.3] Vyjayanti; People's Magazine | Nyapathi Subbarao (monthly; editor)
  [201:2:0.4] Deshabhimani, Sasilekha, Rasikollasini, Gowtami, Vivekavardhani | Among about 20 Telugu journals by 1905
[201:2:1] - **Role:** journals **criticised administrative failures** and spread **nationalism and democracy**.
[201:2:2] > First Telugu journal = **Satyadoota**; first political journal = **Andhra Prakasika** (not Krishna Patrika, Deshabhimani or Golconda Patrika).

## SUB 3 | Andhra Moderate Leaders and Local Politics to 1905
[201:3:0] # Leaders
[201:3:1] TABLE head: Person | Role
  [201:3:1.0] Nyapathi Subbarao | Rajahmundry lawyer; titles Rajabahadur, Padyavinoda; founded Vyjayanti, the Godavari District Association and the Hindu Samaj, Rajahmundry; Congress General Secretary; later first president of the Andhra PCC and of the 2nd Andhra Conference (Vijayawada, 1914)
  [201:3:1.1] Mocherla Ramachandra Rao | "Gokhale of South India"
  [201:3:1.2] G. Subramania Iyer | "Father of South India" (not Telugu)
  [201:3:1.3] Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao | Later (1919, 7th Andhra Mahasabha, Guntur) gave a data-led critique of the drain from Andhra to Madras
  [201:3:1.4] Others | V.V. Jogaiah, Gade Raghava Rao, A.P. Patro, B.N. Sarma
[201:3:2] - Andhra Moderates **repeated the INC's economic critique** (drain of wealth) and its constitutional demands.
[201:3:3] - **After 1908**, with the Extremists crushed, **Konda Venkatappayya and B.N. Sarma** came to the fore.
[201:3:4] # Order of events
[201:3:5] - Madras Native Association (**1852**) → Madras Mahajana Sabha (**1884**) → first INC (**1885**) → Anandacharlu presides (**1891**) → Krishna District Association (**1892**) → Krishna Patrika (**1902**).
[201:3:6] # Local politics and 1905
[201:3:7] - **Guntur district** carved out of Krishna in **1904**; Konda Venkatappayya moved there.
[201:3:8] - **1905:** real political awakening came with **Vandemataram/Swadeshi**; Andhras opposed both the partition of Bengal and the **transfer of Ganjam** from Madras – opposing Ganjam's transfer is called the "**first victory**" of the Andhra movement.
[201:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 Part 1 p.73, 87; NextGen AP History APPSC Part 7 p.19; NextGen Rocket Sheets AP History p.50; old app notes (row 200-201) for titles and district years

=== NOTES 1:202 | Partition of Bengal 1905, Swadeshi and Boycott Movement; Techniques and Impact
## SUB 0 | Partition of Bengal, 1905 – Dates, Curzon, Motive, Annulment
[202:0:0] # Key facts
[202:0:1] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [202:0:1.0] Viceroy | Lord Curzon (1899-1905) – not Minto, Hardinge, Lytton or Napier
  [202:0:1.1] First proposal | December 1903 – Moderate protests 1903-05
  [202:0:1.2] Announced | 19 July 1905 (order issued; published 20 July)
  [202:0:1.3] Took effect | 16 October 1905 – not 15 October
  [202:0:1.4] New province | Eastern Bengal and Assam (Dacca, Chittagong, Rajshahi divisions + Assam), capital Dacca, 31 million
  [202:0:1.5] Rest of Bengal | West Bengal + Bihar + Orissa, 54 million – 18 million Bengalis, 36 million Biharis and Oriyas (Bengalis a minority)
  [202:0:1.6] Lt Governor of Bengal | Sir Andrew Fraser (1903-08), active in framing the partition
  [202:0:1.7] Annulled | 12 December 1911, Delhi Durbar of King George V – capital also shifted Calcutta → Delhi
  [202:0:1.8] Viceroy at annulment | Lord Hardinge II
[202:0:2] - **Stated motive:** **administrative convenience** – province of about 80 million "too big"; Curzon called it a readjustment of boundaries.
[202:0:3] - **Real motive:** **weaken Bengali nationalism** – "the nerve centre of Indian nationalism" (Curzon) – and **divide Hindus and Muslims** (Curzon at Dacca wooed the Muslims).
[202:0:4] - **H.H. Risley:** "**Bengal united is a power; Bengal divided will pull in several different ways.**"
[202:0:5] - **Surendranath Banerjea:** the announcement "**fell like a bombshell**"; he and K.K. Mitra **led the anti-partition agitation**.
[202:0:6] - **NDA 2013 statement:** Curzon **separated Dacca, Chittagong and Rajshahi divisions from Bengal and joined them to Assam** ✓; he did **not** succeed Canning, introduce the subsidiary alliance (Wellesley) or sympathise with the Congress.
[202:0:7] - **Impact:** the partition was the event with the **maximum impact on the freedom movement** of the options usually offered (Prince of Wales 1875, Delhi Durbar 1877, ICS 1861).
[202:0:8] - **Durbars:** 1877 (Lytton, Victoria Kaiser-i-Hind), **1903 (Curzon, Edward VII's coronation)**, **1911 (George V – the only one a sovereign attended; annulment)**. Japan's victory over Russia (1904-05) fuelled the anger.
[202:0:9] > Traps: annulment **1911** (not 1910, 1912 or 1947); it did not last until WWI, the CDM or 1947. "First partition of Bengal" = 1905 (the second = 1947).
[202:0:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-04.txt) p.54-56 (book p.446-448); NextGen Modern India L2 part 6 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-06.txt) p.1, p.4; NextGen Modern India L3 part 1 p.73; Spectrum (Ahir) Ch12 pdf p.294-295
## SUB 1 | Launch of the Swadeshi Movement – Cause, 7 August 1905, Boycott
[202:1:0] TABLE head: Date | Event
  [202:1:0.0] 13 July 1905 | K.K. (Krishna Kumar) Mitra first suggested boycott of British goods in his weekly Sanjibani
  [202:1:0.1] 19/20 July 1905 | Partition announced
  [202:1:0.2] 7 August 1905 | Calcutta Town Hall meeting – boycott resolution passed; formal proclamation of the Swadeshi Movement; boycott adopted as national policy
  [202:1:0.3] 16 October 1905 | Partition took effect – day of mourning, fasting, hartal, Ganga bath, Raksha Bandhan, Federation Hall foundation
[202:1:1] - **Immediate cause:** the **partition of Bengal by Curzon** – not Tilak's sentence, the Lajpat Rai–Ajit Singh deportation (1907) or the Chapekar sentence; not Curzon's universities or municipal measures.
[202:1:2] - **First use:** **Swadeshi and Boycott** were adopted as methods of struggle for the **first time** in the **anti-partition agitation** – not Home Rule, NCM or the Simon boycott.
[202:1:3] - **Movement born of the partition:** the **Swadeshi Movement** (1905-1911) – not NCM, CDM, Quit India or "Purna Swaraj".
[202:1:4] - **National Handloom Day = 7 August**, observed since **2015**, commemorates the **Swadeshi Movement** launched on 7 Aug 1905.
[202:1:5] - **Phases:** Moderates' petitions and meetings (1903-05: S.N. Banerjea, K.K. Mitra, Prithwishchandra Ray) → **Extremists take over from 1906** (passive resistance, Swaraj).
[202:1:6] - **Gandhi** had **no part** in it – he was in South Africa; Khilafat, Individual Satyagraha and Quit India were his movements.
[202:1:7] > "Launched / proclaimed" = **7 Aug 1905**; "took effect" = **16 Oct 1905**; "announced" = **19 July 1905** (BPSC key; many books say 20 July).
[202:1:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.55-57 (book p.447-449); NextGen Modern India L2 part 6 p.1-2; Spectrum (Ahir) Ch12 pdf p.294-295
## SUB 2 | Programme, Samitis, National Education and Swadeshi Enterprises
[202:2:0] # Programme
[202:2:1] - Programmes against the partition: **Boycott, Swadeshi, National education** (plus passive resistance) – **NOT Non-cooperation** (1920).
[202:2:2] - **Boycott:** foreign cloth, salt, sugar; bonfires of foreign cloth; picketing; priests refused foreign sugar, washermen foreign clothes – boycott was the **most successful** form.
[202:2:3] - **Samitis:** **Swadesh Bandhab Samiti** of **Barisal** – **Ashwini Kumar Dutt** (school teacher), who led the **Muslim peasants of Barisal** – not Liaquat Hussain, Pulin Das, Surya Sen or Barindra Ghosh.
[202:2:4] - **Mass mobilisation:** public meetings, processions, jatras, melas, folk songs, akharas and **lathi clubs**; Tilak's Ganapati and Shivaji festivals.
[202:2:5] - **Atmashakti** (self-reliance) – constructive work; the movement was **not "exclusively political"** – it reshaped art, literature, science and industry.
[202:2:6] - Swadeshi = India's **first mass movement**; Barisal Samiti also used **magic lanterns** and **arbitration courts** (old notes); Tilak started Ganapati (1893) and **Shivaji (1895)** festivals.
[202:2:7] - **Calcutta INC 1906 (Dadabhai Naoroji):** **Swaraj** declared the goal; resolutions on Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education.
[202:2:8] # National education
[202:2:9] TABLE head: Institution | Fact
  [202:2:9.0] Dawn Society | Satish Chandra Mukherjee (1902) – education under indigenous control
  [202:2:9.1] Bengal Technical Institute | 25 July 1906
  [202:2:9.2] National Council of Education | 15 August 1906 – later Jadavpur University
  [202:2:9.3] Bengal National College, Calcutta | 1906, first principal Aurobindo Ghosh – not Tagore, Ashutosh Mukherjee, S.N. Banerjea or P.C. Ray
  [202:2:9.4] Rangpur National School | 1905
[202:2:10] # Enterprises
[202:2:11] TABLE head: Enterprise | Founder / year
  [202:2:11.0] Bengal Chemical Swadeshi Stores | Acharya P.C. Ray (1901)
  [202:2:11.1] Swadeshi Steam Navigation Co. | V.O. Chidambaram Pillai, Tuticorin, 1906
  [202:2:11.2] Banga Lakshmi Cotton Mills | 1906, by public subscription
  [202:2:11.3] Swadeshi banks | Bank of India 1906, Indian Bank 1907
[202:2:12] - **Revival of indigenous artisan crafts and industries** ✓ and the **National Council of Education** as part of the movement ✓ (UPSC 2019: both).
[202:2:13] # Spread and extent
[202:2:14] TABLE head: Region | Leader
  [202:2:14.0] Bengal | Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal, Ashwini Kumar Dutt
  [202:2:14.1] Madras | V.O. Chidambaram Pillai
  [202:2:14.2] Bombay / Poona | Tilak
  [202:2:14.3] Punjab | Ajit Singh, Lala Lajpat Rai
  [202:2:14.4] Delhi | Syed Haider Raza
  [202:2:14.5] Andhra (deltaic) | known as the Vandemataram Movement
[202:2:15] - **Participation:** students and **women** took an active part (first time); **some prominent Muslims** joined; the **Muslim peasantry and peasants in general stayed away** (Barisal an exception); it was **not limited to Bengal**.
[202:2:16] - **British journalist H.W. Nevinson** covered the Swadeshi Movement and Surat 1907 (The New Spirit in India).
[202:2:17] - **Sumit Sarkar** – author of *The Swadeshi Movement in Bengal 1903-1908*.
[202:2:18] > UPSC 2002 "not correct": Barisal peasants led by Liaquat Hussain ✗ (Ashwini Kumar Dutt).
[202:2:19] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.56-61 (book p.448-453); Spectrum (Ahir) Appendix pdf p.836-837 (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt); NextGen Modern India L2 part 6 p.3; NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.67 (Tilak's akharas and lathi clubs)
## SUB 3 | Swadeshi in Art, Literature and Song
[202:3:0] TABLE head: Field | Person | Work / fact
  [202:3:0.0] Song | Rabindranath Tagore | Amar Sonar Bangla (1905) – later national anthem of Bangladesh
  [202:3:0.1] Song | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | Bande Mataram (Anandamath) – theme song / slogan of the Swadeshi agitation
  [202:3:0.2] Painting | Abanindranath Tagore | Bharat Mata (1905) – first painted image of Bharat Mata; Bengal School – revivalistic style, wash technique
  [202:3:0.3] Art society | Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore | Indian Society of Oriental Art, Calcutta 1907; Nandalal Bose its first scholar
  [202:3:0.4] Book | Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar | Desher Katha (1904) – banned 1910
  [202:3:0.5] Other songs | Rajanikanta Sen, Dwijendralal Ray, Mukunda Das | Swadeshi songs
[202:3:1] - **Desher Katha (UPSC 2020):** warned against the colonial **"hypnotic conquest of the mind"** ✓; inspired **swadeshi street plays and folk songs** ✓; "desh" meant **India, not Bengal alone** ✗ → **1 and 2 only**.
[202:3:2] - **Tagore:** "**Gurudev**"; first Asian Nobel laureate (1913); preached **Atmashakti**; **critic of the Swadeshi Movement's economic side** (Ghare Baire) and pleaded for **East-West understanding**.
[202:3:3] - **Tagore's poetry, in order:** **Manasi (1890) → Sonar Tari (1894) → Gitanjali (1910) → Gitimalya (1914) → Balaka (1916)**.
[202:3:4] - **Vande Mataram** was the slogan of the **Swadeshi / anti-partition** movement – not 1857, NCM, Champaran, Rowlatt or Quit India.
[202:3:5] > Rabindranath did **not** found the Indian Society of Oriental Art; Nandalal Bose, Asit Haldar and Amrita Sher-Gil are distractors.
[202:3:6] - **Related art facts (old notes):** **Nandalal Bose** led the illumination of the original Constitution manuscript; **Raja Ravi Varma** set up a lithographic press at Bombay (1894).

=== NOTES 1:203 | Swadeshi and Vandemataram Movement in Andhra – Bipin Chandra Pal's Tour, Student Participation
## SUB 0 | Vandemataram Movement in Andhra – Name, Phase, Beginnings
[203:0:0] - **Name:** in Andhra the Swadeshi Movement was called the **Vandemataram Movement** (a **sequel to the partition of Bengal**); Andhra phase **1906-1911**, ended with the **1911 annulment**.
[203:0:1] - **Real political awakening** in Andhra began with it; **students** of Andhra took an active part in politics **from the Vandemataram movement onwards**.
[203:0:2] - **Madras, Sept 1905:** Madras Beach students' meeting under **G. Subramania Iyer** condemned the partition; Kela Sri Ramamurthy sang Vandemataram; Subramania Bharati sang Tamil songs.
[203:0:3] - **Madras, 1906:** an **Industrial Association** and a **Swadeshi League**; the League sent **Nyapati Subbarao and K. Venkataramana Rao** to tour Andhra and popularise Swadeshi – **before Pal's visit**.
[203:0:4] - **S.N. Banerjea's arrest (1906)** → protests at Rajahmundry, Kakinada, Vizianagaram, Gooty; slogan "**Vandemataram – Manade Rajyam**".
[203:0:5] - **Bala Bharati Samiti:** founded at **Rajahmundry, February 1907** by local youths (Chilukuri Veerabhadra Rao, Ganti Lakshmanna and others; members incl. T. Prakasam) – Andhra's response to the **partition of Bengal**; backed by Karanam Guneswara Rao.
[203:0:6] - **Legacy:** the movement roused interest in Andhra's language and history (Andhrula Charitramu, 1910) and **moulded the Andhra Movement** for a separate province.
[203:0:7] # Japan's victory over Russia (1905)
[203:0:8] TABLE head: Person | Work / act
  [203:0:8.0] Adipudi Somanatha Rao | Japan Charitra – history of Japan in Telugu
  [203:0:8.1] Sriram Veerabrahmam | Japaniyam (drama in praise of Japan)
  [203:0:8.2] Munagala Raja | named his sons Togo and Nogi
  [203:0:8.3] Andhra youths | went to Japan for industrial training
[203:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l3-01.txt) p.73-81; NextGen Modern India L2 part 6 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-06.txt) p.2; NextGen AP History APPSC 16 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-16.txt) (Swadeshi League 1906); PMF Modern History Part 4 p.59 (Vandemataram Movement in the deltaic Andhra region)
## SUB 1 | Bipin Chandra Pal's Tour of Andhra, April 1907
[203:1:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [203:1:0.0] When | April 1907 (about 16-27 April) – not 1908, not May
  [203:1:0.1] Why | to spread the Vandemataram movement – Pal was the Extremist leader who promoted it in Andhra
  [203:1:0.2] Organiser | Mutnuri Krishna Rao, editor of Krishna Patrika (he called for an Extremist leader)
  [203:1:0.3] Route | Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam → Kakinada (17 April, two lectures) → Rajahmundry (19-24 April, five lectures) → Vijayawada → Machilipatnam → Madras
  [203:1:0.4] Rajahmundry | the Bala Bharati Samiti organised the meetings; Pal opened the Godavari Swadeshi Stores; Guneswara Rao gave Rs 1,000 for a national school
  [203:1:0.5] Machilipatnam | Pal was the guest of Ramadasu Naidu; Young Men's Swarajya Samiti and a national school committee → Andhra Jateeya Kalasala
  [203:1:0.6] Madras | T. Prakasam presided over Pal's Madras meetings
[203:1:1] - **Pal's message:** **Swaraj the goal, boycott the weapon**; Swadeshi, national education.
[203:1:2] - **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** – the Andhra student leader who welcomed Pal and **went with the Vandemataram campaign to many places**.
[203:1:3] - **Translator:** **Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham** rendered Pal's Rajahmundry speech into Telugu.
[203:1:4] - **Hosts and chairs (old notes):** Kakinada lectures chaired by **Kattiventi Perraju**; at Rajahmundry he stayed at **Madella Sourayya's** house; Vijayawada hosts **Munagala Raja and Nayani Venkata Rangarao**; last Machilipatnam speech "**Matru Murthi**"; the tour **began at Vizianagaram**, not Rajahmundry.
[203:1:5] - Pal (Brahmo, weekly **New India**, 1901) was later **arrested**.
[203:1:6] > Keys disputed in old banks: Rajahmundry body = **Bala Bharati Samiti** (not Young Men's Association); Machilipatnam host = **Ramadasu Naidu** (not Kopalle/Kompalle Hanumantha Rao).
[203:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 part 1 p.77; NextGen Modern India L2 part 6 p.2; NextGen previous papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt) p.21 (guest of Ramadasu Naidu); Rocket AP History (src/ap-history/rocket-ap-history.txt) (Pal – guest of Ramadasu Naidu at Machilipatnam); NextGen AP History APPSC 16 (Kakinada 17 April, Rajahmundry five lectures); NextGen Modern India L2 part 3 p.10 (Chilakamarti translated Pal's speech); old app notes (Prakasam at Madras)
## SUB 2 | Rajahmundry College Incident, 1907 – Student Participation
[203:2:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [203:2:0.0] College | Government Arts and Teachers' Training College, Rajahmundry
  [203:2:0.1] Principal | Mark Hunter – not Pichard, Tyler/Taylor or Reid
  [203:2:0.2] Order | March-April 1907: banned Vandemataram badges and the slogan
  [203:2:0.3] Defiance | student Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao (teacher trainee) presented an address to Pal; with J. Ramachandra Rao organised the protest
  [203:2:0.4] Punishment | 138 students debarred from exams for two years; Gadicherla expelled and blacklisted from government jobs
  [203:2:0.5] Significance | beginning of student participation from Andhra in the freedom struggle – the "Rajahmundry College incident"
[203:2:1] - Not Chittoor, Kurnool or Hyderabad college; the student leader was **Gadicherla**, not Gunneswara Rao, Chidambaram Pillai, Pattabhi or Nyapati Subbarao.
[203:2:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Modern India L3 part 1 p.77-79; NextGen Modern India L2 part 6 p.3; Rocket AP History (Gadicherla – teacher trainee restricted from college)
## SUB 3 | National College, Machilipatnam and Swadeshi Institutions
[203:3:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [203:3:0.0] Name | Andhra Jateeya Kalasala ("National College", Bandar National College), Machilipatnam

=== NOTES 1:204 | Extremists – Lal-bal-pal and Aurobindo; Ideology; Surat Split 1907
## SUB 0 | Moderates vs Extremists – Leaders, Methods and Ideology
[204:0:0] # Who were the Extremists
[204:0:1] - **Extremists** = **Militant / Assertive Nationalists** (Neo-nationalists, **Garam Dal**); trend from the **1890s**, concrete by **1905**; dominated the movement **after 1906**.
[204:0:2] - **Four pillars:** **Lal-Bal-Pal + Ghosh** – **Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh**; Tilak the most outstanding.
[204:0:3] TABLE head: Regional group | Leader
  [204:0:3.0] Maharashtra | Bal Gangadhar Tilak (with Vishnu Shastri Chiplunkar)
  [204:0:3.1] Bengal | Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh (also Raj Narain Bose, Ashwini Kumar Datta)
  [204:0:3.2] Punjab | Lala Lajpat Rai (with Ajit Singh)
  [204:0:3.3] Delhi (Swadeshi) | Syed Haider Raza
[204:0:4] - **Gujarat** was NOT a centre of Extremism (APPSC G1 2002 odd one out).
[204:0:5] - **Moderates (never Extremists):** Dadabhai Naoroji, **Gokhale** (their leader), Pherozeshah Mehta, S.N. Banerjea, M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi, W.C. Bonnerjee, R.C. Dutt.
[204:0:6] > Statement trap: "Tilak, Pal, Lajpat Rai and Aurobindo were Moderates" ✗.
[204:0:7] # How they differed
[204:0:8] TABLE head: Basis | Moderates (1885-1905) | Extremists (1905 onwards)
  [204:0:8.0] Faith in British | Believed in British justice, "providential mission" | No faith in British fairness or generosity; rule exploitative
  [204:0:8.1] Goal | Reforms; self-government within the Empire, gradual | Swaraj – complete freedom, by own effort
  [204:0:8.2] Method | Constitutional agitation; the 3 Ps – prayer, petition, protest | Boycott, Swadeshi, national education, passive resistance, mass agitation; 3 Ss – self-reliance, self-sacrifice, strong will
  [204:0:8.3] Masses | Not ready for politics | Immense faith in the masses
  [204:0:8.4] Inspiration | Western liberal thought | Indian history, culture, Hindu traditional symbols
  [204:0:8.5] Social base | Zamindars, upper middle class | Educated middle and lower middle class
[204:0:9] - **Fundamental difference:** **belief in British fairness and the preferred mode of struggle** (not social base or princely states).
[204:0:10] - **Extremist ideology (UPSC 1998):** **obtaining self-government by aggressive means** in place of petitions and constitutional ways.
[204:0:11] - They called Moderate methods **"political mendicancy"**; **Tilak** attacked the "politics of **prayer, petition and protest**", and the prayer-and-petition policy ended under his lead.
[204:0:12] - Remarks on the Congress: "**begging institute**" – credited to **B.C. Pal** in most keys (NextGen p.371 credits Aurobindo; Pal: Congress "playing with bubbles"); Tilak: "Rights are not begged, they are claimed".
[204:0:13] - **Passive resistance** doctrine – **Aurobindo** (series in *Bande Mataram*, 1907); **Swadeshi** – Aurobindo the main Bengal leader.
[204:0:14] - **Word Swaraj:** first used by **Dayanand Saraswati**; **Deuskar** brought it to Bengal (1902); as a political demand it is **Tilak's** ("Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it").
[204:0:15] - **Atmashakti** = self-reliance (Swadeshi enterprises, national schools); **spiritual nationalism** saw the nation as a **mother goddess** (Bande Mataram, Bhavani Mandir).
[204:0:16] - **Contribution:** turned nationalism into a **mass movement** and made **Swaraj** its goal.
[204:0:17] - **Criticism:** Hindu revivalist symbols (Ganapati, Shivaji festivals, Bhavani) and **harping on the Hindu past** kept most **Muslims** away; politically radical but socially conservative.
[204:0:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 06 p.371-375; Spectrum (Ahir) Ch12 p.257-261, p.263, p.271-272; Rocket Indian History 02 #118-120 p.82-87; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.445, p.497
## SUB 1 | Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856-1920)
[204:1:0] # Life and titles
[204:1:1] - Born **23 July 1856, Ratnagiri**; with Agarkar and Chiplunkar – New English School (1880), **Deccan Education Society** (1884), **Fergusson College** (1885).
[204:1:2] - Joined the Congress **1890**; **never INC President** (Lajpat Rai, Besant, Motilal, Naoroji, Gokhale, Bose, Kripalani, Sanjiva Reddy, M.A. Ansari all were).
[204:1:3] TABLE head: Title | Given by / when
  [204:1:3.0] Lokmanya ("accepted by the people as their leader") | by the people, after his 1897 sedition trial (Rand murder by the Chapekar brothers – revolutionary phase)
  [204:1:3.1] Father of Indian Unrest | Valentine Chirol, *Indian Unrest* (1910); Tilak sued him for libel
  [204:1:3.2] Father of the Indian National Movement | popular title in quiz books
[204:1:4] - **Radical in politics, conservative in social matters** – opposed the **Age of Consent Bill (1891)**.
[204:1:5] # Newspapers, festivals, books
[204:1:6] - **Kesari** (**Marathi – vernacular**) and **Mahratta** (English), both **1881**.
[204:1:7] - Made **Ganapati festival** a public, political festival (**1893**) and started **Shivaji festival** (**1895**).
[204:1:8] - Slogan: "**Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it**"; Kesari: Swarajya the trunk, Swadeshi and Boycott the branches.
[204:1:9] - Books: **Gita Rahasya** (Marathi, written in **Mandalay jail**); **The Arctic Home in the Vedas** (1903 – Arctic as the **original home of the Aryans**); *The Orion* (1893).
[204:1:10] - Quote (1918): "**If God were to tolerate untouchability, I would not recognise him as God at all.**"
[204:1:11] # Trials and death
[204:1:12] TABLE head: Year | Sedition trial
  [204:1:12.0] 1897 | 18 months; Max Muller pleaded for him ("my interest in Tilak is that of a Sanskrit scholar")
  [204:1:12.1] 1908 | Kesari articles on the Muzaffarpur bomb → 6 years in Mandalay (Burma); released June 1914
  [204:1:12.2] 1916 | Acquitted in the High Court
[204:1:13] - **Home Rule League:** **28 April 1916** (Belgaum; president **Joseph Baptista**).
[204:1:14] - Died **1 August 1920** – the day the **Non-Cooperation Movement** was launched; bier lifted by **Gandhi, Shaukat Ali** and Saifuddin Kitchlew.
[204:1:15] > Not Tilak's: **Satya Shodhak Samaj** (Jyotiba Phule, 1873); Bombay Chronicle (Pherozeshah Mehta).
[204:1:16] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 5 p.774-777, p.804-805; PMF Part 4 p.450, p.463 (Rand); Spectrum Ch12 p.272, p.275; Rocket Indian History 02 #96 p.48, #119 p.85; NextGen APPSC 06 p.371-373; newworldencyclopedia.org (Lokamanya after the 1897 trial); en.wikipedia.org Bal Gangadhar Tilak (untouchability quote, Chirol)
## SUB 2 | Surat Split 1907 – Run-up, Causes and Aftermath
[204:2:0] # Run-up
[204:2:1] TABLE head: Session | President | What happened
  [204:2:1.0] Benaras 1905 | Gokhale | Mild resolution condemning partition; supported Swadeshi-Boycott in Bengal
  [204:2:1.1] Calcutta 1906 | Dadabhai Naoroji | Split averted; goal = "swarajya or self-government" like the UK colonies; four resolutions – Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education
  [204:2:1.2] Surat 1907 (26 Dec) | Rash Behari Ghosh (Moderates' choice) | Split
[204:2:2] - **Annulment of the partition** was **NOT** one of the four Calcutta resolutions (UPSC 2010).
[204:2:3] # The split
[204:2:4] - **Extremists (Garam Dal, led by Tilak):** session at **Nagpur**, **Tilak or Lajpat Rai** president, keep the four resolutions.
[204:2:5] - **Moderates (Naram Dal – Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta):** Surat (host-province rule kept Tilak out), Rash Behari Ghosh president, drop the resolutions.
[204:2:6] - **Main reason (UPSC 2016):** **Extremists' lack of faith in the Moderates' capacity to negotiate with the British**.
[204:2:7] - Differences were over **strategy, objectives and mass participation** – all of these; the **Swadeshi Movement** produced the split.
[204:2:8] - **First split of the INC = Surat, December 1907**; scuffle, session suspended; the Moderates pushed the Extremists out and kept the Congress machinery.
[204:2:9] - **A-R (UPSC 1998):** the 1905 partition did **not** end the Moderates' role (A ✗); Surat separated the two wings (R ✓).
[204:2:10] # Aftermath and repression

[204:2:13] - **Andhra Tilak** = **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao**, jailed 1908.

## SUB 3 | Lala Lajpat Rai (1865-1928)
[204:3:0] - **Punjab Kesari / Sher-e-Punjab** (Lion of Punjab); Arya Samaj leader; helped found the **DAV School, Lahore** (1886).
[204:3:1] - Helped found **Punjab National Bank** (Lahore, **1894**).
[204:3:2] - Political guru: **Mazzini**; wrote biographies of **Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji, Shri Krishna**, Dayanand.
[204:3:3] - Deported to **Mandalay** with **Ajit Singh** (May 1907); led protests against Punjab repression.
[204:3:4] - **USA 1917-20:** **Indian Home Rule League of America** (1917); *Young India* (1916); later elected to the **Central Assembly**.
[204:3:5] - **Only one of Lal-Bal-Pal to be INC President** – **Calcutta special session, 1920**.
[204:3:6] - Works: **Unhappy India** (1928, reply to Katherine Mayo's *Mother India*), *The Story of My Deportation* (1908), *England's Debt to India*.
[204:3:7] - Papers: Urdu daily **Bande Mataram** and English weekly **The People** (Lahore, **1920**); The Punjabee.
[204:3:8] - First used the **safety-valve theory** (in *Young India*) to attack the Moderates – Congress was Dufferin's idea; "the Congress movement was **neither inspired by the people, nor devised or planned by them**".
[204:3:9] - Called Congress sessions the "**Annual National Festival of Educated Indians**".
[204:3:10] - Slogan "**Go back Simon**"; lathi-charged at **Lahore** (30 Oct 1928), died **17 November 1928** (Saunders shot by Bhagat Singh and Rajguru).
[204:3:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.417-418, p.454, p.490-492; Rocket Indian History 02 #96 p.48, #119 p.84-85; PMF Part 5 p.777 (Young India, The People, Punjabee)
## SUB 4 | Aurobindo Ghosh and Bipin Chandra Pal
[204:4:0] # Aurobindo Ghosh (15 Aug 1872 – 5 Dec 1950)
[204:4:1] - **New Lamps for Old** (**1893-94**): articles in **Indu Prakash** (Bombay) – systematic critique of Moderate politics; Congress out of touch with the proletariat.
[204:4:2] - Editor of **Bande Mataram** (1906) and **Karmayogin**; first principal of **Bengal National College** (1906); main Swadeshi leader in Bengal.
[204:4:3] - **Alipore Bomb Case** (1908, Maniktala Garden raid): defended by **Chittaranjan Das**; acquitted 1909; retired to **Pondicherry** (1910) – **Sri Aurobindo Ashram**.
[204:4:4] - Sayings: "**Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation**"; "The first principle of true teaching is that **nothing can be taught**" (*A System of National Education*).
[204:4:5] - Works: **The Life Divine**, *Savitri*, *Essays on the Gita*, **The Foundations of Indian Culture**.
[204:4:6] - Titles: **Prophet of Indian Nationalism**; chief ideologue of the Extremists.
[204:4:7] # Bipin Chandra Pal (1858-1932)
[204:4:8] - **Brahmo Samaj** member and social reformer; weekly **New India (1901)**; Bande Mataram (1906, Aurobindo editor); *The Soul of India*.
[204:4:9] - "**Father of Revolutionary Thoughts**"; imprisoned 6 months (1907) for refusing to give evidence against Aurobindo – **not deported to Mandalay**; in England 1908-11.
[204:4:10] - **April 1907: toured Andhra** – the Vande Mataram movement.
[204:4:11] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.492-495; Spectrum Ch12 p.272, p.275; Rocket Indian History 02 #119 p.85; PMF Part 5 p.777 (New India, Bande Mataram)

=== NOTES 1:205 | Morley-minto Reforms 1909; Formation of the Muslim League 1906; Lucknow Pact 1916
## SUB 0 | Simla Deputation and Founding of the Muslim League, 1906
[205:0:0] # Simla Deputation (1 October 1906)
[205:0:1] - Led by **Aga Khan III**; met **Lord Minto** at **Simla (Shimla)**.
[205:0:2] - Demanded **separate electorates** for Muslims and representation **above their numbers** (weightage), citing their contribution "**to the defence of the Empire**"; also safeguards in government services.
[205:0:3] - **Jinnah**, then a Congressman (secretary to Naoroji at Calcutta, 1906), **opposed separate electorates** in 1906 – the Aga Khan called him the only well-known Muslim to do so.
[205:0:4] # Founding facts
[205:0:5] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [205:0:5.0] Date | 30 December 1906
  [205:0:5.1] Place | Dacca (Dhaka), at the session of the All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference
  [205:0:5.2] Initiative | Nawab Salimullah of Dacca, with Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Viqar-ul-Mulk (who chaired the Dacca meeting)
  [205:0:5.3] First president | Aga Khan III (president 1906/08-1913) – not Jinnah, who joined only in 1913
  [205:0:5.4] First annual session | Karachi, 1907 (constitution adopted); 2nd session Amritsar, 1908
  [205:0:5.5] Headquarters | Lucknow
  [205:0:5.6] London Muslim League | Syed Ameer Ali, 6 May 1908 – exam keys call it the League's "London branch" (PMF: strictly an independent body)
[205:0:6] # Character
[205:0:7] - **Loyalist, communal, conservative**: preached loyalty to the Empire, kept Muslim intelligentsia **away from the Congress**.
[205:0:8] - **Supported the partition of Bengal** and sought safeguards in government services – it did **not** oppose the partition (UPSC 2002 "not correct" statement).
[205:0:9] - **Other figures of the 2002 statement question:** **Hakim Ajmal Khan** – a leader of the militant nationalist **Ahrar movement** (with Mohammad Ali, Hasan Imam, Zafar Ali Khan, Mazharul Haq); **Syed Ahmad Khan** opposed the Congress (United Indian Patriotic Association, 1888); **Barkatullah and Obeidullah Sindhi** – Provisional Government of India, **Kabul (1915)**.
[205:0:10] - **W.W. Hunter** (*The Indian Musalmans*, 1871) – exam keys credit him with "The Muslims, if contented and satisfied, would become the greatest bulwark of British power in India".
[205:0:11] # Chronology and dates
[205:0:12] - **INC 1885 → Partition of Bengal 1905 → Swadeshi (7 Aug 1905) → Muslim League (Dec 1906) → Surat split 1907 → Morley-Minto 1909 → Lucknow Pact 1916**.
[205:0:13] TABLE head: Body | Founded
  [205:0:13.0] Brahmo Samaj | 1828
  [205:0:13.1] Indian National Congress | 1885
  [205:0:13.2] All India Muslim League | 1906
  [205:0:13.3] HSRA | 1928
[205:0:14] > Founded at **Dacca 1906**; first session **Karachi 1907**; first president **Aga Khan**; London League **Ameer Ali 1908**.
[205:0:15] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.308; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.77-79; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.51-52, 72; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian History Part 2 p.58
[205:0:16] - **Delhi Durbar, 12 December 1911:** partition of Bengal annulled; capital shifted from **Calcutta to Delhi**.
[205:0:17] - **1911-13 rift with the British:** annulment of the Bengal partition (Delhi Durbar, **12 December 1911**; capital Calcutta → Delhi), refusal of an Aligarh university and of help to Turkey turned the League towards the Congress.
## SUB 1 | Indian Councils Act, 1909 – Morley-Minto Reforms
[205:1:0] # Names and background
[205:1:1] - **Names:** **Indian Councils Act, 1909** = **Morley-Minto (Minto-Morley) Reforms**; exam options also call it the "Government of India Act, 1909".
[205:1:2] - **Persons:** **John Morley** = Secretary of State for India (Liberal, from end-1905); **Lord Minto II** = Viceroy (1905-10), who succeeded **Curzon** in 1905.
[205:1:3] - **Aim:** "rally the Moderates" (carrot and stick) and win Muslim loyalty – the reforms were meant to **divide the nationalist ranks** and check Indian unity.
[205:1:4] # Provisions
[205:1:5] TABLE head: Area | Provision
  [205:1:5.0] Separate electorates | For the first time, separate electorates for Muslims – Muslim members elected only by Muslim voters = communal representation; "legalised communalism"
  [205:1:5.1] Weightage | Muslims got more seats than their population share, and a lower income qualification for voters
  [205:1:5.2] Elections | Elective principle recognised for non-official members – but indirect, multi-tier (local bodies → electoral college → provincial councils → central council)
  [205:1:5.3] Central Council | Additional members raised to 60 (from 16); official majority kept (69 members: 37 officials, 32 non-officials, 27 elected)
  [205:1:5.4] Provincial Councils | 30-50 additional members; non-official majority (but partly nominated)
  [205:1:5.5] Powers | Ask supplementary questions, move resolutions, vote on separate items of the budget – not on the budget as a whole; army spending non-votable
  [205:1:5.6] Executive Council | One Indian could be appointed: S.P. (Satyendra Prasanna) Sinha, Law Member, 1909 – first Indian on the Viceroy's Executive Council
[205:1:6] - **Before the Act (1907):** Morley put two Indians – K.G. Gupta and Syed Hussain Bilgrami – on the Secretary of State's India Council.
[205:1:7] - **Gokhale** went to England to meet Morley for self-government on colonial lines; Moderates co-operated with the reforms and lost popular support.
[205:1:8] # Verdict
[205:1:9] - **Most short-lived** of Britain's constitutional experiments in India (UPSC 1999) – replaced by the 1919 Act (in force 1921); **Ramsay MacDonald:** an incomplete deal between democracy and bureaucracy.
[205:1:10] - Morley: "if this chapter of reforms led ... to a parliamentary system in India, I would have nothing to do with it." The councils stayed **advisory**.
[205:1:11] > "Which Act introduced separate / communal electorates (communal representation)?" → **Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto)** – not 1892, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford) or 1935, which only extended it.
[205:1:12] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.308-310; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.66-70; Laxmikanth Part 1 p.31-32; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.52
## SUB 2 | Lucknow Session and the Lucknow Pact, 1916
[205:2:0] # The Lucknow Congress (December 1916)
[205:2:1] - **President:** **Ambika Charan Majumdar** (a Moderate). The League's Lucknow session was presided over by **Jinnah**; **both** bodies met at **Lucknow**.
[205:2:2] - **Reunion** of Moderates and Extremists – Tilak's group readmitted after **9 years** (Surat 1907). Chief architects of the reconciliation: **Annie Besant** and **Tilak**; Pherozeshah Mehta (died 1915) had blocked it.
[205:2:3] - First Congress session Gandhi attended after returning from South Africa; Champaran peasants' problems were put to him here.
[205:2:4] - **Tilak's slogan** "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it" – exam keys (UPPCS) place it at the **Lucknow session, 1916**; strictly it was the slogan of his Home Rule campaign of 1916 (league founded at Poona, April 1916).
[205:2:5] # The Pact
[205:2:6] - **Brokers:** **Tilak and Jinnah**; Besant also helped; Sarojini Naidu called Jinnah the "Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity".
[205:2:7] - **Main concession:** the **Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims** – the **first time (1916)** the Congress did so; Muslims got a **fixed proportion of seats** (weightage).
[205:2:8] - **Joint demands:** self-government at an early date; expanded councils with **elected majorities**; **half** of the executive councils to be Indians; five-year council term; Secretary of State paid from the British treasury.
[205:2:9] - **Not in the Pact:** no merger (separate sessions continued), no power-sharing deal, no demand for complete independence.
[205:2:10] - **Unity period:** **1916-1922** (Lucknow Pact → Khilafat-Non-Cooperation) = high point of Congress-League unity.
[205:2:11] # Chronology
[205:2:12] - **Lucknow Pact (Dec 1916) → Jallianwala Bagh (13 Apr 1919) → Tilak's death (1 Aug 1920) → Swaraj Party (1 Jan 1923)**.
[205:2:13] > Lucknow 1916: Congress president **A.C. Majumdar**, League president **Jinnah**; Congress **accepted** separate electorates.
[205:2:14] ~~ Sources: Spectrum p.332-334, 515; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.93-95; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 6 p.54; NextGen Modern India L2 Part 6 p.4
[205:2:15] - **Also in the 1916 scheme:** separation of the executive from the judiciary; elected majorities in the provincial councils.
[205:2:16] - **Order:** Muslim League (1906) → Morley-Minto (1909) → Lucknow Pact (1916) → Jallianwala Bagh (1919).
[205:2:17] - **Communal veto:** no bill affecting a community could pass if **three-fourths** of that community's members opposed it.
## SUB 3 | Separate Electorates – Divide and Rule, Father of the Communal Electorate
[205:3:0] - **Stated reason:** protecting the Muslim minority. **Real reason:** part of the British policy of **divide and rule** – to set Muslims against the Congress and maintain British supremacy.
[205:3:1] - **Effects:** checked India's unification, encouraged separatism, became a potent factor in the **growth of communalism** – the "seeds of discord" that ended in partition.
[205:3:2] - **Lord Minto** = "**Father of the Communal Electorate**" – used separate electorates to **turn Muslims against the Congress**. Exam key (BPSC 2018): **Rajendra Prasad** called **Lord Minto** the "**Father of Pakistan**" (attribution not traced in the sources).
[205:3:3] - **Extension:** 1909 Muslims → **1919** + Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans → **1935** + depressed classes, women, labour.
[205:3:4] > Separate electorates = Minto (1909); Congress accepted them = Lucknow (1916).
[205:3:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Modern History Part 4 p.69, 83; Laxmikanth Part 1 p.31-33; Spectrum p.310
## SUB 4 | Acts Compared – 1861 to 1935
[205:4:0] TABLE head: Act | Key feature
  [205:4:0.0] Indian Councils Act, 1861 | Indians associated with legislative councils (nominated)
  [205:4:0.1] Indian Councils Act, 1892 | Discussion of the annual financial statement (budget); questions; indirect (nominated-on-recommendation) members
  [205:4:0.2] Indian Councils Act, 1909 | Separate Muslim electorates (communal representation); elective principle; S.P. Sinha
  [205:4:0.3] GoI Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford) | Provincial dyarchy (reserved and transferred subjects); bicameralism and direct elections at the Centre; communal electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans
  [205:4:0.4] GoI Act, 1935 | All-India Federation; provincial autonomy (dyarchy in provinces abolished); dyarchy at the Centre; separate electorates for depressed classes, women, labour
[205:4:1] - **Match (APPSC G2):** separate Muslim representation – 1909; dyarchy in provinces – 1919; federation – 1935; discussion of annual statement – 1892.
[205:4:2] - **1909 vs 1919:** 1909 = separate Muslim electorates; 1919 = dyarchy. No Act brought dyarchy "at the Centre as well as in the provinces".
[205:4:3] ~~ Sources: Laxmikanth Part 1 p.30-33; PMF Modern History Part 4 p.69
